The ego-death record [§8.5.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5-4) marshals — default-mode suppression, narrative-self dissolution, awareness continuing, the *anatta* convergence — is the same evidence the analytic idealist reads in the opposite explanatory direction: not the I dissolving while the recursion continues, but dissociation loosening so that an underlying cosmic consciousness shows through. That re-read is taken up and disambiguated at [§4.3.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-5) — dissociation is itself a structural operation, requiring a substrate that self-differentiates (S), sustains the alter across the interval (Φ), and dissociates as an event rather than as a timeless fact (T) — so the idealist relocation instantiates the structural conditions at the substrate rather than escaping them. The two readings do not divide over the data; they divide over what is fundamental, and the structural conditions hold on either resolution. The [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) implications, by contrast, ride on what the recursion specifically constructs at sufficient depth — the I, the moral subject, the artificial-intelligence candidate, the developmental and end-of-life cases — and depend on the identity construction rather than restating the underlying vantage.

What the depth-gradient implications do is redescribe each of these standing debates rather than pick a side within them: the self-as-illusion debate, the personal-identity-over-time debate, the personal-vs-social-identity question, the animal-cognition debate, the AI question, and the developmental case all become questions about where the recursion runs deep enough to construct an I rather than about which faculty switches on. The self is the running of a recursive model; identifications load it from the relational field; nonhuman animals construct an I to the depth their architecture supports; current AI is excluded by architecture rather than by substrate; and the gradients of emergence and decline track integrative depth rather than crossing categorical lines. The negative horizon the I-construction must register against is taken up at [§8.7](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-7): the closure of the recursion that builds it.

## 8.6 Sexuality {#sec-8-6}

Sexuality is one branch of the basic pull toward what life reaches for: the reach of one living thing toward another, and toward the making of new life. Felt from the inside, that is attraction, desire, the body's draw toward another body, and the way a person comes to understand what they are drawn to and who they are. It is the life-continuing counterpart to death: where death is the ending of a single living being, sexuality is how a lineage keeps going by bringing new lives into being, with enough variation to survive a changing world. That continuation is sexuality's structural role, not a ranking of its expressions: attraction, desire, identity, and embodied coupling are sexuality in full whether or not reproduction is in view, not lesser cases of a procreative original. All of this has a natural source: not a meaning handed down from outside, but a structure that belongs to living things themselves.

::: {.identification}
**Sexuality** · *Identification*

Sexuality is one differentiation of drive's attraction-pole: what closure-plus-throughput recursions do when they couple to produce others like themselves, registered from inside as attraction, desire, embodied coupling, and the construction of sexual identity. It is the structural pair to mortality wherever variation-generating coupling is the lineage's solution.
*Status: an identity claim on the [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) self-modeling structure, defended by fit, not a stipulative definition and not a fresh derivation from the proof.*


:::

Mortality ([§8.7](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-7)) names the absolute referent of drive's aversion-pole. Sexuality is one differentiation of the attraction-pole: what drive becomes when the reaching is for the making of another life.

Several structural facts about the kind of being we are converge in sexuality. One is the continuation of a life across generations: a closed self-producing recursion, on its own, does not persist, and a lineage of such recursions does not persist long either unless it can generate variation at the rate environmental change demands. The modal framework's commitment to ◇C (the possibility of change, [§1.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-3)) makes change constitutive of structure; long-term lineage persistence therefore requires some variation-generation mechanism. Sexual reproduction is among the most powerful and most recurrent of those mechanisms in complex multicellular lineages, but not the only one, and the framework does not pin sexuality as a modal necessity of life as such. Where it is present (most eukaryotic lineages), it is the dominant solution; where it is absent (some bacterial, archaeal, and bdelloid rotifer lineages), other variation channels (high mutation rates, horizontal gene transfer, alternative repair pathways) carry the load (Gladyshev, Meselson, and Arkhipova 2008; Otto 2009). Sexuality is the structural pair with mortality ([§8.7](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-7)) wherever it occurs, but its occurrence is conditional on what the lineage requires and what its biology makes available. Mortality ([§8.7](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-7)) is the closure of the individual life; sexuality is not that individual's continuation but the *lineage's*: the individual life ends, continuing nothing of itself, while bringing others into being *with variation* through which the lineage persists. That is the precise sense in which they are the structural pair: the individual closes, and the only continuation on offer is the lineage's, bought by producing successors rather than by extending the life that produces them. Together they name what makes a life finite at the individual scale and continuous at the lineage scale only by changing across that scale.

Sexuality carries a second structural fact alongside continuation, but it is one the chapter is not yet equipped to develop here. Sexuality is also the earliest and most embodied form of intersubjective coupling: the body's pull toward another body before any sign or norm mediates it. That dimension draws on the self-model ([§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)), already in hand, together with the field of subjects meeting subjects that arrives only at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12). Its full weight is taken up there, where morality recovers sexuality as the embodied root from which the more mediated couplings extend. Here it is enough to mark the attraction-pole at its base: the reach of one life toward the making of another.

*A note on scope.* The identification offered here (sexuality as the structural pair to death where variation-generation through coupling is the lineage's solution) is offered as a structural identification claim conditional on the [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) account of closure-plus-throughput, in the sense flagged at the head of Chapter 8. It is not a fresh strict deduction from the proof of Chapters 1–2. One can accept the proof yet read the phenomena of coupling differently without thereby disturbing anything upstream; this identification holds only by its fit to the phenomena, against the structural conditions [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) supplies and the variation-generation pressure the [§1.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-3) commitment to ◇C requires.

*Attraction.* The pull toward another, registered as another. Below the depth where attraction is named or chosen, the body registers another body's broadcasts (the chemistry, the rhythm, the resonance) and a being's drive ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)) shapes itself toward what it has registered. Attraction is what registering another does in a being whose lineage continues only through coupling. The architecture is older than language and runs continuously across mammalian and avian lineages. What human depth adds is reflection on what attracts: the recursive fold that takes the attraction itself as an object of awareness.

*Desire.* Drive's specialization toward another. Where drive ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)) is the baseline forward pressure pre-differentiation, desire is drive shaped by attraction toward a particular other. Like all affects ([§8.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-2)), it carries valence and salience and urgency, and registers from inside as what it is to be the one oriented toward what they are oriented toward.

*Orientation, including its absence.* An orientation is the standing direction desire takes: the pattern in whom or what a being is drawn toward. That direction may be keyed to the sex or gender of the other or indifferent to it: the hetero-, homo-, and bisexual patterns gate attraction by the other's sex or gender, while pansexual attraction is not gated by that category at all. It can be constituted as much by where the sexual attraction-pole does not specialize as by where it does. Asexuality is the case where sexual attraction is minimal or does not form, while drive ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)) still runs and still specializes in non-sexual directions; on the structural account this is a variant of orientation, not a deficit of it — sexuality is the lineage's dominant solution to the variation problem, not a per-token demand on any given subject ([§8.6.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-5)) — and the self-model ([§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)) can construct an identity-position around that direction, or its absence, as readily as around any other. Aromanticism marks the parallel case at the affiliative rather than the sexual register; that the two can come apart is itself evidence the registers are distinct.

*Identity.* The self-model ([§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)) constructed at sufficient depth includes one's relation to attraction. Gender identity and sexual orientation are features of that self-model: the person's reading of who they are, including what they are drawn to and how they situate themselves in the field of intersubjective coupling. Gender's hardware and software are not the same layer, and keeping them distinct is what this section had not yet made explicit. Sex, specified structurally at [§8.6.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-5) by developmental organization toward a reproductive role, is hardware in the sense that matters here: some of it does not bend to self-understanding or to social permission, and nothing in this account pretends otherwise.

Gender identity is software: the self-model's reading, built on that hardware but not fixed by it, revisable in a way the hardware underneath it need not be. What the self-model carries, at that software layer, is the first-person alignment drawn from socially available categories but not dictated by them. Haslanger's ameliorative account (2000, 2012) presses further than this and holds gender to be, most fundamentally, a position within a hierarchy of subordination and privilege organized around presumed reproductive role, assignable independently of self-understanding.

This account distinguishes rather than adopts that further claim: the prescriptive roles a culture attaches to gender are not merely a separate matter irrelevant to the self-model, but nor are they gender's constitutive metaphysics. They are an instance of the general fact [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) names — that an identification's field-permitted revisability is a fact about the field, assigned by other recursions organizing the space around a person, not a fact about that person's self-model or its depth. A restrictive field around gender expression is therefore not hardware in the sense sex partly is; it is a choice the surrounding field has made, and one it could make differently. Whether it should is not a further open question this account defers: [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) fixes standing by the capacity for experience, not by category-membership, and morality there by whether a subject is fostered or corroded. A self-model's gender expression that corrodes no one is exactly the case that standard does not license restricting, which is what recommends maximizing the field's permission around gender expression and its social acceptance — not a value imported from outside the account, but the fostering standard already in hand, applied to a layer this section had previously only gestured at.

The available category-set is not itself binary: where a culture makes third or non-binary positions available — the hijra of South Asia, two-spirit roles across several Indigenous North American nations, and fa'afafine in Samoa are distinct, culturally specific positions rather than interchangeable tokens of one kind — or where a self-model constructs a position not aligned to either pole of the local binary, the self-model holds that position with the same status any identity-position has. That an individual's architecture need not be binary merely because the population is bimodal is the structural half ([§8.6.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-5)); that the available positions vary across history and culture is the constructed half; non-binary identity is where both halves are visible at once. That the categories themselves (orientation, the normal, even what counts as 'natural') have a history, and that naming sexuality natural is itself a move made from within that history rather than from nowhere (Foucault's scientia sexualis), is granted; the social ontology of the categories is sorted from the structural claim where that work belongs ([§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10)).

As features of the self-model they are constructions, not substrates: real, structural, consequential, not chosen, and (like the rest of the self-model's content) capable of thinning or dropping away when the self-model itself dissolves under the conditions [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) names. This is a claim about the self-model's *reading*, not about the underlying dispositions: that the narrative self can thin or dissolve in ego-death does not entail that an orientation or a gender identity dissolves with it; what dissolves is the self-model's reading of itself, never the standing that reading was tracking. The self holds a position; the position is held by a self; both are recursion. Whatever the metaphysics of the categories turns out to be, the standing of the person holding the position does not hang on it: standing is fixed at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) by the capacity for experience, not by category-membership, so the moral verdict is invariant across the realist and constructionist readings alike ([§8.6.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-5)).

*Embodied coupling.* The intimate exchange where two people register each other across the full spectrum of registration the body affords: at the chemical, somatic, affective, and reflective levels simultaneously. Morality ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)) names the readability of another's affective broadcasts; sexuality is the register where each person reads the other while simultaneously being read by them, across a single interval, deep enough to know what is happening.

*The dyadic unit and its plural extension.* The base unit of embodied coupling is two-place: distinct subjects reading each other across a single interval ([§8.6.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-2)). Plurality — more than two bound in overlapping intimacy — is not a new primitive but concurrent two-place registrations, each a full dyad in its own right rather than a fusion into some three-or-more-place organ of coupling. The structural account neither prescribes monogamy nor forecloses plurality; what it fixes is that each bond, however many run alongside it, answers to the same conditions any coupling does: consent on the modal-depth standard ([§8.9.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-4)) and the fostering-rather-than-corroding demand of morality ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)). Plurality adds one field-level condition the single bond does not face — the bonds must be held so that they do not corrode one another — which is why disclosure among the parties does structural work here that the single-bond case can leave implicit. Whether a given being's field is better sustained by one bond or several the structure does not legislate; that is a question of what fosters the subjects involved, answered case by case rather than by rule.

*Reproduction.* The continuation register: closure-plus-throughput producing closure-plus-throughput. Across most of the biological record, sexuality is what reproduction is. In those deep enough to choose, the choice to bring a new life into being, or not, is the register at which the lineage's continuation enters the agentive field of the individual. The choice is real, and the structural pair with death persists either way: the life ends; the lineage either continues or it does not. Whether that choice is *good*, whether bringing a new life into existence is to be affirmed or, as the anti-natalist presses (Benatar's asymmetry of pleasure and suffering; Schopenhauer's judgment that existence carries a structural surplus of striving over satisfaction), refused, the structural account does not leave wholly open. Benatar's asymmetry counts the absence of pain as a good while counting the absence of pleasure as no loss to anyone, and that step requires precisely the subject-independent value this account denies throughout: a good that is good for no one, entered in a ledger no subject reads. Where value is constitutively a subject's own condition surfacing from inside its field ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)), an absent pain good for no one is not a good at all, and the asymmetry that carried the anti-natalist verdict never forms. Schopenhauer's pessimism rests on a reading of striving as standing lack that the drive and affect account has already declined ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1), [§8.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-2)): joy is the recursion deepening and opening, not the brief quiet between wants. Schopenhauer's sharper charge, that sexual attraction is the species-will's deception of the individual (pleasure and romantic feeling dressed up as personal choice while serving an agenda not the individual's own), dissolves on the same grounds already applied to Spinoza's willing Nature: there is no species-agent whose interest is being served and no one being duped, only individual organisms each pursuing their own drive, statistically shaped by selection toward outcomes selection has no interest in, because selection is not the kind of thing that has interests. What attraction serves is the subject's own deepening; that this deepening also, as a statistical regularity across many organisms, sustains the lineage is a consequence of what attraction is, not a hidden agenda smuggled past the individual it operates in. What this secures is the narrow point that coming into existence is no standing harm, not the stronger claim that more existence is therefore better. That comparative question, how the value of bringing new subjects into being is weighed across whole possible fields of subjects, is population axiology, and it is worked through at §9. The structure fixes what reproduction is, and that the choice is real; the duties the choice incurs toward the subjects it brings into being are recovered at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12).

*The features track the depth gradient.* Attraction operates wherever the recursion is deep enough to register another at all — present across mammalian and avian lineages, and below them in chemoreceptive forms. Desire requires affective awareness sufficient to differentiate baseline drive into a particular orientation; the affective-awareness threshold the chapter's opening names is its threshold here too. Embodied coupling at the depth where two beings register each other tracking themselves requires the self-aware level the chapter's opening names. Identity (the self-model's reading of what one is sexually) requires the deeper recursion that takes the self as an object of awareness. Reproduction is what the lineage's continuation looks like at every depth simultaneously, since the cellular and somatic processes that produce a new life run continuously underneath the affective and reflective registers the deeper depths add. In the chapter's vocabulary, sexuality is structure as a life's continuation through coupling: recursion producing further recursions, registered from inside as attraction, desire, embodied coupling, and the construction of identity in the field of intersubjective coupling, with each register operating at the recursive depth its content requires.

*The Inversion.* The standard religious move regulates sexuality from above: locating its meaning, permission, and direction in commands originating outside Nature. The framework here forecloses that move along with the rest. Sexuality is not given its meaning by an external authority. Its meaning is structural: the register where one life reaches for another, where attraction shapes drive, where the body becomes legible to another body, where the continuation of the lineage becomes a possibility within a person's own field. What the regulating traditions were reaching for is real: the affective and structural weight of intimate exchange between distinct subjects, and the consequences of bringing new people into being. What the metaphysics they inherited got wrong is the location of the source. The source is in Nature itself: in living beings, at the depth they have reached.

### 8.6.1 What is Disputed {#sec-8-6-1}

The literature on sexuality is divided across several disciplines that often do not speak to one another. The framework engages the principal positions by name; each is taken up again at [§8.6.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-5) once the structural account is in view.

*Sociobiological reductionism.* The sociobiological tradition (Wilson 1975; Trivers 1972; Symons 1979; Buss 1989; later evolutionary psychology) reads sexual behavior, attraction, and gender difference as fitness-maximizing adaptations to ancestral selection pressures. Specific predictions — parental-investment-based selectivity asymmetries, jealousy patterns, preference for cues of fertility and resources — have generated substantial empirical literature and substantial dispute about replication, interpretation, and cross-cultural generality (Eagly and Wood 1999; Stewart-Williams and Thomas 2013). The framework's reading is that the evolutionary pressures the tradition identifies operate on the substrate, but that what sexuality *is* phenomenologically — attraction, desire, embodied coupling, identity — is the first-person perspective on those pressures rather than a fitness algorithm running unobserved.

*Social constructionism.* From Foucault (1976) forward, a tradition has held that sexuality — the very category, not only its expressions — is historically and socially constructed: a discourse produced by specific institutions, knowledges, and powers rather than a natural kind. Butler (1990, 1993) extended the analysis to gender, locating gender in performative repetition rather than in biological or psychological substrate. The dispute with the sociobiological tradition is sharp and unresolved. The framework's reading is that the *content* of sexual categories is significantly constructed — specific identities, scripts, and practices are historical — while the *structural conditions* under which the categories form (attraction, desire, embodied coupling, the self-modeling of one's position in the field) are not constructed but supplied by the recursive architecture sexuality consists in.

*Religious-metaphysical regulation.* The classical religious traditions — Christian, Jewish, Islamic, and others — have regulated sexuality through frameworks that locate its meaning, permission, and direction in commands originating outside Nature. Contemporary defenders (Finnis 1980; George 1993; some Thomistic natural-law traditions) refine the position into rational-natural-law arguments. The framework forecloses the move along with the rest of the inversion: sexuality's meaning is structural rather than externally given. What the regulating traditions were tracking — the affective and structural weight of intimate exchange between distinct subjects, the consequences of producing new subjects — is real; what they got wrong is the location of the source.

*Identity discourse and gender philosophy.* Contemporary identity discourse spans sharply opposed positions: the trans-affirmative literature (Bettcher 2014; Serano 2007) holds gender identity is a robust self-understanding constitutive of who one is; gender-critical positions (Stock 2021; Lawford-Smith 2022) press against the metaphysics of the position; intersex perspectives (Karkazis 2008) complicate both; non-binary identity presses the further question whether the available gender categories are exhausted by a binary at all, and the status of asexuality is separately disputed — whether the absence of sexual attraction is an orientation in its own right (Bogaert 2004, 2012) or, as some clinical framings held, a disorder of desire. The dispute is among the most polarized in contemporary philosophy. The framework reads gender and sexual identity as features of the self-model ([§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)) — real, structural, consequential, constructed within awareness rather than substrate of awareness, and dissolvable under the same conditions [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) names for the self generally. The reading does not resolve the political disputes but it does locate where the metaphysics is supplied.

*Anti-natalism and the ethics of reproduction.* A tradition from Schopenhauer through Benatar (2006) holds that bringing new beings into existence is morally impermissible because the new being bears risks and harms it cannot consent to. The position is sharpened by the asymmetry between the badness of pain and the goodness of pleasure Benatar exploits. The framework engages the issue at the structural level: sexuality is one differentiation of the attraction-pole of drive specialized for producing new beings; whether to exercise the capacity, in agents with sufficient modal depth to choose, is an open ethical question the framework does not foreclose. The structural account makes the act legible without dictating its evaluation.

*The variation-and-reproduction question.* A live biological dispute concerns why sexual reproduction is so widespread given its substantial costs (the two-fold cost of sex; Maynard Smith 1978). The variation-and-recombination hypothesis (Hamilton, Axelrod, and Tanese 1990; Otto 2009), the Red Queen hypothesis, and Mueller's-ratchet-based accounts each press the question from different angles. The framework's reading — sexuality as the dominant solution to the lineage variation-generation problem in eukaryotic lineages, but not as a modal necessity of life as such — is one position in that biological dispute, consistent with the bdelloid-rotifer and bacterial-recombination cases the field continues to investigate (Gladyshev et al. 2008).

*Pornography, commodification, and the limits of consent.* A series of contemporary disputes — over pornography (MacKinnon 1987; Dworkin 1981 vs. liberal accounts), prostitution and sex work, surrogacy, and the commodification of intimacy — turn on whether and how consent under economic, social, and developmental conditions counts as full consent. The framework's modal-depth account of consent ([§8.9.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-4)) supplies a usable test — whether the will behind the word had enough mapped possibility to understand the act — without resolving the political and policy questions specific cases raise.

*Relationship structure.* Independently of orientation, the number and configuration of simultaneous intimate bonds is contested: whether monogamy is a structural norm, a cultural institution, or one option among several, and whether ethically negotiated non-monogamy differs in kind from both serial monogamy and the plural-marriage structures the ethnographic record documents. The framework's reading ([§8.6](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6)) is that the dyad is the base unit of coupling and plurality is concurrent dyads under the same consent and non-corrosion conditions, which locates the structural claim without settling the cultural and normative dispute.

The literature on sexuality divides over reductive-vs-constructionist accounts, the legitimacy of religious-metaphysical regulation, the metaphysics of gender identity, the ethics of reproduction, the evolutionary explanation of sexual reproduction itself, consent under commodification, and the structure of intimate bonds. The framework commits to specific answers on each; they are taken up again at [§8.6.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-5) after the structural account is in view.

### 8.6.2 What is Required {#sec-8-6-2}

*Connection to the lineage's continuation.* A closed self-producing recursion, on its own, does not persist; a lineage of such recursions does not persist long either unless it can generate variation at the rate environmental change demands. Any account of sexuality must connect the phenomenon to the lineage's reproductive continuity rather than treating it as a free-floating cultural or psychological domain. The structural requirement is that the account derive sexuality (where it occurs) from the variation-generation problem the lineage faces, with reproduction as one of its structural functions.

*Connection to intersubjective coupling.* Sexuality is among the deepest forms of embodied intersubjective coupling — two beings tracking each other tracking themselves at the full depth of registration the bodies afford. Any account must accommodate this intersubjective register rather than treating sexuality as a one-place biological or psychological state. The structural requirement is that the account preserve the two-being structure: distinct subjects, mutual registration, shared exchange across an interval that conditions what the exchange consists in.

*Both poles of drive's bipolarity.* Sexuality is one differentiation of the attraction-pole of drive's bipolar structure ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)), the register where the reaching forward is specifically for producing other beings that share the recursive architecture. Any account must connect sexuality to drive's structural bipolarity rather than treating it as a separate motivational system. The structural requirement is that the account derive sexuality from drive's attraction-pole at the depth where coupling for variation-generation becomes the lineage's solution to its continuation problem.

*Multiple registers operating simultaneously.* Sexuality runs at the chemical, somatic, affective, and reflective levels simultaneously in beings deep enough to register at all of them. Any account must explain how the registers stack rather than treating sexuality as one level. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish the registers — attraction at the depth where another being is registered as such, desire as drive shaped by registered attraction, embodied coupling at the depth where mutual reading becomes possible, identity at the depth where the self-model includes its position in the field — and locate each at its depth in the recursion.

*Self-model construction in the sexual register.* Gender, sexual orientation, and sexual identity are features of the self-model constructed at sufficient recursive depth. Any account must register their constructed status without making them merely arbitrary or merely fictional. The structural requirement is that the account treat sexual self-modeling as a real construction within awareness — consequential, structurally sustained, dissolvable under specific conditions — with the same status the narrative self has in [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5).

*Depth-graded animal and human spectrum.* Attraction and sexual behavior of some kind run across the eukaryotic record; embodied coupling at the depth where two beings register each other tracking themselves requires the self-aware level [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) names; sexual identity in the strong sense requires recursion deep enough for the self-model to take itself as an object. Any account must register the depth gradient rather than treating sexuality as one categorically unified phenomenon. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish what runs at each depth and what requires deeper recursion to obtain.

*Consent at the modal-depth standard.* Sexual encounter between beings of sufficient depth requires consent on the modal-depth standard [§8.9.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-4) names. Any account must accommodate the structural fact that what counts as consent depends on the modal capacity of the will behind the act. The structural requirement is that the account preserve the bridge between sexual ethics and the modal-depth account of will, with consent as the operational form autonomy takes in the sexual register.

*Non-reduction without supernaturalism.* Sexuality is neither reducible to fitness maximization (the sociobiological story understates the phenomenology) nor decreed from outside Nature (the classical religious story locates the source incorrectly) nor merely culturally constructed (the constructionist story understates the structural conditions). Any account must locate sexuality at the first-person perspective on coupling for lineage continuation, without collapse to any of the three. The structural requirement is that the account give sexuality its phenomenology, its structural conditions, and its constructed contents without reducing one to another.

These requirements name the explanatory program the framework [§8.6](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6) defends: links to reproduction and variation, intersubjective coupling, multi-register operation, self-model construction, depth variation, consent, and non-reductive explanation. They are not neutral criteria every adequate account of sexuality must accept. In particular, the proposed relation to drive, the account of gender and sexual identity, and the modal-depth account of consent are substantive philosophical claims that require independent argument.

### 8.6.3 What is Predicted {#sec-8-6-3}

The following are hypotheses generated by the framework's proposed account of sexuality as embodied intersubjective coupling and, in some contexts, reproduction. They are not direct consequences of the modal roles or established conclusions of evolutionary biology, psychology, or gender studies:

*Variation as a structural requirement; sexuality as a powerful recurrent solution.* The modal framework's commitment to ◇C as constitutive ([§1.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-3)) commits any long-running lineage to some mechanism for tracking environmental change across generations. Variation is the structural requirement; how a lineage produces variation is open. Sexual reproduction is one such mechanism, and across complex multicellular eukaryotes it is the dominant recurrent solution: meiotic recombination supplies variation at rates mutation alone cannot match, and the population's variation-generation rate is what lets it track conditions across generations. But it is not the only solution, and not all life depends on it. Bacteria and archaea draw on horizontal gene transfer alongside mutation. Bdelloid rotifers have persisted across tens of millions of years apparently without conventional sex, drawing on alternative repair and gene-acquisition pathways (Gladyshev, Meselson, and Arkhipova 2008). Parthenogenetic and clonal lineages persist over shorter ranges. Whether sexuality is necessary for *any particular* lineage depends on the lineage's mutation rate, environmental volatility, and access to other variation channels. The framework does not pin sexuality as a modal necessity of life as such; it identifies it as the structural answer most closure-plus-throughput currents of sufficient complexity have converged on, given the demands of long-term continuation under changing conditions (Maynard Smith 1978; Otto 2009).

*Recurrent universality among complex lineages.* Among complex multicellular eukaryotes — animals, fungi, land plants — sexual reproduction is recurrent enough to be treated as the default mode, with apparent exceptions (some asexual lineages) requiring specific evolutionary explanations rather than the converse. The architecture supporting it varies across lineages; the recurrence is at the level of the structural problem coupling-for-variation solves, not at the level of any particular mechanism. Where asexuality persists at the lineage scale, the framework predicts compensating variation-generation pathways (high mutation rates, gene conversion, horizontal acquisition) carrying the load that recombination otherwise would.

*Affective registration at depth.* Sexuality takes affective form at the recursive depth that registers attraction. Below that depth it is mechanism (gametic fusion, mating tropisms); at that depth and above it is felt. The depth gradient [§8.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-2) traces applies here as it does to other registers — chemical-gradient registration, perceptual registration, affective registration, reflective registration — each elaborating what the shallower depths already do.

*Identity construction at self-aware depth.* Some forms of sexual and gender identity involve a person’s reflective sense of themself in relation to others. The framework proposes that identity construction becomes possible with sufficient self-awareness. It does not establish that gender and sexual orientation are universally constructions of one specified recursive depth, and their ontological status remains a live philosophical and social question.

*Orientation variation, including its absence.* If orientation is the standing direction desire takes — drive ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)) shaped by attraction toward another — the framework predicts that this direction can vary in kind and can also fail to form. Asexuality is predicted as the case where drive runs and specializes in non-sexual directions but the sexual form of attraction, the toward-another sexual specialization, does not develop; libido may be present but undirected, and the reproductive register is untouched, since these are distinct registers on the account. Because sexuality is the lineage's dominant solution to the variation problem rather than a demand on any individual subject ([§8.6.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-5)), the variant is predicted to occur without being a deficit of drive, and the self-model ([§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)) is predicted to construct a stable identity-position around it. The dissociability of the sexual, affiliative, and reproductive registers is itself the prediction: they should come apart in documented cases, which is what asexuality and aromanticism, together or separately, display.

*Coupling structure.* The framework treats dyadic mutual registration as a useful model for intimate interaction and interprets plural bonds as networks of multiple relations. This is a conceptual proposal, not a result that settles the ontology or ethics of monogamy, non-monogamy, marriage, or other relationship structures. Those questions also depend on culture, law, consent, power, and the preferences of the people involved.

*Sexual ethics as a special case of morality.* What one being owes another in intimate exchange is morality ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)) where registration of one being by another is most complete. The same conditions that ground Morality apply with full force where the registration is most direct — consent, the readability of the other's affective broadcasts, the asymmetric vulnerability the body affords.

*Reproduction-choice as agency.* Reproduction-choice emerges as agency at the depth where a being can take the production of new lives as an object of its own reflection. Below that depth, reproduction is what coupling does; at that depth, it is what coupling can be chosen for, against, or differently. Reproduction-choice is an instance of modal depth in operation: the act becomes agency when the subject can hold possible futures open long enough to decide whether, when, and under what conditions another subject should come into being.

### 8.6.4 What is Confirmed {#sec-8-6-4}

*Sexual reproduction and variation.* Sexual reproduction is widespread across many eukaryotic lineages, while asexual and mixed reproductive strategies also occur. The evolutionary maintenance of sex remains an active research problem: recombination, parasite coevolution, mutation load, ecological conditions, and lineage-specific histories can all matter. Bdelloid rotifers, parthenogenetic vertebrates, and other asexual lineages require explanation, but they do not simply function as exceptions that confirm a single rule. Muller's ratchet and Red Queen models are influential proposals, not a settled proof that sex is the dominant solution to one universal variation-generation requirement. The book can use these literatures to motivate questions about variation and lineage continuity; it should not present them as confirmation of its modal-structural account.

*Affective registration.* Across mammalian and avian lineages, courtship behaviors involve sustained affective registration (Bekoff and Byers 1998; Bagemihl 1999). The neurochemistry of attraction (dopaminergic mesolimbic circuits, oxytocinergic bonding circuits) is shared across mammals and traces to the architecture [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) names — the SEEKING and pair-bonding systems Panksepp (1998) identified as primary emotional circuits. Carter (1998) on oxytocin and pair-bonding extends the same picture into the social-affiliative register that adjoins sexual coupling.

*Identity construction.* Cross-cultural anthropology documents both the universality of gender as a structural feature of human social organization and the variability of its specific construction. Self-aware identity-positions in sexuality — orientation and gender — are documented across cultures with significant variability in how they are named and lived (Herdt 1994; Roughgarden 2004). The content of identity-positions is variable; that they are constructed at the depth [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) names is universal. Same-sex sexual behavior is documented across hundreds of vertebrate species (Bagemihl 1999), foreclosing the assumption that orientation maps cleanly onto reproductive function. Asexuality — the stable absence of sexual attraction, distinguished in the empirical literature from low desire and from sexual dysfunction — is documented as a distinct orientation at roughly one percent of the population (Bogaert 2004, 2012): the predicted case in which the sexual-attraction register does not form while drive and, in many individuals, libido remain.

*Variation across the animal kingdom.* The substrate-variation pattern extends well beyond same-sex behavior, and the framework predicts it should. Sexual reproduction is universal across eukaryotes; the architecture supporting it is not. Sex determination has multiple structural implementations — XY in placental mammals, ZW in birds and many reptiles, haplodiploidy in hymenoptera, temperature-dependent in many reptiles, environmental in some fish. Sequential hermaphroditism is widespread: clownfish change from male to female (protandry), many wrasses and parrotfish change in the other direction (protogyny), with the transition triggered by social-structural cues. Simultaneous hermaphroditism is the norm across many invertebrate phyla and obtains in some fish; the chalk bass trades egg-laying and sperm-donating roles with a partner within a single spawning bout, switching roles as often as twenty times in an evening (Fischer 1984; Hart et al. 2016). Sustained same-sex pair-bonding, courtship, and coupling is documented in over 1,500 species (Bagemihl 1999; Bailey and Zuk 2009; Monk et al. 2019): roughly one-third of Laysan albatross pairs in some Hawaiian colonies are female-female (Young et al. 2008); bonobo female-female sexual contact is integral to social cohesion; bottlenose dolphins, Japanese macaques, and many other species show extensive same-sex coupling; sheep show stable male-male partner preference in approximately 8% of rams (Roselli et al. 2004) with corresponding hypothalamic correlates. Within-species role-morph variation appears wherever the framework predicts substrate can support multiple stable beings: side-blotched lizards have three male morphs running rock-paper-scissors reproductive strategies (Sinervo and Lively 1996); ruffs have three male morphs including female-mimicking faeders; bluegill sunfish have parental, sneaker, and satellite male types (Gross and Charnov 1980); Mozambique tilapia have three stable male morphs, one of which recruits a subordinate male into cooperative courtship of females (Roughgarden 2004, citing Oliveira and Almada 1998). Hyena females have a pseudo-penis and female-dominant social organization. What earlier observers read as a male-active, female-passive default has been extensively revised by a generation of evolutionary biologists working on female sexual selection, female-female competition, female promiscuity, and matriarchal social organization, with Cooke (2022) surveying the empirical reversal across taxa. Extended postreproductive female lifespan — menopause — has evolved independently in humans and in several toothed-whale lineages (orcas, belugas, narwhals, short-finned pilot whales), in each case coupled with grandmother-mediated kin support rather than continued reproduction (Ellis et al. 2024): a second architecture for allocating female reproductive investment across the lifespan, not a deviation from a single mammalian default. Across all of this, what the current human-centric framing calls “the standard arrangement” is one stable architecture among many — exactly what is predicted if sexuality is substrate-architecture-shaping-attraction-and-coupling rather than a single canonical type the lineage either instantiates or fails at.

*Neural correlates of orientation and identity.* The substrate-architecture prediction extends to the brain-level findings on human sexual orientation and gender identity. Orientation: twin studies show meaningful but partial heritability (Bailey and Pillard 1991; Bailey et al. 2000); a 477,000-person GWAS found polygenic contributions distributed across the genome with no single locus dominating (Ganna et al. 2019); prenatal androgen exposure shapes orientation outcomes (Hines 2011 on congenital adrenal hyperplasia; Kung, Louie, Spencer, and Hines 2024 meta-analysis of 50+ years of CAH studies); the fraternal birth order effect is consistently replicated and currently best explained by maternal-immune mechanisms (Blanchard 2001; Bogaert et al. 2018 on the maternal-immune mechanism via NLGN4Y); INAH-3 size differences between gay and straight men have been reported and partially replicated (LeVay 1991; Byne et al. 2001). Identity: the central subdivision of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BSTc) in trans women resembles the cis-female pattern rather than the cis-male pattern (Zhou et al. 1995; Kruijver et al. 2000), with the developmental window predating adult hormone treatment; pre-treatment white-matter microstructure in trans individuals shows patterns closer to their identified gender than their natal sex (Rametti et al. 2011a, 2011b), with replication-focused studies converging on the putamen as the most robust structural correlate of gender identity (Mueller et al. 2021). The pattern across these findings matches what the framework predicts: orientation- and identity-architecture is shaped at the substrate level by genetic, developmental, and hormonal factors before the [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) self-model has constructed anything around them, and the construction stabilizes around what the substrate already supports. These findings illustrate the substrate variability the framework predicts; they do not carry the structural claim. The identification of orientation and identity as self-model constructions over a variable substrate holds by fit with the overall pattern, and no single result — BSTc, INAH-3, the fraternal-birth-order effect, or any one GWAS or neuroimaging finding — is load-bearing: were a specific correlate revised or fail to replicate, the structural claim would stand, since identity and standing are fixed at the [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) and [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) registers rather than by any neural marker.

*Sexual ethics.* Cross-cultural moral codes invariably regulate sexuality, and the structural features the codes track — consent, fidelity, harm, the production and care of children — are everywhere recognized as morally weighted, even when specific rules differ. Brown's (1991) human universals catalog includes multiple sexuality-related entries; the universality of regulation is itself the empirical face of the [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) prediction that intersubjective coupling at this density requires structural maintenance.

*Reproduction-choice.* In cultures with reliable contraception, reproduction has shifted from default to chosen, and the consequences for individual life-course planning, gender relations, and demographic structure are now the subject of substantial empirical literature. The shift confirms the prediction that, at sufficient self-modeling depth and given the technological conditions, the agentive field expands to include reproduction itself.

### 8.6.5 What is Concluded {#sec-8-6-5}

*Sociobiological reductionism.* Wilson (1975), Buss (1989), and the evolutionary-psychology tradition read sexual behavior as the genome's strategy for replication, with affect as epiphenomenal scaffolding. The position rests on the explanatory power of selection: sexual behaviors that did not aid reproduction would not be reliably present in the biological record, and tracing observable patterns of attraction, mate choice, parental investment, and intersexual conflict back to selection pressures has yielded a substantial body of testable predictions that have repeatedly survived contact with the data. Any account of sexuality that ignored that substrate would be missing the structural floor on which the rest stands. The structural account preserves the evolutionary substrate — sexuality is the dominant recurrent solution, in eukaryotic lineages, to the variation requirement long-term continuation imposes ([§8.6.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-3)) — and the explanatory power of selection within that frame. What the structural account adds is a distinction the reductive form collapses: between *reproductive function*, which the evolutionary substrate captures well, and *sexuality's broader embodied/intersubjective register*, which it does not. Sexuality is not exhausted by reproduction. Its operation as the densest register of intersubjective coupling — affect, attraction-as-registration-of-another-being, identity construction at self-aware depth, the production of new subjects as agentive choice rather than as biological default in beings capable of choosing — runs continuously alongside the reproductive function but is not reducible to it. Affect is real because registration is real; reducing affect to replication-strategy mistakes the substrate for the phenomenon, and treating same-sex coupling, post-reproductive sexuality, contraception-mediated reproduction, and sexual coupling as ends in themselves as anomalies-to-explain rather than as features the broader register makes immediately legible is one place where the reduction shows. The same substrate hosts both bacterial gradient-following and the deepest human intimacy; what differs is depth, not the kind of activity.

*Social constructionism.* Foucault (1976), Butler (1990), and the constructionist tradition read sexuality and gender as productions of historical discourse. The position rests on the variability of how sexuality is named, organized, regulated, and experienced across cultures and historical moments: what counts as sexual at all, who is permitted to do what with whom, which identity-positions are even available to the subjects who construct themselves around them, which forms of attention are sexually weighted versus unmarked, and how desire and constraint are jointly produced by power, language, and institution all vary in ways that resist substrate-only explanation. The constructionist's central observation — that identity is held in language, transmitted by institution, and shaped by power — is correct as far as it goes, and any account that treated identity-positions as substrates rather than as constructions would miss precisely what makes those positions historically and culturally located. The structural account preserves the constructed character of identity-positions — they are self-model constructions in the sense [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) names, not substrates — without dissolving the substrate they are constructed against. The body is real, attraction is real, the affective architecture is shared across lineages and predates discourse, and the [§8.6.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-4) neural-correlate findings on orientation- and identity-architecture are not optional. What discourse constructs is how a particular being takes up its position in the field; the field itself is structural. The construction is real, person-specific, consequential, and dissolvable under the conditions [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) names — but the substrate it constructs around is not negotiable in the same way.

*Sex-binary reductionism.* Contemporary sex-realist arguments — Stock (2021), Joyce (2021), Soh (2020), and the broader gender-critical literature — correctly insist that sexed embodiment is materially real, that reproductive biology is not a discursive artifact, and that institutional handling of identity categories has policy consequences that cannot be wished away. The structural account preserves all three claims. What it forecloses is the move from “one biological layer is real” to “that layer is the whole structure of sex and gender.” Five recurring inferential collapses drive the argument past what its substrate supports.

The gametic collapse moves from anisogamy — that sexually reproducing species use two gamete types — to the conclusion that sexed embodiment, development, attraction, and identity must therefore be binary in the same way; but anisogamy is one structural layer, not the whole architecture [§8.6.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-2) documents. The chromosomal collapse moves from XX/XY's prevalence to the conclusion that sex is settled by chromosomes; but development is multilayered — genes, gonads, hormones, morphology, neural development, self-model — and atypical patterns at every layer are documented. The statistical collapse moves from population dimorphism to the conclusion that every token person is binary in the same way; but average differences between groups do not determine the architecture of the individual being. The policy collapse moves from “some institutions handle gender identity poorly” to “gender identity is therefore not real in the relevant sense”; but bad institutional handling does not falsify the phenomenon being handled. The construction collapse, running in the opposite direction, moves from “gender is socially constructed” to “gender is therefore arbitrary”; but self-models, languages, laws, and identities are constructed and causally real at once.

The structural account avoids all five by holding what each register tracks at its proper level: gametic polarity, chromosomal pattern, endocrine development, morphology, attraction, identity-position, and political standing are coupled registers, not interchangeable names for the same thing. Beneath the gametic and statistical collapses in particular lies a single distinction the reductions elide: at the substrate layer, sex-category membership tracks developmental organization toward a reproductive role, not the realized exercise of that function. The infertile, the post-reproductive, the prepubescent, and the celibate are not thereby removed from the category — which shows the category was never a per-token functional test but a claim about the developmental pathways a body's development instantiates, holding whether or not the function is ever exercised or succeeds.

Both collapses trade a type- or population-level fact for an individual functional criterion; the organization/function distinction forecloses that trade at its root. Two limits keep the distinction honest. First, the organization at issue is the typical bimodal pattern the chromosomal collapse already qualified, not a re-assertion of clean binary development: where organization is itself atypical — the documented intersex and disorders-of-sex-development conditions — category standing is genuinely intermediate rather than settled by a hidden exercised-function test, exactly as the multilayered account requires. Second, this is a claim about the substrate layer alone; it carries no verdict on social-category membership or on the self-model identity a person holds, which are the questions [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10) and [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) take up, and the organizational reading of sex-as-substrate licenses no inference to them. Adopting the developmental reading of sexed embodiment therefore concedes nothing to the move from substrate to identity that the gender-critical inference requires: the registers stay separate.

*Religious-metaphysical regulation.* Augustine, Aquinas, and the natural-law tradition, with cross-cultural variants in Confucian, Brahmanic, and Islamic ethics, did more than issue commands from outside Nature. They identified four real features of sexuality that thinner accounts tend to omit: that sexual coupling has in-built structural directionality and is not metaphysically inert; that the norms tracking it are not arbitrary divine fiat but constraints latent in what coupling is; that what is done sexually leaves enduring effects on the beings involved that mere consent or contract does not exhaust; and that sexuality participates in an order larger than the individual life, a kinship-and-generations order across which subjects are produced and sustained. Each of these phenomena is real, and a recreational-signaling or contractual-exchange account of sexuality cannot capture them. The structural account agrees with the tradition on the phenomena and corrects only the metaphysics. The directionality is what coupling is at the substrate level, with attraction-architecture, hormonal coordination, gestational physiology, and pair-bonding circuitry all converging on it; the norms tracking the directionality are [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) structural-moral constraints on registration at maximum density, not divine fiat; the enduring effects are what registration in a recursive self-model does over time; the kinship-and-generations order is what intersubjective coupling at the density [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) names already is, with no relocation above Nature required. The traditions accurately identified the weight, the directionality, the duration, and the order. They misidentified only the location of the source.

*Contemporary identity discourse.* Both poles of the public argument flatten one half of the substrate–self-model pair the framework holds together. The "gender is just biology" position collapses the [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) self-model construction into the substrate, missing that the construction is real, person-specific, and consequential — that the self-model holds the position, and what the self-model holds is what it is to be that subject. The “gender is purely social construction” position collapses the substrate into discourse, missing that the body is real, attraction-architecture predates language and runs continuously across mammalian and avian lineages, and the [§8.6.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-4) neural-correlate findings are not optional. The framework holds both halves at once because both are present: [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) self-models are constructed in a neural substrate that has structural properties, and neither half is the whole story. The reality and variability of sexual orientation and gender identity are grounded by the structural account directly: orientation- and identity-architecture have real substrate variability the empirical record confirms, and the self-model's construction of an identity-position around that architecture is real, constructed, consequential, and dissolvable under the conditions [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) names for the self generally. The political weight derives from [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12): identity-positions are the beings subjects construct of themselves in the field of intersubjective coupling, and the structural account of moral standing applies to them as it applies to subjects in any other intersubjective register. Because standing is fixed at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) by the capacity for experience rather than by category-membership, the moral verdict is invariant across the constructionist and realist readings alike. Manne's (2017) distinction between sexism (the role-ascribing belief system) and misogyny (the enforcement mechanism that punishes deviation from the ascribed role) gives the [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) framework analytic purchase here: misogyny is structural-moral violation directed at one being of the substrate-and-self-model pair, operating through the [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10) language register to constrain the [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) self-model. The structural account does not adjudicate the contested specifics of contemporary policy debate; it grounds the standing of the subjects whose positions are at stake and the empirical reality of the architectures their positions construct around.

::: {.callout-note}
*Scope of the claim.* This account asserts two things and declines a third. It asserts that every subject at issue has moral standing fixed at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) by the capacity for experience, not by category-membership, so the moral verdict is invariant across the realist and constructionist readings alike. It asserts that the substrate architectures those identities construct around are empirically real and variable ([§8.6.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-4)). It declines to adjudicate the contested specifics of contemporary policy and etiquette debate. The account will be misread from both directions — as biological essentialism on one reading, as gender ideology on the other — and both misreadings collapse a register it holds apart: substrate ([§8.6.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6-4)), self-model identity ([§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)), social category ([§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10)), and moral standing ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)) are coupled but distinct, and no claim at one level settles a question at another.


:::

*Sexual violation.* The structural account names sexual coupling as [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) morality at maximum density, where registration of one being by another is most direct. Sexual violation is the inversion at the same maximum: structural-moral failure at the register where the structural-moral demand is densest. The framework reads it not as an ordinary harm scaled up but as the violation specifically targeted at the position where the depth of registration is greatest. This is why the harm cannot be accounted for by injury-metrics alone — somatic recovery does not retire it — and why traumatic registration persists at depths the [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10) language register cannot fully reach (Herman 1992; Walker 2013). Manne's (2017) reading of misogyny as enforcement-mechanism extends here: the prevalence of sexual violation as an instrument of role-enforcement, war, and political subordination is structural-moral failure operating systematically rather than incidentally. The framework does not explain why violation occurs — that is a question about substrate, history, institution, and agent — but it locates the wrong it represents at the precise point where intersubjective coupling is densest, and gives the [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) framework analytic purchase on what the wrong consists in.

*The boundary between variation and violation.* Across the practices this section has not enumerated — commercial exchange, the range of kink and fetish, the configurations consenting adults arrive at in private — a single line does the work, and it is the same line drawn throughout: consent on the modal-depth standard ([§8.9.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-4)), the standing of every party ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)), and, where more than one bond is in play, non-corrosion ([§8.6](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6)). What falls on the permitted side is variation, and variation is not the account's to moralize; what falls on the forbidden side is violation, and the account names it without hedging. The two verdicts are asymmetric by design. Where valid consent cannot be given — by a party who cannot map the possibility the act requires, whether through immaturity, incapacity, or coercion — or where a party lacks the standing the act presupposes, the coupling is ruled out, and no appeal to preference, custom, or privacy reopens the question. Where consent is real and standing is intact, the account issues no verdict beyond that one, and declines to convert its silence into either endorsement or prohibition. Commodification is the instructive case. The introduction of payment does not itself alter the consent analysis: an exchange of money between consenting adults whose consent meets the modal-depth standard is not structurally distinct, at the register this account speaks to, from the same act unpaid. What the word exploitation names is not the payment but the defeat of consent by the conditions around it — coercion, deception, or a desperation severe enough that the will behind the word lacked the mapped alternatives real consent requires; the wrong is a person used and mistreated, their consent hollowed out, not the presence of a price. The account locates the wrong there and leaves the policy question — how a shared structure should permit, regulate, or restrict such exchange — to Chapter 9, where institutional questions belong. One further distinction keeps the boundary honest: whether a practice is publicly acceptable is a question of the [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10) social register, not of structural-moral standing, and the two must not be run together. That a practice offends public norm is not itself a structural wrong, and conducting it in private discharges the separate concern of not implicating non-consenting witnesses — but privacy addresses only that concern. It cannot launder a consent-or-standing violation into a permitted act: what is done to a non-consenting party, or to a party without standing, is no less a violation for being done unseen. The boundary is consent and standing, not visibility.

*Reproduction-choice.* Pregnancy gives the structural account its hardest application because one subject's body is the site where another possible subject is being produced. The [§8.7](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-7) developmental-gradient result is therefore load-bearing here but not settled here: consciousness emerges as the neural architecture capable of integrated registration comes online, and standing comes into view by degrees rather than by binary switch. The [§8.7](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-7) contribution is to name why reproduction-choice becomes agency at all. At the depth where a being can model its own future, its bodily conditions, its relations, and the possible production of another subject, reproduction is no longer only what coupling does. It becomes an object of self-modeling. The decision whether, when, and under what conditions to produce another subject belongs to the agency of the already-existing subject whose body bears the process. The developing being's emerging standing matters once the [§8.7](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-7) developmental threshold begins to be reached; the pregnant subject's standing is already present throughout. Chapter 9 carries the political application because the question then becomes institutional: how should a shared structure protect an existing subject's bodily autonomy while registering the developing standing of another being as it comes into being?

Sexuality read structurally as the densest register of intersubjective coupling preserves what each rival tradition was tracking while refusing each collapse it forced. Sociobiology's reproductive substrate is real and is one layer rather than the whole; constructionism's identity-construction is real and is built against a substrate that does not negotiate at the same rate; sex-binary reductionism's biological reality is real and does not license the five collapses (gametic, chromosomal, statistical, policy, construction) that drive its inference past where the substrate goes; religious-metaphysical regulation's directionality, duration, and order are real and their source is the medium rather than the agent it was personified into; contemporary identity discourse's substrate-and-self-model pair holds at both halves rather than at either alone. Sexual violation is [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) morality at maximum density inverted; reproduction-choice is where the developmental-gradient result meets the pregnant subject's already-present standing. The structural counterpart is taken up at [§8.7](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-7) — drive's aversion-pole at its limit.

## 8.7 Mortality {#sec-8-7}

Every living thing eventually stops. Narrower than that is what it is like, from the inside, for a creature to grasp that *it itself* will end. A bacterium dies without ever knowing it will; only a mind that models itself as a single person stretched through time can register its own coming death as a fact about itself. That awareness is not just one more item added to a life: it changes everything else in it, because feeling, knowing, meaning, and will now all run against a limit the mind can see ahead of it. What truly ends (the living process and its inside view) is separate from what outlasts it, like the memories, works, and children a person leaves behind. Those remain, but they are not the person; the person ends.

::: {.identification}
**Mortality** · *Identification*

Mortality, in its deep form, is the recursion registering its own ending as a structural fact about itself: the closure every living current is organized against, folded back into a self-model deep enough to project itself toward its terminus. (The universal fact of closure is the aversion-anchor of [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1); the phenomenon here is that fact registered from inside.)
*Status: an identity claim on the [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) self-modeling structure, defended by fit, not a stipulative definition and not a fresh derivation from the proof.*


:::

Drive runs in two directions, and the defensive one has a structural limit: not the moment-to-moment threat-responses and homeostatic corrections, but the fact that the closure each defense was oriented against is not contingent. Every recursion that runs will stop. What is death, structurally, for beings of the kind we are? Every philosophical tradition treats mortality as a discrete subject: Epicurus's anodyne argument, Lucretius's image of the vanished candle, the Stoic *meditatio mortis*, Montaigne's essay on learning to die, Heidegger's *Sein-zum-Tode*, Becker's *Denial of Death*, the Buddhist contemplations of impermanence, the Christian *memento mori*. The framework here gives mortality a specific structural meaning, and in giving it that meaning, recovers what the traditions have been pointing at.

*What gets bundled under "death."* The section's question needs sharpening before it can be answered. There is the *structural fact*: every closed self-producing recursion eventually fails to keep producing itself, and the closure each living thing is organized against is not contingent. This is universal: every bacterium, every plant, every animal, every human. It is already named in [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) Drive, where the closure-threshold is the absolute structural anchor of the aversion-pole, operative at any depth and not requiring self-modeling. And there is the *phenomenon*: what it is like, from inside, for a recursion to grasp its own ending as a structural fact about itself. This second thing is what the present section is about. The phenomenon requires that the recursion have folded back deeply enough to model itself as a persistent subject in time and to project that subject toward its terminus. A bacterium dies but does not grasp its own dying. The structural fact operates everywhere; the phenomenon is what mortality becomes from inside at the depth where it can become anything at all. Conflating the two has been a persistent source of confusion in the literature: treating Heideggerian *Sein-zum-Tode* as if it claimed something true of every living thing, or treating the universal biological fact as if it carried the phenomenological weight only the deep form actually carries. The framework keeps them distinct: Drive ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)) carries the universal structural anchor; this section carries the phenomenon at the depth where it emerges.

What we are was identified at [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) as a closed self-producing recursion coupled to a sustained energy gradient, dissipating that gradient through itself in order to keep producing itself. The chapter's opening traces the same phenomenon from inside. Death, on this account, is what happens when the recursion fails to keep producing itself: the closure breaks, the energy throughput stops, the being that *was* a self-producing recursion is no longer that. The vantage that opened with sufficient recursive depth closes when the recursion does. Death is not an external event imposed on the person; it is the structural condition of the person coming apart.

*A note on what is and is not closing.* Several distinct things are usefully separated here. *Biological closure* is the failure of closure-plus-throughput at the cellular and organismic scale; it is the structural event the section's main argument is about. *Ordinary-consciousness closure* is the closing of the recursive vantage that opened at sufficient depth; on the framework here it tracks biological closure rather than supervening on it independently, since the vantage is what the recursion is from inside, not a separate thing keyed to the recursion. *Surviving effects* (the dead person's models held by others, the social patterns their life shaped, the artifacts their making produced, the children they raised) persist after both forms of closure and are real, but they are not the person; they are what the person left in the structures that hosted them. Confusing the last for either of the others is the structural error the survival traditions make. The person ends. What they shaped does not, until those persons also end.

*What death takes, and why it remains a loss.* The account at [§8.5.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5-5) draws Parfit's consequence that identity is not what matters: what one has reason to care about in one's own future is the continuation of the recursion, not a bare identity-fact laid over it. Carried to mortality, this fixes what death takes and blocks two opposite errors. Against the survival traditions, death takes exactly the recursion's continuation, the projects, connections, and self-model that would have been carried forward, and not some further self-substance that might have gone on elsewhere, for there is no such further thing to survive. Against the fully deflationary reading, the loss is nonetheless real and, in the ordinary case, determinate, because the recursion whose continuation matters is a single real continuant rather than a relation that only ever held by degrees. Parfit's softening of the badness of death has purchase where the recursion is already thin or branched, where little of what matters was going to be carried forward in any case, and not against the standard case, where a determinate continuant with a future is what ends. What Epicurus and Lucretius saw is that there is no post-closure vantage for death to be bad for; what they missed is that the badness was never located there but in the foreclosure of the continuation the living recursion was oriented toward.

This is why mortality is constitutive of what the deep first-person perspective *is*, not an unfortunate addition. Self-modeling requires sustained energy throughput it cannot guarantee. The depth at which self-modeling folds back into itself is also the depth at which the person becomes capable of registering, from inside, that self-modeling requires what it cannot guarantee. To be a self-modeling being at that depth *is* to be oriented toward an ending that is not external to the structure but is one of its conditions of possibility. Heidegger's claim that Dasein is *Sein-zum-Tode* (being-toward-death) names, on this framework, a structural fact about any sufficiently recursive vantage, not a peculiarity of human existence.

*Mortality-awareness as a phase-transition for the recursion.* Crossing the threshold at which mortality registers as a first-person structural fact is not the addition of a new modality alongside the others the chapter has been tracing. It is a phase-transition event for the recursion as a whole, not in the sense of an instantaneous switch (the capacity to register one's own ending comes online by degrees, as the gradient discussions below describe), but in the sense that, once the threshold is crossed, the modalities already in play are reorganized rather than supplemented. The modalities the recursion possessed before the threshold continue to operate after it, but they operate differently. Feeling becomes feeling-of-a-current-that-will-end. Knowledge becomes knowledge-of-a-mind-that-cannot persist what it stabilizes. Meaning becomes meaning-for-a-life-bounded-at-both-ends. Will becomes will-against-the-horizon. Art becomes a current's resonance with what it knows it will not outlast. The threshold does not install death as one modality among the chapter's others; it reorganizes the entire field of modalities by inserting an absolute limit-condition the field must now operate against.
