Empirical psychology confirms the shape from a different angle. Baumeister and colleagues (2013) find that meaning, distinct from happiness, tracks integration across time, connection to others, and orientation toward projects larger than the self — exactly the three coordinates the structural argument predicts, and exactly the three features that evolutionary psychology has independently identified as correlates of persistence and reproductive fitness in social organisms (Tooby and Cosmides 1990; Buss 2019). Meaning and survival correlate in the empirical record because they share a structural ground — the persistence of a self-modeling subject whose continuation depends on integrated orientation toward what sustains it. This does not reduce meaning to reproductive fitness: the persistence at issue is the persistence of the subject's exchanges with its medium, not narrowly its gene-propagation, and the empirical correlations track the broader structural fact rather than the narrower evolutionary one. Reproductive success is one specific subset of the broader persistence-pressure; meaning tracks the broader pressure.

Frankl’s (1946) observations in the Nazi concentration camps make the link unmistakable. In conditions where starvation, cold, forced labor, arbitrary violence, and systematic dehumanization had collapsed every other component of wellbeing, meaning persisted wherever orientation persisted — and wherever orientation persisted, the probability of survival rose. The correlation is not accidental. Meaning is the internal aspect of the orientation that sustains a person against what threatens them: a model of a future that has not yet arrived, a relational interval between the self and what the self reaches toward, and a substrate that continues under conditions designed to erode it. Meaning tracked T, S, and Φ (the three structural roles derived through Modal Identity and Conditions-as-Nature, §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7) before the framework was named, and tracked them in their role as conditions of persistence.

Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan 2000) reaches the same structure through motivational psychology: autonomy (an agent with causal reach), competence (the reach connecting to what matters), and relatedness (a relational interval between self and other). The three basic psychological needs are the three structural conditions of orientation, restated in motivational vocabulary.

Comparative cognition extends the prediction across species. Animals reach toward what sustains them through orientations that involve real relational intervals — mate selection, territory maintenance, bond formation, the long-running attachments documented across mammals, birds, and cephalopods. Meaning in the structural sense — the internal registration of one's direction within the medium — obtains wherever a self-modeling subject registers its own reach, regardless of substrate. What human meaning adds is not the registration but the depth at which the registration takes itself as an object: articulating directions, naming projects, transmitting purposes across generations through language and culture. Birds returning to last season's nest and humans returning to a vocation are running the same operation at different recursive depths.

These literatures offer partial points of contact with the structural account, but their methods, constructs, and normative commitments differ. Their overlap is suggestive background for the model rather than confirmation that the structural argument predicts the settled shape of meaning.

### 8.8.5 What is Concluded {#sec-8-8-5}

*Constructivism* — the view that meaning is imposed by sovereign subjects onto a universe indifferent to value (Sartre 1946) — rests on the insistence that without some imposing subject, no meaning would obtain anywhere; meaning is the kind of thing that exists only where someone meant something, and any account that locates it elsewhere either smuggles in a subject under another name or equivocates on what *meaning* is. The structural account agrees that meaning requires a self-modeling subject to register direction, and that no meaning lives in the medium prior to the subjects that hold it. Where constructivism then misidentifies the structure is in the imposition image itself. Any imposition presupposes a ground on which it lands. No one can impose direction onto a medium that lacks the conditions for direction, any more than a hand can press onto a surface that lacks extension. The structural ground is not optional for the constructivist either. What constructivism correctly identifies is the contingency of content. What it mistakes is the necessity of the conditions under which any content can be meant at all.

*Theistic prescription* — the view that meaning requires a transcendent lawgiver to inscribe purpose from outside (Craig 2008; Swinburne 2004) — rests on the experiential weight of moral and meaningful demands: when something matters, the mattering does not feel like something the subject could simply withdraw at will; it presents itself with the authority of what is owed, not what is preferred. A view on which the subject just makes up its own meaning struggles to capture that weight. The structural account agrees that the weight is real, that it is not invented at will, and that any adequate account has to ground rather than dismiss it. It locates the source differently. The pressure the tradition attributed to a transcendent source is real; people oriented toward shared exchange do experience a normative pull that exceeds their own preferences. But the source of that pull is the modal gradient of the medium itself, not an agent beyond it. A designer outside T, S, and Φ could not inscribe direction into a medium it does not share; inscription requires contact, contact requires the medium, and the medium is what is being identified as the ground. The tradition’s intuition — that meaning is not invented by the individual — survives. Its ontology does not.

The same point explains how religion produces genuine meaning while getting its metaphysics wrong. Religious communities connect people to each other across real relational intervals and orient them toward shared outcomes sustained through time — the structural conditions of meaning, met whether or not the outcome exists as named. A congregation oriented toward a heaven that is not real still connects: to each other, across the interval the community holds open; to a direction that organizes collective life across time; to a tradition whose persistence exceeds any single member. The meaning is not imaginary; the connection is actual. The terminus of the shared reach is imaginary; the reach itself is not. Religion has been one of the most effective meaning-producing technologies humans have built (Durkheim 1912; Geertz 1973; Atran 2002), and the modal account inherits the phenomenon without inheriting the ontology. What the tradition's metaphysics located beyond Nature was not where it claimed to be; what the gathering itself produced — connection across the relational interval, shared orientation across time, communities held open by what they reached toward — was real all along.

One heuristic sharpens the contrast. Meaning under theistic prescription works like a paint-by-numbers kit: the subject traces a fixed scheme whose authority is pre-supplied; the picture is right when it matches the template. Meaning under the structural account is more like the open studio where the curriculum has been genuinely absorbed — the medium, tools, tradition, and the constraint that some marks are technically incoherent are all real — but what gets made within them is authentically the maker's own. The studio version is not emptier than the kit. The constraints are found, not invented; the expression is genuinely one's own; the tradition is shared; the conversation with other makers continues across the making. What the kit supplies that the studio does not is not richer meaning but fewer choices — and the fewer choices, not the meaning, is what its adherents sometimes mourn when they leave.

The concession is mortality. Religion did not only host meaning; it hosted meaning eternalized — security against all contingency, survival without end, a witness that never looks away. The structural account can relocate meaning because the arrangements that secure possibility are real, and the connections they hold open are real. It cannot relocate the fantasy that those arrangements cannot be lost. Meaning returns to the finite world intact but without the guarantee against loss. That is not nihilism; it is the mature cost of the relocation. The full burden of that cost is carried at [§8.7](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-7), because mortality is where the wish for permanence has to be faced directly.

*Nihilism and absurdism* — the view that the universe is silent on the question of meaning, and that the human demand for meaning confronts a neutral or indifferent cosmos (Camus 1942; Nagel 1971) — rest on the honesty of the refusal: once the external sources of meaning have been withdrawn, no consolation prize should be smuggled back in to fill the gap, and any account that surreptitiously reintroduces a substitute under a new label is not earning its result. The structural account agrees that no external prescription is restored by its own move and accepts the discipline that constraint imposes on what can be claimed. What the nihilist hears as silence is the medium’s refusal to supply prescribed content, not the absence of structure. What the absurdist names as the confrontation between demand and silence is the encounter between a self-modeling person and a medium that supplies the conditions of orientation without supplying the direction. The modal account keeps the honesty of the absurdist’s refusal of cheap comfort while correcting the metaphysics. Camus correctly identified that no external authority hands down the answer; he misread this as no answer being available. The activity of asking is itself the answer.

A fourth position deserves separate treatment rather than assimilation — Wolf's hybrid (1997, 2010), which is the framework's nearest analytic neighbor and the position most likely to be read as a predecessor the structural account has absorbed. Wolf holds that meaningful activity requires both genuine subjective engagement and objective worth — *fitting fulfillment*, the subjective attraction to something objectively worth caring about. The structural account cannot accept the objective-worth component in Wolf's sense. Wolf's objective worth is a *north*: a fixed set of right things to love, their worth a normative fact about the objects that no further reduction explains. The structural account cannot install a north without reintroducing, under a new name, the external prescription Chapters 6–7 foreclosed — a prescribed destination is exactly what the Inversion denies the universe has. Two further problems compound the difficulty: a north is positional and exclusive, so rival traditions each posit different norths and on Wolf's reading these must adjudicate as competing absolutes rather than complementary directions of reach, which makes the absoluteness itself the source of conflict rather than its resolution; and the postulated north has no determinate referent the framework can point to in the way the outward points to actual others and the medium reaching is conducted through — one phantom referent against which everything is to be measured, where the outward has many real ones. What it offers in place of a north is an *outward*: the objective component of meaning is not a target the current is meant to reach but the real directedness of its reaching — extension into the genuinely other, the interval held open, coherence with the medium (Spatiality, [§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4)). The difference is between a compass needle that should point toward a fixed pole and the fact that the needle is pointing at all.

The disagreement has to be settled in the currency Wolf's worth-condition was minted to provide: discrimination. Worth is what lets her tell a meaningful life from an empty one, and if the outward replaces the north it must go on telling them apart, or the replacement has dropped what the north was for. The first thing to see is that worth was never the object-property it presented itself as. Worth is always worth *to*: the pilot in the cockpit has more of it than the passenger asleep behind him, not because a value adheres to his person, but because in that frame the survival of everyone aboard routes through his functioning. Move the frame and the ranking moves with it. What posed as an absolute pointing at fixed objects resolves into a relation, and the relation bottoms out in the fact the account has leaned on since [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1): beings find their own lives worth living. Worth is what appears when many such stakes converge on what keeps them going.

That relation has two layers, and Wolf's single criterion collapses them. Beneath everything is a floor: each subject's stake in its own continuation, indexed to no frame and rankable against no one else's, the aversion [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) marks as structurally prior. Every subject carries it in full. On top of the floor sits a positional layer: worth to others within a frame, contingent and rankable, and it is all the pilot example ever measures. Keeping the layers apart is not bookkeeping. It is what stops relational worth from sliding into the doctrine that useful lives count and useless ones do not. Positional ranking decides who should occupy a scarce role; it never licenses spending a floor. The pilot flies the plane, and the infant who cannot is not thereby a lesser stake. Who fills the function and whose stake counts at all are different questions, and the north answered them with one word because it could not see they were two.

With worth deflated this way, the two lives the worth-condition was built to exclude come apart, and they come apart in opposite directions. The first is the trivial life that is nonetheless richly connected: a subculture organized around something an outsider finds empty, genuine others reached, a tradition shared, the arrangement surviving across time. This is not a defect the account should set out to correct. To call it thin is to rank it from outside, the very move worth-as-object licensed and worth-as-relation forbids.

The framework has already granted, in the congregation oriented toward a heaven that is not real, that connection across the interval is genuine meaning even when its terminus is not; the same verdict holds here. The meaning is the reaching, and no standpoint outside the reach is positioned to strike it down. What Wolf read as absent worth is only her frame declining to share the subject's: her discrimination is real, but it discriminates from somewhere, and that somewhere holds no authority over a meaning registered from inside.

The second life is refused, and the reason it is refused is the reason worth deflates rather than vanishes. Take the cohesive cruelty-project: a movement bonded among its members, reaching, persisting, tracking its own survival, organized around the degradation of others. It satisfies connection, reach, and survivability, and on the criteria taken flatly it should pass. It does not, and not because cruelty offends a taste. Worth was just shown to bottom out in the convergence of self-valuing stakes; cruelty is the project aimed at the floor those stakes stand on, the negation of the very fact that lets worth mean anything.

Its reach is parasitic on its own condition: it uses the relational interval to close other subjects' fields rather than hold them open, and so it consumes the ground it would need in order to be meaning at all. Its members register orientation, and that first-person face is as real as anyone's; the account does not reach in and strip it. What the arrangement lacks is standing: the constitution in the inter that turns registered orientation into meaning that holds. That there is an objective inter to be failed against is not a forward promise but Theorem 9 (Modal Convergence, [§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)), already in hand; the standing is withheld here because the inter is the very thing the project is set against, and its objectivity is not the project's to revoke (the medium that develops it is taken up at [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10)). The monstrous life is excluded not for loving the wrong object but for being self-liquidating, meaning that feeds on what it requires. So the outward keeps what the worth-condition was for and splits it along the seam the single criterion could not: the shallow-but-connected life is left its meaning, because ranking it was never anyone's to do, and the connected-but-monstrous life is refused, because it cannot coexist with its own ground. Wolf was right that meaning discriminates and wrong about the coin. It sorts lives not by the worth of what they love (perspectival, unrankable from outside) but by whether the reach can stand on the ground it reaches from (structural, and self-enforcing).

The moral-sainthood observation (Wolf 1982) tightens the disagreement. A perfectly virtuous agent who devotes every moment to morality loses the engaged particularity that makes a life feel meaningful — loses the projects and persons they have *their own* stake in, the directions that carry *their* weight rather than the universal weight of what morality assigns. The observation sits uncomfortably inside Wolf's own hybrid account — on her view, morality is one of the items of objective worth, so more devotion to it should be better for meaning, not worse. The framework's reading dissolves the discomfort: morality is what the inter requires of a subject among subjects; meaning is what that subject's own weighting of its modal field produces. A subject can honor what the inter requires and still have a life that is, in terms of the weighted field, particularly *theirs*. The three evaluative dimensions — meaning (internal direction-registration), happiness (affective quality of integration), and moral worth (what the inter requires of one subject among others) — are distinct, and Wolf's moral-sainthood observation is the diagnostic that shows why they must be kept that way.

The convergence the preceding analysis develops is not an accident of selective reading — though the right way to take it is not quite Parfit’s. Parfit (2011) argued that Kantian ethics, contractualism, and consequentialism — traditions that spent the twentieth century in apparent opposition — were each converging, in their most defensible forms, on substantially the same verdicts; and that the agreement was itself evidence about the moral terrain rather than a coincidence of three independent projects happening to err in the same direction. The traditions of meaning do not agree in that way — they divide over meaning’s very source — and so the pattern here is not shared verdicts but shared ground, each holding one face of a single structure. Existentialism tracked the contingency of content — the fact that what a given person finds meaningful is authored, not received. Theism tracked the genuine weight of meaning — the fact that the mattering does not feel like something the subject could simply revoke. Nihilism tracked the discipline of honest refusal — the fact that no cheap consolation can replace what the withdrawal of external prescription removed. Each tradition preserved one face of the structure the account has been developing; each went wrong in the metaphysics it built around that face. This is not evidence in the same sense Parfit’s convergence was, and the difference is worth marking: Parfit’s traditions agreed on the same verdicts, whereas these three preserve complementary faces of one structure — a weaker inference, but a real one. What makes it evidence is the common source they all stand on. Before any of the three gets a vote, some things already matter to a being of this kind, because it has conditions to meet; and those conditions are, in the first instance, negative — survival, health, safety, and protection are not yet a structure of significance but what a subject registers on the way away from its own dissolution, the aversion [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) identifies as structurally prior. Meaning is that aversion read forward — as [§8.12.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12-3) puts it on the moral side, “not the absence of pain but the optimum the avoidance points at” — the field held maximally open once the floor is secured and the freed drive has somewhere to go ([§8.1.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1-5)). That three traditions built from incompatible starting points each preserved a distinct genuine component of one structure is what would be unlikely if the structure were not there, and exactly what is predicted once meaning is read as the forward face of a persisting subject’s aversion to its own dissolution. The same logic is applied to morality at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12).

Meaning collected against constructivism, theistic prescription, nihilism, religion, and Wolf's hybrid alike is neither invented, nor inscribed, nor absent — it is the constitutive relation between a self-modeling subject and what its orientation connects to, a relation the medium necessarily supports and the subject necessarily instantiates. Each tradition was tracking something the structural account preserves: constructivism's contingency of content, theism's refusal that meaning is invented at will, nihilism's discipline against cheap consolation, religion's effective production of connection across the relational interval, Wolf's insistence that meaning needs more than subjective grip. What the convergence corrects is not the tracking but the metaphysics each tradition built around it. What can be anticipated from the [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10) result already shapes what can be said here: the inter across which subjects exchange is constituted as objectively as the Spatiality that makes any relational interval possible, and the arrangements of a life mean what they mean not by private registration alone but by their standing in an inter that has already constituted them as meaning-bearing. The first-personal registration is real and irreducible; it is one face of an intersubjective constitution the medium provides. The medium that makes that inter possible is taken up at [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10).

## 8.9 Will {#sec-8-9}

Will is the power to choose among the options you can actually see. The surprising part is that freedom is not a matter of somehow escaping cause and effect; it is what choosing becomes when a creature understands its own situation deeply: what is really possible, and what follows from what. So freedom comes in degrees. A choice made over a field you barely grasp, or under pressure that stops you from acting on what you do grasp, is barely free; a choice made with real understanding and real room to act is about as free as choosing gets. That means freedom can grow, with knowledge, upbringing, education, and everything else that widens the field you choose within.

::: {.identification}
**Will** · *Identification*

Will is a living being's capacity to *select* among the options its modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) presents: the point at which causation has been mapped deeply enough, from inside, for that being to participate in which possible line becomes actual. Drive supplies direction, feeling valence, knowledge the stable map, reasoning the navigation, meaning the weighting; will is the selection that turns those possibilities into action. Freedom (*modal freedom*) is not standing outside causation. It has two dimensions: how deeply a person grasps the options they are choosing among (modal depth: what is possible, and what follows from what), and how much latitude they have to act on that understanding. A choice made over a barely registered field, or under constraint that blocks action on what is understood, is barely free; a choice made with deep understanding and room to act is as free as a living being can become. So freedom admits of degree, grows with understanding, and can be cultivated.
*Status: an identity claim on the [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) self-modeling structure (Principle 5), defended by fit, not a stipulative definition and not a fresh derivation from the proof.*


:::

Will appears twice in the cascade. In its thin form, it has been present since drive: directedness through whatever field of possibility the being can register, however small. A bacterium moving up a gradient, an animal orienting away from threat, and a person trying to hold attention on a task all display forms of directedness, but the fields through which they move differ in depth. This section names will in its thick form: the capacity of a living being to act through a mapped and meaningful field of possibility.

That is why will belongs here in the cascade: after drive, feeling, knowledge, reasoning, and meaning. A choice is only as free as the modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) through which the agent understands it. Thin will operates on a sparse field, thick will on a dense one, which is why parenting, education, and the cultivated breadth made available through language and art bear directly on the freedom of the resulting agent. Each is, mechanically, the deliberate installation of modal-field content the agent will later select from. Drive supplies direction; feeling supplies valence; knowledge stabilizes the map; reasoning navigates alternatives; meaning weights the map as worth pursuing or avoiding; will acts through it. The willing subject is not outside causation. They are the point at which causal conditions have been understood deeply enough for the person to participate in which possible line becomes actual.

The chapter's structural reach is sharpest here. Everything traditionally placed above causation (libertarian exemption, divine simplicity, freedom transcendent of Nature) turns out to be what modal depth *within* Nature consists in at sufficient recursion. Will is the register where the inversion is hardest to accept and most precisely available: not because the framework denies the phenomenon the tradition has been naming, but because it locates the phenomenon one register deeper than the tradition placed it. Freedom is not what stands above the modal field; it is the modal freedom a sufficiently recursive being realizes within it: the modal depth it brings to its own selection, together with the latitude to carry that selection into act. The detailed dialectical engagement with libertarian, compatibilist, and semicompatibilist alternatives follows in §[§8.9.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-1)–.5. Language is taken up at [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10) as the technology of shared interiority: one way willing beings externalize their models, claims, refusals, and invitations into another being's field.

### 8.9.1 What is Disputed {#sec-8-9-1}

The literature on will is organized around a small number of standing positions, each of which the framework engages directly. The engagement runs on three terms formally specified at [§8.9.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-2) — the modal-mapping network (the structure that holds an agent's live alternatives), modal depth (how far that structure extends), and the modal field it presents — introduced here in their working sense. Each is taken up again by name at [§8.9.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-5) once the structural account is in view.

*Libertarian free will.* The classical libertarian tradition (Chisholm 1964; van Inwagen 1983; Kane 1996; O'Connor 2000) holds that free will requires exemption from the causal structure of the natural world: a genuinely undetermined act, or an act produced by an agent acting as a first cause. The motivation is that if every act traces back to prior conditions the agent did not author, no act is properly the agent's own. The structural account presses where the position meets its own commitments. An agent acting outside any modal field acts on no possibilities, because possibility is the structure the field provides; an act with no modal context is not a free act but no act at all. Grant the libertarian the modal field, then, and press where freedom actually lives: in the *selection* among the live alternatives the field presents. That selection is either grounded in the agent's prior states — character, conviction, the modal map accumulated and installed in them — or it is not. If it is, the act issues from what the agent is, which is determination by the agent's own structure, not exemption from it; that is the structural account, not a rival to it. If it is not, then nothing about the agent explains why this outcome occurred rather than that one, and an unexplained selection is luck, not control — the very thing the libertarian invoked freedom to secure the agent against. The agent-causal refinement (Chisholm, O'Connor) — the agent *qua* substance as an irreducible first cause — appears to name a third thing, but the appearance depends on a self standing apart from its own structure, and [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) and [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) have already foreclosed one: the agent just *is* the structured recursion, the self just *is* the self-model built within it. There is no substance over and above the modal-mapping network for an irreducible agent-cause to be. So the refinement collapses back into the fork: operate *through* the map and it is structure under another name; select with no basis in the map and the luck horn returns intact. The dilemma is general, and it is why the result is stronger than the mere actual absence of contra-causal freedom. Given the identification of the agent with a structured recursion ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8), [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)), no contra-causal locus survives specification: pressed for its content, contra-causal freedom resolves into determination-by-structure or randomness, with no third thing available. The claim is modal, not merely actual — contra-causal freedom picks out no possible act — and it stands exactly as far as that identification does. The agent-causal theorist who would resist it must supply a self that is not its structure, which is the [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) result over again. What libertarianism needed was depth within structure, which is what the modal-depth account supplies; the rejection of structure was the wrong move on a correct intuition.

*Hard determinism and hard incompatibilism.* The hard-determinist tradition (Pereboom 2001; Caruso 2012; Strawson 1994) holds that because every act is caused by prior conditions the agent did not author, no one is ever ultimately morally responsible for what they do. The structural account agrees that no agent authors itself from nothing and rejects the inference that responsibility therefore disappears. Responsibility tracks modal depth — the capacity to hold alternatives open, model consequences, inhibit response, and revise the field — not ultimate metaphysical sourcehood. Hard incompatibilism is correct that libertarian sourcehood is unavailable and incorrect that anything moral practice cares about depended on it.

*Classical compatibilism.* Compatibilist accounts from Hume forward (Hume 1748; Hobbes 1654; Frankfurt 1971; Watson 1975; Fischer and Ravizza 1998; Wolf 1990) hold that free will is compatible with determinism because what matters is the right kind of internal cause — desires endorsed by higher-order desires, reasons-responsive mechanisms, sanity-relative reasons-tracking. The structural account is the deepest version of this thought. The internal structure that does the work is a modal-mapping network: its depth supplies the alternatives a higher-order desire or a reasons-responsive mechanism would range over, while the agent's identification with one of the valuations the network holds is what those criteria were approximating. Compatibilism named the location; the structural account names what is there.

*Frankfurt cases and the principle of alternate possibilities.* Frankfurt (1969) argued by counterexample that responsibility does not require the ability to have done otherwise: an agent who acts on their own reasons, while unbeknownst to them a counterfactual intervener would have forced the same act had they tried to deviate, is still responsible despite lacking genuine alternatives. The literature has multiplied increasingly elaborate versions (Fischer 1994; Widerker and McKenna 2003; Pereboom 2001). The structural account dissolves the dispute by distinguishing what alternatives consist in. Frankfurt cases manipulate the external-world branching while leaving the agent's modal-mapping network — the inside of the act — intact. The freedom that matters is the depth of the internal map, not the count of metaphysically open branches. Responsibility therefore tracks modal depth even when external alternatives are foreclosed, exactly as Frankfurt argued, but on a structural reading rather than a counterexample-driven one.

*Hierarchical will and volitional necessity.* A second strand locates freedom not in how many alternatives lie open but in the agent's relation to their own desires. Frankfurt (1971) gives the hierarchical version: a wanton, moved by whichever first-order desire is strongest without caring which one moves them, is unfree with options to spare, while an agent is free when the desire that moves them is one they endorse by a higher-order desire. Watson (1975), routinely filed alongside Frankfurt but in fact the locus classicus critique of him, presses exactly the objection the hierarchy invites — a higher-order desire is only another desire, with no standing to confer authority, so ranking desires by order begins a regress rather than ending it — and substitutes a valuational reading: what makes a desire the agent's own is that it expresses what the agent values, the deliverance of a valuational system distinct from the mere strength of the motivational one. Bratman (2007) develops the same identificatory thought in terms of self-governing plans. The distinction is load-bearing here, because the endorsement criterion this chapter adopts is Watson's valuational one rather than Frankfurt's higher-order-desire one, and [§8.9.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-5) answers Watson's regress worry rather than inheriting it. A later refinement (Frankfurt 1982, 1988) adds that the deepest form of such endorsement — volitional necessity, being unable to act against what one cares about most — is a height of freedom rather than a limit on it, and stands as the analytic tradition's most developed reply to the demand for open alternatives. The everyday failure of the same structure is the weakness of will tracked since Aristotle and sharpened by Davidson (1970): judging one course best and being carried into another. These positions press the modal-depth framing from a direction the alternatives-based disputes do not, since they turn on which valuation governs rather than on how many alternatives lie open; how depth and endorsement combine is taken up at [§8.9.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-5).

*The Eden story.* The most developed classical reading of the Genesis narrative — present in Augustine and Aquinas, refined in the contemporary Catholic tradition — holds that Adam and Eve were created with perfectly oriented wills and full modal competence by divine endowment, so that the choice they faced was a free turning of an already-competent will rather than a choice that lacked the depth to count. The structural account presses where this reading meets its own commitments: a will competent to choose moral evil already requires a modal field rich enough to contain the alternative as live, and the field's structure is what the present account calls Nature; the endowment view relocates rather than removes the modal-depth requirement. And the endowment cuts against what the defender needs from it. A will acting on an *infused* map — competence conferred whole, as Aquinas's original justice and infused knowledge have it — is acting on modal-field content it did not author, so its selections are grounded in that installed structure: freedom in precisely the structural, modal-depth sense, not the contra-causal one. That modal content can be *installed* at all is no concession against this — education, language, and art install it piecemeal, divine infusion all at once, and in neither case does the will that acts on the map act independently of the map. Infusion therefore yields a structurally free will, not a contra-causally free one, and cannot rescue the libertarian reading of the first choice; the only question it leaves open is whether the infused map was *deep* enough for the choice to count as fully responsible — a question internal to the structural account, and one its account of accumulated, lived modal depth answers in the negative. On the structural reading — modal depth as accumulated terrain — the first humans are placed before a morally decisive choice before they have accumulated the modal depth required to understand it. They have no history of deception, no developed map of death, no prior moral failure, no experience of shame, alienation, guilt, punishment, or irreversible consequence. The act is formally voluntary, but formal voluntariness is not freedom. Freedom requires a modal network deep enough to understand what is being selected. On that standard, Eden is not the origin of fully responsible rebellion. It is the exposure of undeveloped will to a consequence it could not yet understand.

*Divine will.* The same analysis returns to divine will. The most developed classical reading — Aquinas's *actus purus* (pure actuality — being with no unrealized potential), refined in Stump (2003) and the contemporary Thomistic tradition — holds that divine willing is not the operation of selection across alternatives but a single, simple, eternal act in which what God wills and what God is are not distinct; on this view divine simplicity is preserved without surrendering the language of will, and the apparent absence of modal depth is not a defect but a higher-order feature of the divine mode of being. The structural account presses the dilemma the picture leaves intact. Classical God can be assigned modal status, but not modal depth. If God is pure actuality, there are no live alternatives, no delay, no unrealized possibilities, no selection, and no distance between willing and obtaining. That is not will; it is necessity wearing the grammar of will. If God has maximal modal depth instead, then God stands within a modal field rich enough to contain alternatives, contingencies, unrealized possibilities, and distinguishable possibilities. But to stand within such a field is to instantiate the structure God was supposed to transcend. The first option gives no will. The second gives Nature.

The standing positions in the philosophy of will divide along a single load-bearing axis: whether free will requires exemption from causal structure or admits some form of embedded freedom within it. [§8.9.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-2) takes up the structural conditions any willing must meet, [§8.9.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-3) the architecture those conditions predict, [§8.9.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-4) the empirical record, and [§8.9.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-5) the disputed positions reframed.

### 8.9.2 What is Required {#sec-8-9-2}

*Distance.* There must be distance between the willing and what is obtained by willing. The obtained state is not yet actual; possible lines toward it must be distinguishable; and a persisting medium must carry the transition from present condition to obtained condition. Where willing and obtaining are identical, will disappears into identity. Where they differ, the structure of the difference is already in play.

*The three modal axes.* The distance just identified decomposes into three conditions that map onto Time, Space, and Substance (T, S, Φ — the three roles derived through Modal Identity and Conditions-as-Nature, §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7). *Time* supplies the not-yet: a state not yet actual, so that what is willed differs from what is. *Space* supplies the distinction among lines: more than one path from present to obtained, so that selecting one displaces the others. *Substance* supplies continuity: something holds together across the transition, so that the agent who acts and the agent who obtains the result are the same agent. Strip any of the three away and willing collapses. A timeless agent has no not-yet to will toward. An agent without distinct lines has nothing to select among. An agent without persistence cannot be the same one at the moment of willing and at the moment of obtaining. T, S, and Φ are not philosophical categories grafted onto agency from outside; they are what willing consists in.

*Modal depth.* The bare three-axis distance is necessary but not sufficient for what the literature has called *free* will. Free will is the depth of the distance — not libertarian exemption from structure but modal depth within structure: the expanded capacity to hold alternatives open, model their consequences, inhibit immediate response, and revise the map. Whether the agent can then enact the line it selects — participate in which possibility becomes actual — is a further condition, *latitude*, external to depth rather than part of it ([§8.9.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-5)). At shallow depth, life is responsive. A bacterium follows a nutrient gradient or avoids a toxin; that is directed responsiveness, not free will in the relevant sense. At greater depth, response becomes mapped line. At still greater depth, mapped lines can be held open before action. The more alternatives an agent can hold, compare, and revise before one path runs, the freer the will becomes. A bigger mind, in the sense relevant here, is a modal-mapping system with greater depth, broader integration across modules, more capacity to inhibit immediate response, and longer reach into both modeled futures and accumulated pasts — not a brain with more storage.

*Asymmetric freedom.* The depth of will is asymmetric across the present moment. The forward side of will is the field of possible futures ahead: what can be done, what can be avoided, what can be obtained, what may follow. The back side of will is the accumulated modal network behind: memory, experience, learned consequence, social pattern, emotional calibration, bodily habit, and prior encounter. A person's freedom depends on both. Two agents may face the same external option while not possessing the same freedom toward it, because they do not bring the same modal map to the choice. The structural requirement is therefore not just that a modal field be present at the moment of willing but that the agent bring sufficient accumulated depth to register what the field affords.

*Two kinds of registered constraint.* A modal-mapping system deep enough to support will must register constraint of two kinds. Some constraint distinguishes possibilities from one another — the wall is not the doorway, the closed door is not the open one, the past is not the future, this object is not that one. Some constraint settles which possibility becomes actual — the line taken excludes the line not taken, the door once opened cannot also be left closed in the same moment, the chosen action displaces its alternatives. Both are required: the structure that keeps possibilities distinct, and the structure under which one possibility comes to occupy the place the others could have.

*Placement in the cascade.* These conditions explain why will belongs after meaning in the cascade. Drive supplies direction ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)). Feeling supplies valence ([§8.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-2)). Knowledge stabilizes the map ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)). Reasoning navigates alternatives ([§8.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-4)). Meaning weights the map as worth pursuing or avoiding ([§8.8](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-8)). Will acts through it. A choice is only as free as the modal network through which the agent understands it — and the network is what the prior registers have built. The willing subject is not outside causation but is the point at which causation has been internally mapped deeply enough for it to participate in which possible line becomes actual.

The framework models willing through temporal, spatial, and persistent dimensions of action, and models freer action through a capacity to represent alternatives, consequences, and prior learning. This is a philosophical account of agency, not an established result that free will requires the book's specific modal-depth architecture. Other accounts of agency, responsibility, and consent remain live.

### 8.9.3 What is Predicted {#sec-8-9-3}

The framework proposes that willing involves a system capable of representing alternatives, constraints, and anticipated consequences before action. In humans and other animals, neural systems are relevant to this work, but the relation between neural architecture, conscious access, and agency remains actively debated. The following are hypotheses generated by the framework, not a specific cognitive architecture established wherever willing occurs.

*A note on scope.* The empirical sketches that follow — the brain as modal-modeling network, modular sensory architecture, the subconscious as accumulated modal terrain — are offered as structural identifications consistent with cognitive-neuroscience practice, not as load-bearing empirical premises of the structural argument. The load-bearing claim is the modal architecture itself; the empirical realizations name what that architecture looks like in the human case. Wherever willing occurs in other substrates, the same structural features must obtain, though their implementation will differ.

*The brain as modal-modeling network.* The brain is the organism's modal-modeling network. It does not merely represent what is actual. It models actuality as possibility-space: what can happen from here, what cannot happen from here, what must happen for another state to obtain, what blocks a line, what opens a line, what threatens continuation, what enables it, and which response-pathways remain available. At reflective depth that map can take propositional form: *if I do this, that may follow; if that follows, this future closes; if I wait, another line may open.* Beneath reflective depth the same operation is embodied, affective, spatial, temporal, and procedural. The organism maps condition, response, consequence, and constraint before it names any of them.

*Three modal dimensions of the map.* The map is structured by the same Triconditions that organize Nature itself (Time, Space, and Substance: T, S, and Φ). Temporal modal mapping registers sequence, delay, what must come before what, what is ripening, what is closing. Spatial modal mapping registers distinction, reach, separation, what blocks passage, what opens onto what. Substantial modal mapping registers persistence, identity, capacity, what holds together under change, what a thing can and cannot do given what it is. The dimensions are not chosen by the brain; they are the modal dimensions a living current must map to act at all.

*Modularity.* That modeling is modular. A subject does not build one undifferentiated map of everything at once. The work is distributed across specialized modules that map regions of possibility-space at different scales and through different channels. Each sense is a modal-mapping module rather than a passive sensor. Vision builds a navigable visual possibility-space rather than recording pixels — what is present, what is reachable, what blocks what, what is likely to move next, what is hidden but inferable. Hearing builds a directional, source-attributing acoustic possibility-space. Proprioception builds a possibility-space of available bodily motion. Memory, language, social recognition, threat-detection, and future-simulation are likewise modular: each maps a kind of modal structure the organism must navigate. Will and reasoning operate on the integrated field these modules produce, which is why damage to a module does not merely subtract data; it subtracts a region of livable possibility from the subject's world.

*Concepts, language, technology, institutions.* Concepts are portable modules of this kind. A concept like *door* is not a label for an image. It is a stable modal map: passable when open, blocking when closed, separating inside from outside, available through handle or push or key, changing what lines are live. Language ([§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10)) is the sharing of such modules between agents. Technology ([§8.11](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11)) is their externalization into the world. Institutions are modules for coordinating recurring modal problems across many subjects at once. Each is a structural extension of the same predicted architecture beyond the boundaries of any single brain.

*The subconscious as accumulated modal terrain.* The subconscious is the accumulated modal network operating beneath reflective attention. It is not a hidden second self but the stored terrain of prior condition-response-consequence pairings: habit, skill, aversion, trauma response, bodily anticipation, social recognition, procedural memory. Autopilot is not irrational in itself. It is the map running where the system does not reopen the whole field. Beneath even this stored terrain lies a faster layer that does not run through the field at all: the withdrawal of a hand from a hot surface is run by a protective reflex arc that fires before the field is consulted and before the act could be selected or refused, so that the body executes it *for* the current rather than through it. Such a movement is not a shallow exercise of will but the absence of will — directed, adaptive, and wholly involuntary, which is why it is felt as something that happened rather than something done. Will begins above both layers, where the current can delay, inspect, inhibit, or redirect the stored line before it becomes action — predicting a specific functional architecture in which prefrontal inhibition, working-memory holding, and conscious access selectively reopen subconscious channels for revision.

*Depth gradient across lineages.* The framework predicts that richer capacities for foresight, delay, learned revision, and counterfactual reasoning may correlate with more complex integrative cognitive systems. This is a graded hypothesis about agency, not a settled cross-species measure of free will or responsibility. The empirical record can inform this model but does not uniquely establish its three-axis architecture, modular theory, or account of conscious and subconscious control.

### 8.9.4 What is Confirmed {#sec-8-9-4}

*Premeditation and passion in criminal law.* The legal distinction between passion and premeditation tracks the same structure. A crime of passion is not innocent, but its modal depth is contracted toward reaction: provocation, panic, rage, fear, or bodily activation narrows the field and accelerates response. At the extreme, intense affect does not merely narrow the field but overrides the agent's access to it, so that the body discharges ahead of any selection the agent could have made — a partial return toward the involuntary reflex ([§8.9.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-3)), which is why provocation mitigates culpability rather than aggravating it: the agency premeditation exercises in full was, in the moment, partly displaced. Premeditation is more will-saturated because the agent had more distance: time to model the act, foresee consequence, inhibit drive, revise intention, abandon the line, or continue anyway. Criminal law has long tracked modal depth under other names. It punishes premeditation more severely because the agent participated more fully in keeping the harmful possibility live until it became actual. The differential sentencing across common-law jurisdictions (first-degree murder, second-degree murder, voluntary manslaughter, involuntary manslaughter) is not arbitrary: it is a centuries-old empirical calibration of culpability against modal depth, refined under adversarial pressure across millions of cases. Hart's (1968) analysis of mens rea, and the Anglo-American tradition more broadly (Moore 1997; Robinson 1997; Husak 2010), names the structural variable without naming it as such.

*Consent.* Consent depends on modal depth. Consent requires more than verbal selection: it requires a subject whose modal network is developed enough to understand what the option means — what is being asked, what consequences may follow, what alternatives exist, whether refusal is safe, whether power is asymmetrical, and what future self-states may be affected. A choice can be formally available while the agent lacks sufficient modal competence for the choice to count as consent. The relevant question is whether the will behind the word had enough mapped possibility to understand the act as a choice, not whether a word was spoken. Contemporary work in bioethics (Beauchamp and Childress 2019; Faden and Beauchamp 1986) and sexual-consent law converges on the same finding from clinical and legal directions: informed, voluntary, and competent consent are the three conditions, each tracking a dimension of modal depth (information = forward map, voluntariness = inhibition capacity, competence = accumulated map). Read through the two axes of free will ([§8.9.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-5)), consent is the exercise of will over one's own field: knowing what a decision makes possible — *if I do this, these outcomes; if I do that, those* — and weighing those outcomes oneself, with the latitude to act on the weighing. Its two failure modes follow directly. Deception and immaturity corrupt the field, so that the outcomes weighed are not the real ones — the lied-to and the child assent to a decision whose scope they cannot map. Coercion ordinarily leaves the field intact and removes the latitude, so that the outcomes are understood but cannot be freely acted on — the threatened assent to what they would otherwise refuse, though pressure severe enough to contract the field as well returns the case to the impairment analysis above. The child is the limiting case of the first: a real selection over a field too shallow to hold the decision, which is consent in form without consent in substance.

*Impairment.* Impairment cases show why the modal-depth test must remain general rather than scenario-bound. Intoxication, panic, coercive pressure, dissociation, developmental immaturity, and other contractions of the modal field can narrow the subject's capacity to understand the act as a choice. The principle is not that one external marker mechanically settles consent or blame. The principle is that consent requires enough modal depth for self-rule, and responsibility intensifies where one will knowingly uses another subject's contracted agency as the medium for its own end. Where impairment is shared, ambiguous, or symmetrical, the analysis cannot simply assign predatory asymmetry by formula; it must ask whether one subject's will actually governed, exploited, or overrode the other's. The framework therefore gives a general structural test, not an endless catalog of moral or legal scenarios. Forensic and clinical practice — from the *M'Naghten* rules forward through *Durham* and the Model Penal Code — has been refining versions of the same test across more than a century of case law.

*Developmental neuroscience.* The progressive maturation of prefrontal inhibitory capacity through adolescence and into the mid-twenties (Casey, Jones, and Hare 2008; Steinberg 2008; Giedd et al. 1999) confirms the predicted architecture from a third direction. The capacity to hold alternatives open, inhibit immediate response, and revise the map develops slowly across the lifespan of the human brain, and legal-moral practice has independently calibrated to it: minors are presumed to have contracted modal depth and are held to differentially weighted standards. The structural prediction — modal depth as a function of accumulated map plus current inhibitory capacity — and the developmental record converge.

*Pathology.* Damage to prefrontal cortex (Damasio 1994; Bechara et al. 1994), severe addiction (Volkow et al. 2016), and certain dissociative and impulse-control disorders all narrow the modal field in measurable ways, and the narrowing produces behavioral patterns the structural account predicts: contracted future modeling, weakened inhibition, line-locked responding, and impoverished alternative-holding. The phenomenology, the neuroscience, and the legal-clinical assessment converge on the same variable from independent directions.

*Decision neuroscience and predictive processing.* Computational accounts of action selection — model-based versus model-free reinforcement learning (Daw, Niv, and Dayan 2005), active-inference frameworks (Friston 2010; Hohwy 2013), and the role of prefrontal cortex in deliberate line-comparison versus habitual response (Miller and Cohen 2001) — describe the same gradient from a fourth direction. Model-free responding is the modal-mapping system running its accumulated lines without reopening the field; model-based deliberation is the system holding alternatives open, simulating consequences, and revising before action. The literature does not name the variable modal depth, but the variable it tracks is the same.

Criminal law, bioethics, forensic practice, developmental neuroscience, neuropsychology, and computational decision research all address capacities relevant to deliberation, control, and consent. Their constructs and purposes differ, and they do not independently confirm the book's modal-depth architecture. The framework offers one way of integrating these literatures, while the philosophical debates about free will and responsibility remain live.

### 8.9.5 What is Concluded {#sec-8-9-5}

*The reframing.* The dispute between libertarianism, compatibilism, and hard determinism has been organized for centuries around a single load-bearing question: does free will require exemption from prior causation, or is some form of causally embedded freedom sufficient? The structural account dissolves the question by relocating the variable. Freedom is neither metaphysical exemption nor any single compatibilist criterion (higher-order endorsement, reasons-responsiveness, sanity); it is the modal depth an agent achieves within the field that the modal pressures (T, S, Φ — see [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)) make available. Libertarianism named depth and called it exemption. Compatibilism named depth and called it the right kind of cause. Hard determinism noticed that exemption was unavailable and concluded freedom must therefore be illusory. Each tracked a real feature of the same architecture from an incomplete angle.

*Depth is necessary but not sufficient: fidelity and endorsement.* Modal depth names the space freedom requires but not the whole of its structure, and the cases that follow show why. A wanton — Frankfurt's (1971) agent who is moved by whichever first-order desire is strongest without caring which one moves them — can command an enormous field and still fail to be free, because nothing in the agent settles which mapped line counts as their own. The agent under volitional necessity runs the other way: Luther's *Here I stand, I can do no other* (Frankfurt 1982, 1988) has the field collapsed to a single option by the depth of what is cared about, and is not thereby less free but more. Depth points the wrong direction in both — the wanton has it without freedom, the resolute agent has freedom without it — which shows that freedom is the degree to which an act is governed by the valuation the agent identifies with, operating over a field that is both deep enough and uncorrupted.

This is the point at which Watson's regress must be stopped rather than relocated. Were the valuation the agent identifies with authoritative merely by being a higher-order desire — one more want ranked above the rest — the question would simply climb a level: what confers authority on that desire, and why not one higher still? The structural account does not rank desires at all. Identification, on the [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) result, is not a further-order preference the agent happens to hold but the operation by which the self-model is constituted — the recursion's identifying with some valuations and against others is the same operation by which it builds the I. A valuation the agent identifies with is authoritative not because it wins a contest among desires but because it is partly constitutive of who the agent is; there is no higher tribunal to appeal to, because the identifying is the self any appeal would be made to. This is the move that dissolves agent-causation earlier in the section — the agent is the structured recursion, not a substance behind it ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8), [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)) — applied to endorsement: the regress halts at the self-model, because the endorsement is not a desire the self has but the self the desires are had by.

The modal-mapping network must therefore meet several conditions, each of which fails recognizably. Its *depth* can be too shallow: an agent who does not know an option exists is not free with respect to it, however available it is in the world — the diner who never learns the kitchen will prepare a dish that is not on the printed card has exactly the freedom the card's depth allows and no more, which is why part of the relevant competence is knowing that one's field has edges and can be probed. Its *fidelity* can be compromised: a field that misrepresents what an act makes possible defeats freedom even where depth is intact, which is why honest disclosure expands freedom without adding any new act — the consumer who learns a product carries a lethal long-term risk gains freedom over the identical choice once the consequence-branch is installed, and why the law counts consent obtained by concealment or fraud as no free consent at all (the competence-and-consent variable [§8.9.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-4) tracks). Knowledge feeds the field directly at this point: since whatever is actual is possible, every fact an agent holds is already an entry in the modal field, and inference projects from those entries to the further possibilities they license — the precise sense in which knowledge ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) is a condition of will.

Corruption can also be internal rather than external: where the salience-weighting that decides which valuation governs is set so that it reliably under-serves the agent's endorsed priority — as in conditions of executive-function dysregulation such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder — the endorsed valuation can remain wholly intact and still lose, which marks the seam where a corrupted field shades into a defeated endorsement. Its *endorsement*, finally, can simply be overridden in the moment: judging one course best and being carried by the stronger immediate pull into another is the weakness of will the tradition has named since Aristotle and sharpened in Davidson (1970) — the episodic form of the wanton's standing failure. Beneath all three, will rides on a substrate it does not author. The thick will of this section is the thin directedness of drive ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)) brought under a field that is deep, faithful, and owned, and like all drive it stays embodied: a current can override a standing drive such as hunger by the valuation it endorses, but only to the limit the body itself permits. Freedom is depth, fidelity, and endorsement together, instantiated by a living current — none alone suffices, and the tradition's single-criterion accounts each seized one and mistook it for the whole.

These conditions concern the field and the agent's ownership of the act made over it; freedom needs one thing further, external to them all. It also requires *latitude* — the standing room to act on the selection once made — which coercion removes without touching depth, fidelity, or endorsement: the coerced agent can map the field truly, endorse the refusal, and still be made to act against it. Depth, fidelity, and endorsement settle whether a selection is genuinely the agent's; latitude settles whether the agent can enact what has genuinely been selected. So *modal freedom*, the whole of which freedom consists, resolves into two pillars — modal depth (the grasp) and latitude (the room to enact) — with fidelity and endorsement as the conditions under which the depth-side selection is truly the agent's own.

*Frankfurt cases reconsidered.* The proliferation of Frankfurt-style counterexamples in the late twentieth century revealed that something about responsibility was decoupled from metaphysical branching, but the literature could not say what. The structural account names it. What the cases preserve while removing external alternatives is internal modal depth: the agent's mapping network, the alternatives the network holds open at the time of action, and the agent's participation in which mapped line runs. Branching in the world matters less than branching in the map. The Frankfurt literature was right that responsibility survives the loss of external alternatives and could not specify why because it had no account of the modal-mapping variable.

*The Eden challenge revisited.* The reading developed in [§8.9.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-1) — that Eden subjects undeveloped will to morally decisive choice — does not depend on rejecting the classical endowment view's conceptual coherence; it depends on the structural-depth account being the correct read of what freedom is. If freedom is modal-mapping depth accumulated through encounter, no act of divine endowment can substitute for the encounter. A perfectly oriented will with no developed modal terrain has the form of a will and lacks the substance the form requires. The endowment view answers a structural-depth requirement with a metaphysical decree, and the decree cannot do what the depth would. What the classical reading offers as a higher-order resolution is on the structural reading a relocation of the problem one register deeper.

*The divine-will dilemma revisited.* The dilemma at the end of [§8.9.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9-1) — *actus purus* has no modal depth, maximal modal depth gives Nature — admits no escape that preserves the classical view of divine will as both transcendent of structure and genuinely will-shaped. Stump's (2003) refinement secures simplicity at the cost of the modal architecture *will* names; alternative refinements that secure the modal architecture surrender the transcendence. The dilemma is structural, not rhetorical. Will is what modal depth makes available within Nature, not what stands outside it.

*The inversion at the level of will.* What the inversion of greatness names at the level of consciousness ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)) returns at the level of will. The freedom traditionally located above Nature — exempt from causation, prior to creation, transcendent of structure — is what modal depth within Nature looks like at sufficient recursion. The motion is again inward, not upward. Free will is not what we have despite being natural creatures. It is what being a sufficiently deep natural creature consists in.

*Responsibility, asymmetry, and moral practice.* The structural account does not collapse responsibility into determinism. Two agents facing the same external option may bring different modal maps to it, and the moral practice that tracks responsibility — praise, blame, punishment, gratitude, resentment, forgiveness — calibrates against those maps. Strawson's (1962) reactive-attitudes account, the Hart-Honoré tradition in legal philosophy, and the bioethical apparatus of competence and consent are all calibrations of the same variable. The framework explains why the calibrations work without committing to libertarian sourcehood and without surrendering moral practice to hard-determinist deflation.

The framework models will as action mediated by a representation of alternatives, accumulated experience, valuation, and practical latitude. It proposes that richer modal mapping supports more reflective forms of agency. This does not dissolve the standing debate between libertarian, compatibilist, and hard-determinist accounts; it supplies one compatibilist-leaning framework for interpreting it. The relation between reasoning, knowledge, valuation, will, and responsibility remains a substantive philosophical question. The medium through which such an agent makes itself legible to others is taken up at [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10).

## 8.10 Language {#sec-8-10}

Language is how one mind gets a piece of what is inside it across to another. A shared word is really a shared chunk of mental map: when two people are trained to the same word, they load roughly the same patch of 'how things are and could be.' Understanding does not require that your version be identical to mine, only close enough that we can coordinate, predict, and go on together. This is why teaching, writing, and specialist jargon all work: each installs a region of one person's map in another. And the gap between separate minds is not a flaw language has to defeat; it is the very thing language exists to cross: there has to be a gap for anything to be said across it.

::: {.identification}
**Language** · *Identification*

Language is the technology of shared interiority: the structured practice by which one mind externalizes a region of its modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) (a model, a claim, a refusal, a promise) into another mind's, across the interval that separates self-modeling minds. A shared word is a shared region of map; understanding is the sufficient reproduction of one field's structure in another, never identical, but enough to coordinate. The interval is not a barrier to that transfer but its condition: there must be a gap for a claim to cross.
*Status: an identity claim on the [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) self-modeling structure (Principle 5), defended by fit, not a stipulative definition and not a fresh derivation from the proof.*


:::

A will acting through its modal field ([§8.9](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9)) eventually has to make the field legible to other actors. Language is the first technology of that making. The central question is not how sound, gesture, posture, or marks become meaningful, but how the structural content of one mind's model can be reliably transferred (imperfectly but systematically) into another's.

Language carries the claim while art ([§8.13](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-13)) carries the feel. Each depends on T, S, and Φ, requires self-modeling at both ends, and crosses the same interval under the same conditions. What distinguishes them is the content each is structured to carry, and the fact that each can carry what the other cannot. Language reaches as far as propositions reach. Beyond that boundary, the work belongs to art.

What language transfers, mechanically, is regions of the speaker's modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) into the hearer's. A shared vocabulary is a shared region of map: every speaker trained to a word has the same chunk of possibility space loaded under the same label. Jargon is what compressed labels look like for densely-mapped specialist regions: a single technical term invokes a region of modal field that took a discipline decades to lay down, available now in one syllable for anyone who has been trained into the region. This is why teaching is modal-representation installation, why documentation freezes a region for asynchronous transfer, and why a discipline's evolution toward shared vocabulary is, structurally, the formation of a consensus map across the bodies who practice it. The interval language crosses is the interval between maps; the fact that the same words can install nearly the same regions across millions of bodies is what makes coordinated knowledge possible at all.

*Communication's expressive and referential functions.* Communication runs on a continuum from pure expressive function (direct externalization of the sender's drive-state) to referential function: externalization of modeled objects in the sender's modal field, displaced from the immediate context. A cat backed into a corner rearing itself, a dog snarling, a bird's alarm call, a baby's cry, a wince at unexpected news: these are expressive; they make the sender's drive-state public so other beings can register and respond. Symbolic language carries the expressive function all the way up; "stop that" is functionally a snarl with words, "I love you" is functionally a purr with grammar, and a great deal of everyday speech is more articulated drive-state externalization than referential transmission. What symbolic language adds at sufficient depth is referential function: the capacity to externalize content that *is not* the sender's current drive-state, referents displaced from the here-and-now, other times, other places, hypothetical states, abstract types, counterfactual branches, the absent friend, last week's meeting, next year's plan, the square root of two. A cat cannot rear at the threat that was here yesterday or at the threat its modal field is projecting forward; the cat's body has no apparatus for that displacement. The recursion that performs displacement is the same modal-field machinery [§8.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-4) named in its account of reasoning, applied here to externalize modal-field content rather than to operate on it internally. Referential function does not replace expressive function (almost all human utterance carries both), but it is the structural addition that emerges as the depth gradient deepens, gradually rather than at a sharp break. Vervet predator-calls have a thin form of reference (type-of-predator, not just here's-something-bad). Bee waggle dances have thin displacement (food at a location not currently visible). Toddler pointing at an absent ball is fuller displacement. Adult abstract reference is the upper end. The [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10) section's specific work is on the deep-form referential capacity; its expressive function remains continuous with the signaling that runs all the way down the depth gradient.

Two self-modeling configurations persist, occupy genuinely different positions, and remain in causal exchange across the interval between them. Distinction, persistence, succession (Spatiality, Physicality, Temporality) are not features the linguistic situation happens to require. They are what propositional transmission consists in. Without distinct positions, there is no separation for a claim to cross. Without persistence, there is no speaker whose claim remains the same claim a hearer can take up. Without succession, there is no before-and-after to the act of saying or the act of being understood. A proposition is a structure that can survive the journey between minds because the journey passes through the same three conditions every other concrete transition passes through. The exchange can hold content mutually across the interval: each speaker contributes to what the other can take up, rather than merely passing an asymmetric signal. Theorem 9 (Modal Convergence, [§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) remains the narrower epistemic theorem of collectively held knowledge; language is one means by which such knowledge can be formed and transmitted, not an automatic application of the theorem.

This relocates the standing positions in philosophy of language. Saussure's conventional signs, Chomsky's generative competence, Wittgenstein's meaning as use, Frege's sense and reference, Kripke's rigid designation, and Davidson's truth-conditional semantics were each tracking real features of how minds reach each other through propositional form. What the structural account corrects is the assumption common to all of them: that language is a system separable from the structure it describes, a layer of signs or rules or uses that coordinates with reality through some external relation. Language is not separable. Its structure is the structure it carries because there is no other structure for it to carry, and what each tradition was tracking is what propositional transmission looks like from the angle that tradition approached. That there is a mind-independent structure for language to carry, rather than a scheme the mind lays over a formless content, is the realism defended once at [§8.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-4).

The charitable readings sharpen the point. Wittgenstein (1953) is right that meaning is bound to use: a proposition that does not function in the practice of any community of speakers does not transmit, because there are no shared procedures by which a hearer can recover its content. Kripke (1980) is right that names refer through causal-historical chains rather than through descriptions speakers can articulate, because reference must survive disagreement and error about what is being referred to. Davidson (1967, 1973) is right that the systematic compositionality of truth-conditions is what makes infinite production from finite resources possible: recursive grammar is the structural feature that lets propositions of arbitrary complexity transmit without each one requiring a new convention. Quine (1960) is right that translation underdetermines: no observable behavior fully fixes the model in another speaker's mind; the gap between minds is real, and what closes it sufficiently is alignment under shared conditions rather than identity of internal representation. Chomsky (1965, 1986) is right that linguistic competence requires the recursive structure linguistics describes, because that recursion is what allows propositions to embed propositions: the structural condition for any speaker to articulate a thought *about* what another speaker has said. Each position locates one face of the same structural fact: a configuration capable of modeling itself, modeling another, and modeling what passes between them must coordinate across distinct positions, across time, and across whatever sustains the exchange. Where the literature has competed over which face is fundamental, the structural account reads them as views of one transmission from different angles.

*The private-language pressure.* One charitable credit is not yet an answer to Wittgenstein's private-language challenge, and the section's own vocabulary is what stands exposed to it.
