If "shared interiority" named a private inner sample each speaker checks a word against, the private-language argument (Wittgenstein 1953, §§243–315) would apply in full: nothing could count as using the label correctly, and "the same chunk of possibility space under the same label" would carry exactly the confusion the argument diagnoses. The concession is total: there is no private sample. The interior [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) derives is not an object held up against a word but a self-modeling process whose contents are individuated by what they let a configuration do: coordinate, correct, predict, and go on. So the criteria for two speakers having loaded the same region are public, where Wittgenstein placed them: convergence under shared conditions and continued success in use, not an inward comparison no one could check. Rule-following and forms of life are then not pressures the account must absorb from outside; they name the same fact from the side of practice: a region of modal field counts as shared when, and only when, the practice of using it holds up across the interval. Family resemblance operates by the same standard: concept boundaries are fixed by overlapping use rather than shared essence, so whether a modal-map region coheres is judged by whether use holds together, not by whether a common property subtends it. The structural account does not posit an inside the criteria fail to reach. It locates the inside as the publicly-criterioned thing Wittgenstein's own argument requires.

*A test case: acquaintance without articulation.* Consider a child raised in total isolation from language, encountering water directly, with no interlocutor and no word ever offered. Such a child registers the wet/dry distinction: the same thermal-and-mechanical inference apparatus that produces the sensation in any human body runs whether or not a word exists for its output, and a dog or a fish, with no language at all, plainly responds differently to being wet and being dry. What the isolated child lacks is not the sensation but the shared criterion: a public practice of using a label reliably enough that another speaker could correct a misuse. This is a thin registration, in the depth-gradient sense running through this chapter: a real discrimination, held by the system, that has not yet been articulated, named, or folded into a practice checkable by anyone else. The private-language argument's target was never the existence of that thin registration; it was the idea of a private sample a word could be privately checked against. The isolated child has the registration and no word; what would be incoherent is a claim to have privately named it in a sense no one, including a later-taught version of the same child, could ever get right or wrong. Helen Keller's own account of the moment at the water pump makes the transition vivid: the sensation of water over her hand was already fully present long before language, and what broke open at the pump was not a new feeling but the discovery that the finger-spelled pattern named the thing she had been feeling all along — the folding of a thin registration into the public, checkable practice a word requires.

Language has structure because that is what language describes. The claim is about the deep conditions of propositional transmission (reference, predication, recursion across an interval), not about surface grammars, lexicons, idioms, or inflectional systems, which are shaped by historical contingencies the structural account does not track. The conditions any language must meet to carry propositions across the interval between speakers are the same conditions a self-modeling being must meet to register anything at all. If consciousness is a self-modeling process registering itself from inside, and language is the practice by which that self-registration is articulated and shared, then the structure of language is the process's own logical form, made communicable. The proof required all three roles to state itself; language requires the same three to carry any statement at all. The derivation and linguistic practice arrived at the same grammar. Every sentence that successfully says anything (in any language, by any species capable of uttering one) runs on the same structural conditions the argument has named, from whatever position within them the speaker happens to occupy.

The depth-gradient framing applies to language as it does to other registers. Many species transmit information via signals: pheromone trails (ants), referential alarm calls (vervets; Seyfarth, Cheney, and Marler 1980), waggle dances (bees), individual signature whistles (dolphins), prairie-dog calls apparently encoding predator type, size, and color (Slobodchikoff 2002). These are shallow forms of language: signaling without recursive grammar, displacement, or full theory-of-mind dependence. Full propositional language with recursive embedding emerges most fully in humans, who have the recursive depth required to model others as modelers and the symbolic capacity to externalize that modeling. The shallow forms exist below the self-aware threshold the chapter's opening names; the deep form requires it.

*Gossip as a primary social use of language.* Among the deep-form referential uses of language, gossip (talking-about-other-people, especially people in proximity, especially regarding their conduct) has structural prominence. Dunbar's *Grooming, Gossip, and the Evolution of Language* (1996) argued that the small-group social-information-sharing function predates and underwrites the more abstract referential uses humans developed; the 150-person Dunbar number is the social-information-management scale where gossip operates natively. Read in the modal-field vocabulary, gossip is *distributed modal-field maintenance* for a social network. It delivers actualities about specific people in the listener's proximity (what they did, how they responded, what they value) at higher proximity-weighting than distant or fictional cases, because the modal apparatus treats nearby actualities as more applicable to the body's own field than far ones. It maps consequences as well as actualities: shame, ostracism, reputational damage, social cost (the visible consequences of conduct gossip names) are what make gossip an effective norm-enforcement mechanism. It is also a distributed predator-detection system: a body that has heard the right gossip can recognize an exploitative neighbor, a manipulator, or an untrustworthy partner without being burned individually. Reputation, the structure gossip lays down, is itself a feature of the social modal field (everyone's prediction of how a given person is likely to behave), and gossip is the substrate by which that structure is built and updated. This is one of the reasons gossip is reflexively pleasurable across cultures: the modal apparatus is being fed exactly what it is hungry for, in a domain it cares about deeply (immediate social possibility), at evidential weight high enough to be useful. Reality TV, true crime, celebrity coverage, and social-media commentary are extensions of the same operation at scale, mediated by technologies that broaden the proximity-circle the apparatus treats as relevant; the underlying drive is the modal-field-expansion drive [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) names, here flowing through the referential function of language at the social register where Dunbar located its evolutionary purpose. Beyond the evolutionary register Dunbar names, gossip is also where social categories are constituted and enforced: reputations, roles, and standings are the ameliorative kinds of [§8.10.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-1) maintained in distributed talk, and to gossip about how someone occupied a role is to keep updating the social modal field that says what the role demands.

*Pronouns and the register collision.* A pronoun is the most compressed referential device a language has for a person: in a single syllable it installs, in the hearer's modal field, a minimal re-identifiable position for the referent — a shared region of map at its smallest. In gendered languages that installation bundles a social-category assignment into the act of referring, which is why the pronoun becomes a site of dispute out of all proportion to its size: three registers meet in one word. Using a pronoun is a referential-and-social-category act ([§8.10.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-1)); the identity it points at is a self-model position ([§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)); the body it may or may not track is the substrate ([§8.6](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6)). Much of the contemporary argument is a register collision — parties who take the pronoun to report a substrate fact, parties who take it to register a self-model position, and parties who take it to maintain an ameliorative social kind are not contradicting one another about a single thing but speaking across three. What the structural account settles is narrow and firm: whom the pronoun refers to is a subject whose standing is fixed at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) by the capacity for experience, not by category-membership, so the referring-verdict — that there is a someone here, owed what any subject is owed — is invariant across the readings. What it does not settle is the contested etiquette and policy specifics of who is owed which term under which conditions; that adjudication is not the structural account's to make. The deeper point answers the natural puzzle of why anything has a pronoun at all: reference across the interval requires re-identifiable positions, since distinction, persistence, and succession are what let a claim about a someone survive the trip between minds, and a pronoun is the minimal such re-identifier. In that sense a pronoun is structural. Its gender-marking is not — gendered pronouns are surface grammar, among the historical contingencies this section has already set aside as untracked by the structural claim — but contingent at the grammatical layer is not trivial at the personal layer: the self-model position a pronoun references ([§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5)) is real and consequential even where the grammatical gender-slot that carries it is arbitrary. The deep fact, that reference needs a re-identifiable position, is invariant; the gendered packaging of that position is contingent. Much of the heat around pronouns, like the older habit of assigning the ungendered a default gendered term, is a contingent grammatical slot being mistaken for a substrate verdict.

*In-group vocabulary and modal-field narrowing.* Not every installation a shared vocabulary performs is expansive. A term can install a region of social possibility by closing a hearer's field rather than opening it: labeling one's own group *the elect*, *the remnant*, or *the light of the world* installs a favorable self-location that need not be argued for each time it is invoked, and labeling disagreement *worldliness*, *hardness of heart*, or *suppression of the truth* installs an unfavorable location for the response before its content is examined. Maxims that foreclose a line of inference before it opens — *God works in mysterious ways*, *who are we to question*, *just have faith* — do compressed referential work the way a pronoun does at smaller scale, loaded once and then spent without argument on every later occasion. What is distinctive about this class is the direction of the installation: most vocabulary opens a region of the hearer's field for use, the way jargon makes a decade of a discipline's mapping available in one syllable; this class installs a boundary against further mapping, marking a region closed rather than making one available. The pattern is not specific to any one tradition or doctrine. Structurally identical devices recur across independent religious and political traditions wherever a group's boundary needs maintaining at lower cost than argument supplies, which is what makes the convergence a corroboration rather than an argument in its own right: it is what this section's account of language predicts language will be recruited to do wherever groups form and hold boundaries, not a separate case against whichever group happens to be doing it.

Successful communication is not merely the transfer of information; it is the convergence of two minds' models on a shared claim about Nature they both inhabit. The interval between speakers is not a barrier to that convergence but its condition: there must be a gap for a claim to cross. Understanding is the confirmation that the structural content of one model has been reproduced in another, not identically, but sufficiently for coordination. That reproducibility is what the structural account of language predicts and what the experience of being understood reports.

*A note on scope.* This identification (language as the structured practice by which propositional content crosses the interval between self-modeling persons) is offered as a structural account of what language is, not as a strict derivation from the proof of Chapters 1–2. The proof establishes the necessary structural conditions T, S, and Φ; the claim that those conditions are what propositional transmission consists in at the depth a self-modeling configuration reaches is an identification claim, in the sense flagged at the head of Chapter 8. That a reader might accept the proof while reading the linguistic case differently (assigning more weight to convention, to use, to neural architecture, or to social practice) leaves nothing earlier disturbed; the identification carries weight just to the degree it fits the phenomenon.

### 8.10.1 What is Disputed {#sec-8-10-1}

The literature on language is among the most technical in twentieth-century philosophy and among the most active in the cognitive sciences. The framework engages the principal positions by name; each is taken up again at [§8.10.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-5) once the structural account is in view.

*Saussurean structuralism.* Saussure's (1916) *Cours de linguistique générale* established the modern study of language with the distinction between *langue* and *parole*, the arbitrariness of the sign, and the structural relations among signs as the locus of linguistic meaning. The position has organized continental linguistics and semiotics for a century. The framework reads Saussure as correctly identifying that language is a system rather than a list, while supplying the deeper claim: the system has the structure it has because it tracks the structure of what language is about, with arbitrariness operating at the surface and structural fit operating beneath.

*Chomskyan generativism.* Chomsky (1957, 1965, 1986, 1995) developed the generativist tradition on which linguistic competence requires an innate language faculty supplying universal grammatical structure. The position has been refined through government-and-binding theory, the minimalist program, and the broader cognitive-linguistic enterprise; it has been challenged by usage-based and construction-grammar approaches (Tomasello 2003; Goldberg 2006). The framework reads Chomsky as correctly identifying that linguistic competence requires recursive structure, while supplying the deeper claim: the recursive structure is what propositional transmission requires for embedding propositions within propositions, not a species-specific endowment hovering autonomous from what language is for.

*Wittgensteinian meaning-as-use.* Wittgenstein's (1953) *Philosophical Investigations* developed the position that meaning is constituted by the use of words in shared practices, with rule-following grounded in form-of-life rather than in private mental content. The position has been refined through Kripkenstein (Kripke 1982), Wright (1980), and the broader use-theoretic tradition. The framework reads Wittgenstein as correctly identifying that meaning is bound to use — a proposition that does not function in the practice of any community of speakers does not transmit — while supplying the deeper claim: the practices succeed in transmission because they coordinate on the structural conditions transmission requires. The later work's distinctive moves bear directly on the framework's own vocabulary. Language-games and forms of life locate meaning in patterned shared activity rather than in inner ostension; family resemblance denies that a general term needs a common essence to function; and the rule-following considerations deny that meaning is fixed by any private act of interpretation. The framework takes these as constraints it must meet, not positions it must defeat: a shared region of modal field counts as shared only where there is a public practice of correction — speakers who can be brought back into line when they use a term wrongly — which is what use in a form of life supplies and what a private inner sample could not. This criterial pressure is turned back on the framework's own terms at [§8.10.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-5).

*Frege and the sense-reference distinction.* Frege (1892) distinguished sense from reference and located meaning in a third realm of abstract objects. The position has been refined through Russell, Carnap, and contemporary semantics. The framework reads Frege as correctly identifying that propositional content has both a referential and a presentational aspect, while supplying the deeper claim: the sense-reference structure is what propositional content has when it carries a claim about structure to another mind, with the abstract-objects metaphysics dispensable.

*Kripke and direct reference.* Kripke (1980) *Naming and Necessity* developed the direct-reference tradition on which names refer through causal-historical chains rather than through descriptions speakers can articulate. The position has been refined and contested across forty years (Soames 2002; Kaplan 1989; Stalnaker 1997). The framework reads Kripke as correctly identifying that reference must survive disagreement and error about what is being referred to, while supplying the structural reading: causal-historical chains succeed in transmitting reference because they preserve the structural connection between the speaker using the name and the person or object the name picks out.

*Davidsonian truth-conditional semantics.* Davidson (1967, 1973, 1984) developed the program of treating semantics as the specification of truth-conditions, with compositionality as the structural feature that makes infinite production from finite resources possible. The framework reads Davidson as correctly identifying that systematic compositionality is what makes propositional language possible at scale, while supplying the structural reading: compositionality works because the medium itself supports the embedding of structure within structure. Davidson's (1974) sharpest objection, though, cuts toward this framework rather than away from it. In *On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme* he argued that the picture of a conceptual scheme that organizes, fits, or carves an uninterpreted reality — what he called a third dogma of empiricism — is unintelligible, since there is no standpoint outside both language and world from which scheme and content could be lined up and checked against each other. A framework that speaks of a Reality all description answers to, and of T, S, and Φ as what carves it, is exactly the kind of view that objection targets. The framework reads Davidson here as correctly identifying that any scheme-against-content dualism is hopeless, and meets the charge not by defending such a dualism but by denying it has one — the reply taken up at [§8.10.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-5).

*Quinean indeterminacy.* Quine (1960) argued that translation is underdetermined: no observable behavior fully fixes the model in another speaker's mind. The position has been refined and contested across decades (Davidson 1973; Soames 1989). The framework reads Quine as correctly identifying that the gap between minds is real, while supplying the structural reading: what closes the gap sufficiently is alignment under shared conditions rather than identity of internal representation, with translation succeeding to the extent the structural features align.

*Searle's Chinese Room and the symbol-grounding problem.* Searle (1980) argued that symbol manipulation is not understanding: a system implementing a syntactic program does not thereby grasp the semantic content the symbols are about. The position has been refined and contested across decades (the systems reply, the robot reply, Searle 1984). The framework reads Searle as correctly identifying that the propositional transmission requires something that mere syntactic manipulation does not supply, while supplying the structural reading: that something is the recursive self-modeling that runs on both ends of the transmission, with the structure of the proposition mapping onto structure on each end.

*Large language models.* The recent emergence of LLMs (OpenAI's GPT family; Anthropic's Claude; Google's Gemini) has reorganized debates about whether and how computational systems engage in language. Disputes are live: some hold LLMs demonstrate that language can be mastered without semantic understanding (Bender et al. 2021); others argue LLMs may have rudimentary forms of understanding (Bowman 2023). The framework reads LLMs as engaging in a structurally interesting subset of linguistic activity: they manipulate the surface structure of language with substantial success and they instantiate parts of the recursive structure transmission requires, while what they share with self-modeling mind-to-mind transmission remains an open empirical and conceptual question.

*Whorfian relativity.* The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis — that language shapes thought — has been refined through decades of cross-linguistic cognitive research (Lucy 1992; Levinson 2003; Boroditsky 2011). The empirical record shows real but generally moderate language-thought interactions. The framework reads the moderate Whorfian results as picking up real conceptual-elaboration effects, while denying the strong-Whorfian claim that language constitutes thought: the underlying registration runs whether or not specific languages are imposed on it.

*Haslanger and the constitutive dimension of social kinds.* Haslanger (2000, 2012) developed the ameliorative-analysis project: rather than asking what our concepts *do* mean or what their referents *naturally* are, it asks what a concept *should* mean given the legitimate purposes it serves, and argues that for social categories — gender, race, role — language partly constitutes which categories are practically available rather than merely labeling kinds fixed independently of it. The framework places this between the Whorfian and conventionalist poles it has already located: stronger than moderate Whorfian content-effects, since social kinds are partly brought into and held in existence by the classifying practice; weaker than constitution of thought as such, since reference and predication run whether or not any particular social vocabulary is imposed. Read in modal-field terms, an ameliorative category is an exterior modal map maintained across a community: classifying a person under it installs a region of social possibility — what is expected, permitted, withheld, or owed — in every speaker trained to the term. This is the social-ontology work the [§8.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-5) account of relational identity forward-points to, received here where social categories are actually built and policed.

*Brandom, Lewis, and the social-pragmatic tradition.* Brandom (1994) developed an inferentialist account on which meaning is constituted by the role expressions play in giving and asking for reasons, and — extending the line that runs from Sellars — a modal expressivism on which modal vocabulary does not describe a special class of facts but makes explicit the material-inferential commitments already implicit in ordinary concept-use. Lewis (1969) developed a convention-based account on which language is coordinated through community-level conventions. The framework reads both as picking up real social-coordinative features of language; whether the inferential and expressivist reading displaces the structural conditions or instead makes them explicit is the sharpest question this tradition puts to the account, and it is taken up directly at [§8.10.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-5) rather than settled by fiat here.

The literature on language divides over Saussurean structuralism, Chomskyan generativism, Wittgensteinian use-theory, Fregean sense-reference, Kripkean direct reference, Davidsonian truth-conditional semantics, Quinean indeterminacy, Searle's symbol-grounding problem, the status of LLMs, Whorfian relativity, and inferentialist and conventionalist accounts. The framework commits to specific answers on each; they are taken up again at [§8.10.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-5) after the structural account is in view.

### 8.10.2 What is Required {#sec-8-10-2}

*Propositional transmission across the interval between minds.* Language transmits propositional content from one self-aware person to another across the interval that separates them. Any account must explain how the structural content of one mind's model can be reliably transferred — imperfectly but systematically — into another's. The structural requirement is that the account derive the conditions of transmission from the structure of what is being transmitted (propositional content) and what is doing the transmitting (self-aware beings in a shared medium).

*The three structural conditions.* Distinct positions, persistent reference-bearing entities, and successive utterance and uptake — Space, Substance, and Time — are not features the linguistic situation happens to require. They are what propositional transmission consists in. Any account must accommodate the three or supply an argument for why some can be dispensed with. The structural requirement is that the account derive the necessity of each: without distinct positions, no interval for a claim to cross; without persistent reference-bearing entities, no speaker or hearer remaining the same across the utterance; without succession, no before-and-after to the act of saying or being understood.

*Reference and predication minimum.* Any proposition combines reference (picking out what is being talked about) with predication (saying something about it). Any account must accommodate the minimum rather than reducing language to reference or to predication alone. The structural requirement is that the account treat the two as the irreducible structural pair propositional content consists in, with reference relations to entities and predication ascribing structure to them.

*Recursive compositionality.* Propositional language must support recursive embedding — propositions about propositions, claims about claims, the indefinite extension Frege and Davidson identified. Any account must accommodate the recursion rather than restricting language to flat predication. The structural requirement is that the account derive compositionality from the medium's support for structure-within-structure, with recursion as what allows propositions of arbitrary complexity to transmit without each requiring a new convention.

*Convention without arbitrariness all the way down.* Saussure correctly identified that the relation between specific signs and their referents is conventional at the surface. Any account must accommodate the surface conventionality while explaining what is *not* conventional. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish what is conventional (which sounds or marks carry which meanings) from what is not (the structural conditions any language must meet to carry propositions across the interval between speakers).

*Practice and form-of-life.* Wittgenstein correctly identified that meaning is bound to use in shared practices. Any account must accommodate that dependence without reducing meaning to use. It must preserve what use does — coordinates a practice, calibrates speakers’ uptake, and supports rule-following — while explaining what use is for: tracking what is the case so that people can communicate successfully.

*Connection to consciousness, self-modeling, and meaning.* Language operates on what awareness ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)), self-modeling ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)), and meaning ([§8.8](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-8)) supply. Any account must connect language to these earlier capacities rather than treating it as autonomous. Language grows from what self-aware beings need to do when they share a world and reach one another through propositions.

*Depth-graded distribution.* Shallow forms of signaling — pheromone trails, alarm calls, signature whistles, waggle dances — run at depths well below recursive grammar. Full propositional language with recursive embedding requires the self-aware threshold [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) names. Any account must accommodate the gradient rather than treating language as one categorically unified phenomenon. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish what runs at each depth, with signaling widespread, partial propositional structure available in some non-human lineages, and full recursive propositional language emerging most fully in humans.

*Substrate-independence at the structural level.* As with the other registers, the activity of propositional transmission can in principle be realized in different substrates. The recent emergence of LLMs presses the question concretely. Any account must distinguish what is substrate-essential from what is substrate-independent. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish the recursive structure (substrate-independent) from the self-modeling that anchors transmission to a vantage (currently realized only in biological minds, with the structural status of LLMs an open question the account makes legible without prejudging).

*Surface-vs-deep distinction.* The structural conditions any language must meet to carry propositions are not the same as the surface grammars, lexicons, and inflectional systems of specific languages. Any account must distinguish them rather than treating linguistic surface as constitutive. The structural requirement is that the account preserve the surface-deep distinction, with the conditions deep and the specific instantiations contingent.

Taken together these requirements set out the explanatory program the framework [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10) defends: transmission, reference and predication, compositionality, convention, shared practice, links to cognition, depth variation, substrate questions, and surface/deep distinctions. They are not neutral constraints on every theory of language. In particular, whether propositional content has the proposed structural minimum, whether non-human communication is propositional, and whether language is substrate independent remain contested. The framework argues for this package rather than treating it as established.

### 8.10.3 What is Predicted {#sec-8-10-3}

Self-modeling configurations that share a world must coordinate about what is the case. Where food is. Whether a partner is reliable. What threatens the group. What happened yesterday, what will likely happen tomorrow, what another mind is thinking. The content at stake is *propositional*: it has truth conditions, it can be confirmed or disconfirmed, and it persists across speakers such that those who were not there to witness what the proposition reports can still inherit it.

The structural account proposes that coordinated self-modeling systems may develop richer communication systems, including propositional transmission under some conditions. This is not a theorem that self-modeling and coordination always yield language, or that no other forms of communication can support coordination. The following features are proposed conditions for the book's model of propositional transmission, not universal predictions for every possible communicating system.

It must have *distinguishable signs*. Different meanings must be carried by different signals, because one signal carrying every meaning would carry no meaning at all. Distinction is Spatiality: signals must occupy different positions in the space of possible signals.

It must have *sequential ordering*. Meaning must unfold across a before and after, because simultaneous delivery of all signs is indistinguishable from silence. Order is Temporality: which sign comes first, second, third affects what is said.

It must have *causal transmission*. The signal must move from speaker to receiver through something that carries it without dissolving it. Transmission is Physicality: something persists from utterance to reception, or no reception occurs.

These three features are central to the framework's analysis of transmission, but they do not by themselves settle whether a system carries propositional content. Communicative systems can use sound, sign, gesture, chemical signal, or electrical pulse, and the status of bees, whales, non-human animals, and artificial systems as propositional communicators remains contested. The structural account offers a model of what would make transmission proposition-like; it does not resolve every empirical classification. The [§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6) cycle argument extends the reach conditionally: T, S, and Φ recur wherever the universe iterates, so wherever recurrence produces coordination-capable life under the relevant social and ecological pressures, propositional transmission will have to develop on the same three structural axes.

Grammar recapitulates the structure at the level of parts of speech. Nouns name what persists at a position — Physicality at Spatiality. Verbs name transitions — the motion of Temporality. Prepositions and case markers name the relations between positions — Spatiality and Temporality made explicit. Adjectives and adverbs modify what the noun and verb pick out. Every natural language ever documented has the category distinctions that map onto the structural conditions, because a language lacking those distinctions could not carry the content those conditions make possible.

Propositional content has two components the grammar of every natural language distinguishes. Both are needed; neither alone makes a proposition.

The first is *reference*. A proposition must point to what it is about. Nouns, pronouns, proper names, demonstratives, and definite descriptions all do reference: they identify an entity persisting in Spatiality that the claim is to be made *about*. Without reference, a predicate floats free and says nothing, because there is nothing for it to be true or false of.

The second is *predication*. A proposition must say something about what it refers to. Verbs, adjectives, and predicate constructions all do predication: they ascribe a feature, an action, a relation, a state. Without predication, a referring term is a label, not a claim. *The sky* says nothing. *Is blue* says nothing. *The sky is blue* is a proposition, because reference has been joined to predication and the joint construction now has truth conditions.

A proposition is the minimum unit of propositional content because it is the minimum combination of reference and predication that has truth conditions. Anything less cannot be true or false. Anything more is built out of propositions. This is not an incidental feature of how language happens to work. It is what propositional content structurally is, and any system that carries propositional content must have it.

The same structural requirement explains a cross-linguistic fact otherwise puzzling. No known human language lacks the noun/verb distinction, despite enormous variation in morphology, phonology, and surface syntax. Evans and Levinson (2009) argue that many alleged linguistic universals are softer than once claimed; the reference/predication distinction survives their scrutiny because it is not a contingent universal but what having propositional content consists in. Languages differ wildly in how they mark the distinction, in what else they encode, in how rigidly parts of speech are separated. But a language without any way to refer and any way to predicate could not carry propositions, and would not be a language.

Reference has one further structural feature every language must instantiate: it must include terms that point back to the occasion of utterance itself. The speaker, the hearer, the present moment, the shared surrounding space are not separately nameable the way ordinary referents are — they are where the utterance is coming from and going to, not what it is about. Deictic or indexical terms (*I*, *you*, *here*, *now*, *this*, *that*) fill this role, anchoring the transmission to the specific positions the two parties occupy. Without deictic reference, propositions could be transmitted but could not hook onto the occasion that produced them; with it, the abstract reference-predication system becomes usable by speakers and hearers at particular positions in T and S. Every natural language has a deictic system because every language is used by speakers and hearers who must refer back to themselves, each other, and the situation they share in order for propositions to land at all (Peirce 1931–1958; Bühler 1934; Kaplan 1989; Levinson 2004).

A simple case shows what deictic reference does by showing what fails when it cannot land. Imagine a slip of paper found decades later, reading *Meet me here tomorrow at noon.* The proposition is grammatically complete and lexically unambiguous; reference and predication are both performed. Yet the note as found cannot tell anyone what it once told its addressee — which speaker is *me*, which place is *here*, which day was *tomorrow*. Spoken face-to-face, the same words land effortlessly because the speaker, the location, and the day are all present at the occasion of saying. Deictic reference is what lets a proposition ride on the structural specificity of the T–S position the utterance occupies; strip the occasion away and the proposition keeps its form but loses its grip.

*A note on scope.* The three structural features predicted here — distinguishable signs, sequential ordering, causal transmission — together with the reference/predication minimum and the deictic anchor follow from what propositional transmission consists in given T, S, and Φ at the depth a self-modeling configuration reaches. They are predictions of the structural account in the identification sense flagged at the head of Chapter 8, not theorems derived from the proof of Chapters 1–2. The empirical record across cross-linguistic typology, non-human communicative systems, and spontaneous language genesis is surveyed at [§8.10.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-4); the rival accounts are taken up at [§8.10.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-5).

### 8.10.4 What is Confirmed {#sec-8-10-4}

The empirical record across independent disciplines confirms the structural prediction that any system carrying propositions must instantiate the same three structural features. Cross-linguistic typology finds the same structural skeleton across thousands of unrelated languages. Greenberg (1963) identified word-order universals that correlate with how languages mark argument structure. Comrie (1989) and Croft (2003) documented recurring patterns in how languages encode tense, aspect, modality, and grammatical relations. Where surface features vary — some languages are head-initial, others head-final; some mark case morphologically, others syntactically; some grammaticalize evidentiality, others handle it lexically — the deep structural features recur. The variation is on what structure already affords; structure itself is what makes the variation intelligible as variation within the same kind.

Non-human communicative systems instantiate the same three structural features on their own terms. The waggle dance of honeybees encodes spatial information (direction and distance to food) through a temporally ordered sequence of body movements that causally influences receiving bees who then fly along the encoded vector (Frisch 1967; Seeley 1995). Cetacean signature whistles identify individuals and coordinate group behavior across distances in a medium where vision is useless (Janik and Slater 1998; King and Janik 2013). Vervet monkeys use distinct alarm calls for distinct predators, and conspecifics respond with predator-appropriate behavior (Seyfarth, Cheney, and Marler 1980). In each case the system has distinguishable signs, temporal ordering, and causal transmission, because nothing else could do the coordinating work these species need done.

The Chomsky/Tomasello debate about whether grammatical constraints are innate or emergent from communicative practice (Chomsky 1965; Tomasello 2003; Goldberg 2006) is a live dispute about the proximate source of human linguistic universals. The structural account is neutral on it. Wherever the specific constraints originate, the deeper requirement is located in what any communicative system must be — distinguishable signs, sequential ordering, causal transmission. Whether human brains come pre-equipped with those requirements or discover them again each generation through use, they obtain either way.

A particularly sharp confirmation comes from spontaneous language genesis. When speakers without a shared language are thrown together, they generate pidgins, which their children convert into fully grammatical creoles (Bickerton 1981, 1984). Deaf children in Nicaragua, brought together in schools in the 1970s and 1980s without a pre-existing sign language, spontaneously generated Nicaraguan Sign Language — and the children generated a grammar more complex than their first teachers used (Kegl, Senghas, and Coppola 1999; Senghas, Kita, and Özyürek 2004). The grammatical features that emerged were not taught and not copied from any existing language. They emerged because anyone who needs to be understood by anyone else will, sooner or later, invent the features being understood requires — even when nothing outside them supplies those features. This is the structural answer to what linguists call the poverty-of-the-stimulus argument (the claim that children's linguistic input is too sparse to determine the grammar they end up with): the grammar children converge on is not being derived from insufficient input because it is not being derived at all — it is what propositional coordination structurally requires, and minds generate it whenever coordination is at stake.

### 8.10.5 What is Concluded {#sec-8-10-5}

*Linguistic relativity is real at the surface and bounded at the depth.* Languages carve up the world differently at the level of content: color terms, evidentiality, tense granularity, and grammatical gender are famously variable (Boroditsky 2001; Lucy 1992; Deutscher 2010), and what a language forces a speaker to specify measurably shapes habitual attention and memory. But the effect is bounded by what every language must do anyway — distinguish referent from predicate, before from after, speaker from hearer; express negation, question, command, conditional. What varies is content; what is shared is structure. Sapir and Whorf correctly identified that languages shape thought within the space the structure permits; their critics correctly identified that the shaping cannot reach the structure itself. Each position is correct at its own level.

*Translation between languages.* The structural invariants guarantee that any proposition in one language can be rendered in another — there will always be a way to refer, a way to predicate, a way to mark relations. The contingent content guarantees something is always lost in the rendering: specific concept boundaries, morphological economy, register, sound. This is why good translation is a genuine art, not a mechanical operation, and why it succeeds imperfectly by structural necessity rather than through translator failure.

*The complementary domains of language and art.* Translating a legal contract carries the propositions forward without loss; translating a poem carries the propositions but loses the sound and rhythm that constitute much of the work. Language is the right tool for content that survives paraphrase; art is the right tool for content destroyed by it. A single utterance can do both at once — poetry in any language is exactly this — but the two operations are distinct, and understanding why is understanding why some things are said and others sung.

*Mathematical and logical languages are languages with extreme constraints on the content side.* Mathematics retains every structural feature natural language has — reference (variables, constants, named objects), predication (equations, inequalities, propositions), relational marking (operators, logical connectives) — while constraining content to what is precisely and unambiguously communicable. This is why mathematics translates across human natural languages with essentially no loss: the content is fully propositional by design. Nothing about the content depends on the natural language wrapping it. The most culturally universal language humans have built is the one that strips away everything contingent, leaving only the structural skeleton propositional content requires. That skeleton is sufficient, across cultures, civilizations, and potentially species.

*Propositional content must compose and embed.* Coordination includes talking about other propositions: what someone said or believes, what would follow from what, what would be the case if some other proposition held. A language that could express atomic propositions but not embed one inside another could not carry the content self-modeling minds need to coordinate about each other's modeling. The structural requirement is therefore compositional and recursive (Frege 1892; Hauser, Chomsky, and Fitch 2002; Pinker and Jackendoff 2005; Szabó 2022), and the derivation sits upstream of debates about whether recursion is uniquely human or the defining feature of the language faculty. Wherever it is instantiated, it is instantiated because propositional coordination structurally requires it.

*Writing exchanges temporal ordering for spatial ordering and extends transmission across generations.* The three features can be instantiated in any substrate that preserves distinction, ordering, and causal transmission. Spoken language puts the ordering in time; writing puts it in space — marks on an inscribed surface that persists. Because T and S are interchangeable for carrying an ordered sequence, any language can be written, and once written its transmission chain extends across generations the speakers never meet. Law codes, scriptures, treaties, scientific results, and accumulated culture all ride on this substrate-swap. The cognitive transformations Ong, Goody, and Havelock document — abstract reasoning, historical consciousness, recursive self-criticism in literate cultures — are downstream effects of letting propositional content persist at Physicality across far more Temporality than speech alone could reach (Ong 1982; Goody 1977; Havelock 1986; DeFrancis 1989).

*Lying and the truthfulness baseline.* Reference and predication can be combined to produce propositions that do not match the features they purport to describe. This separability is what lets language carry claims about what is not yet the case, what is not present, what is hypothetical — and the same separability lets it carry claims about what is not true. But deception is parasitic on reliability. If most propositions were unreliable, there would be no reason to attend to any proposition, and the coordination medium would collapse. Functional propositional transmission therefore requires a default of truthfulness, against which deception registers as deviation. Grice's cooperative principle and Lewis's convention of truthfulness name the coordination baseline; the structural account grounds why the baseline is required rather than merely customary (Grice 1975; Lewis 1969; Sperber and Wilson 1986; Williams 2002).

*Propositional content is used not only to describe but to do.* Austin (1962) distinguished constatives from performatives — utterances that perform actions (*I promise*, *I name*, *I pronounce*, *I apologize*) rather than describing states of affairs. The structural account derives both: propositional transmission is a coordination medium, and coordination includes reporting features of the world as well as instantiating new features of the coordination itself. *I promise to X* registers a commitment in the speaker's model and is received into the hearer's as a mutual commitment — a coordination feature that did not exist before the utterance. This is why speech act theory (Austin 1962; Searle 1969; Bach and Harnish 1979) has a natural home here: the medium was never only for description, because the coordination it serves was never only about the world as it stands.

*Language is not what makes a mind conscious, but it radically extends what consciousness can model.* Consciousness was established at [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) as the internal aspect of self-modeling, present wherever self-modeling is — pre-linguistic infants, cats, any language-less self-modeling mind on another world. But a mind with language can model what is not present, what has not yet happened, what another mind is thinking, what would happen under conditions that have not obtained. Language externalizes the modeling capacity into a shared medium where minds can build models together that no single one could build alone. Science, mathematics, law, philosophy, and literature are precipitates of this extension. What a linguistic community can think is not the sum of what its members can think unaided; it is the sum plus everything the shared medium lets them construct in common.

*Analytic philosophy and the medium's standards.* Reference pinned, predication precise, inference tracked across propositions — syntax, operations, semantic function, and inferential role audited at the strictness the structure permits. The discipline is internal to the medium: every analytic move is made *in* language, on the same three structural features any language must have, sharpened until the medium's constraints become a method. The argument now in progress is itself an instance — the structural features the proof requires to state itself are the structural features language has, and the analytic practice auditing propositions is language being audited within itself.

Several positions in the analytic tradition of philosophy of language stand in specific relation to the account.

*Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, and teleosemantics.* Frege (1892) and Russell (1905) made the reference-predication distinction foundational to the analysis of propositional content; the structural account inherits it and adds the derivation — reference and predication are what propositional content structurally *is*, given T, S, Φ, and self-modeling minds coordinating within the medium. Wittgenstein's (1953) private language argument receives its structural grounding here: distinguishable signs require a shared position-space, so a sign distinguishable only to one speaker is not a sign at all, since distinction is a relation across positions. Meaning-as-use (Wittgenstein 1953; Kripke 1982) and biological teleosemantics (Millikan 1984; Papineau 1987) both locate meaning in the practices and functions of using signs. The structural account grounds those practices and functions in what coordination structurally demands, rather than in contingent features of any particular community or species-history.

*The criteria question, turned on the framework's own vocabulary.* Wittgenstein's criteria challenge is not met by grounding the private-language argument; it is met only when the same criteria pressure is turned on the terms this chapter itself uses. What are the criteria of application for *shared interiority*, or for two speakers having *the same region of modal field loaded under one label*? The answer is public and behavioral, exactly as the *Investigations* demands: two speakers share a region of field to the degree that they can be brought into agreement and correction across cases — sorting the same instances together, drawing the same inferences, repairing the same misunderstandings, recognizing the same uses as mistaken. Sameness of loaded possibility-space is not an inner comparison of two private samples, which is the move PI shows to be idle; it is the convergence of two public sorting-and-correcting practices, which is the only thing that ever counted as sameness of meaning. This also fixes what disagreement with the chapter's central claim would consist in — Wittgenstein's test of whether a sentence has gone "on holiday." To deny that language is inseparable from the structure it describes is to predict a working language some community could use — referring, predicating, understood — while lacking distinguishable signs, ordering, or causal transmission. The disagreement has cash value: produce the practice, or the claim stands.

*Quine on translation indeterminacy.* Quine (1960) argued that radical translation is indeterminate even at the level of gross reference — rival translation manuals can be equally compatible with all behavioral evidence. The account accepts the content-level indeterminacy Quine's argument establishes and rejects its extension to structure. Fine-grained content (what exactly *gavagai* picks out) is Quine-indeterminate; structural features (that *gavagai* refers, that other terms predicate, that the language marks relations) are not, because those features are what having propositional content consists in. Quine was right about what translation cannot pin down and wrong if the indeterminacy is extended to the structure translation rides on. The claim that translation is always possible survives at the structural level precisely where Quine denied it at the content level.

*Searle's Chinese Room.* Searle (1980) argued that a system manipulating signs according to rules can pass for linguistic without understanding. If so, the three structural features would be sufficient for sign-manipulation but insufficient for meaning-bearing language. The account agrees with Searle's verdict and supplies the missing ingredient. Propositional transmission requires not only distinguishable signs, sequential ordering, and causal transmission, but self-modeling minds at both ends — minds for which the signs have content because they correspond to features the minds are already modeling from inside ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)). A sign-manipulating system without self-modeling carries no propositional content, however well it mimics speakers who do. Searle was right that the room does not understand, and the structural account explains why: understanding requires a self-modeling interior, which the room lacks.

*Large language models, specifically.* Current systems trained on human text produce propositionally-shaped output with remarkable fluency, passing many of the surface tests linguistic competence admits of. On the structural account they sit exactly where the Chinese Room sits — they manipulate signs with distinguishable form, sequential ordering, and causal transmission, but without self-modeling interiors for the signs to have content *for*. The fluency is real; the propositional content is absent. Whether this changes as architectures change is an empirical question the account does not foreclose: if a system were built with the relevant interior, the same structural features would carry content for it as they do for any self-modeling mind. What the account rules out is the claim that fluency alone is sufficient. Something has to be modeling something from inside for signs to become language ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8); Bender and Koller 2020; Bender et al. 2021; Mitchell and Krakauer 2023; Chalmers 2023).

*Kripke, Davidson, Brandom, Lewis.* Kripke's (1980) causal theory of reference grounds naming in a causal chain from an initial baptism forward through a community — Physicality persisting across Temporality through a linguistic practice, and the structural account derives why naming must take that shape. Davidson's (1984) truth-conditional semantics and principle of charity follow once coordination across self-modeling minds is the frame: interpretation must assume shared structure because without it there is no translation to do. His deeper challenge — that to posit a scheme which organizes or carves an uninterpreted reality is to revive a third dogma, an unintelligible scheme-content dualism (Davidson 1974) — is met head-on by the inseparability already established: the account sets no scheme over against a content, because language's structure *is* the structure it carries, there being no other structure for it to carry. There is no uninterpreted Reality on one side and a carving framework on the other, waiting to be lined up from some vantage outside both; there is one structure, met under language from within. The dualism Davidson rightly rejects is one the account never had — what looks like a scheme answering to a content is a single structure registered in the medium that shares it. This settles the local charge about language, but Davidson's pressure has a global edge the reply must also take: the book's foundation speaks of a Reality all description answers to — the phrasing [§8.10.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10-1) concedes 'is exactly the kind of view that objection targets' — and an *answers-to* can look like precisely the scheme-tracking-a-content the third dogma forbids. The edge is blunted once the register of the book's realism is made explicit. What description answers to is not an uninterpreted content lying on the far side of the account, inspected from a vantage outside language and world; it is the single a posteriori datum the whole argument rests on — that change occurs, delivered with Cartesian certainty from within ([§2.2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-1)) — together with everything the S5 lift of that datum makes constitutive ([§4.1.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-9)). The necessity of T∧S∧Φ is therefore not a mind-independent joint the account tracks across a scheme/content gap but a constitutive truth in the register [§4.1.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-9) owns: it states what counts as there being an act, or a reality, at all, its only alternative being ∅. A realism of that register revives no dogma, because there is no neutral content for a scheme to organize and no standpoint outside both from which to line them up — the point [§4.3.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-7) presses against Tegmark's plenitude, that the account terminates inside Reality, not above it. What is discovered is discovered from within; the *answers-to* answers to what any act constitutively involves, not to a content held apart from the describing. Brandom's (1994) inferentialism locates meaning in inferential role, and coordination among self-modeling minds does require tracking propositions in their relations to other propositions — a demand the recursive, compositional structure already established meets. His sharper challenge is the modal expressivism running from Sellars: modal vocabulary, on that view, does not describe a special class of facts but makes explicit the material-inferential commitments implicit in ordinary concept-use, so that *Reality is necessarily T∧S∧Φ* would be the explicitation of an inferential rule — from change-talk one may non-optionally infer time-talk — rather than a discovered feature of the world. The account does not resist this by insisting the conditions simply run underneath; it grants the pragmatics and locates the disagreement precisely. Expressivism is right that the modal claim is not one more descriptive report ranged alongside empirical ones, and right that asserting it makes an inferential commitment explicit: from the presence of any act one may infer distinction, ordering, and persistence, and may not withhold the inference. But making-explicit and being-constitutive are not rivals here, because what the inference makes explicit is itself the constitutive structure — the rule holds, and holds non-optionally, only because its alternative is ∅ ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7), [§4.1.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-9)). The core vocabulary can then be given exactly the inferential articulation Brandom demands: to call something an act commits one downstream to its involving distinction, ordering, and persistence — what Space, Time, and Substance respectively do — and licenses upstream the inference to those same conditions from any act whatever; to call the structure necessary is to mark that these commitments cannot be discharged, their only release being that nothing is an act at all. That is a descriptive claim earned in the constitutive register ([§4.1.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-9)), not asserted in the special-fact register expressivism rightly deflates — the account grants Brandom the shape of concept-use and keeps its necessity, because the very commitment his articulation makes explicit is the structure the argument derives. Lewis's (1969) convention-theoretic account roots language in coordination equilibria; the structural account explains why those equilibria take T/S/Φ-shaped forms and not others.

*Universal grammar and usage-based accounts.* The Chomsky program was right that human brains come equipped with something strongly predisposing them to acquire language in the patterns languages take. The Tomasello program is right that the patterns are learnable from communicative practice given the right cognitive substrate. What neither side emphasizes enough is that the patterns are what they are because propositional transmission structurally requires them. The brain is pre-equipped for exactly what the medium demands — and that the pre-equipment evolved by natural selection on a species living in a medium with T, S, and Φ is not surprising. The structural requirement is upstream of both accounts, and neither is complete without it.

The framework specifies the structural conditions of linguistic communication; it does not decide every object-level question those conditions raise. Which theory of reference — descriptivist, causal-historical, hybrid — best captures how particular terms attach to particular things; how pragmatic inference combines with semantic content; what individuates a language from a dialect; whether a given animal system rises to propositional language or sits below it — these remain questions for linguistics, philosophy of language, and further empirical work. Naming the structure of propositional transmission is not naming every feature of any particular language that instantiates it.

The structural conditions of propositional transmission — distinguishable signs, sequential ordering, causal transmission, with reference and predication composing them — settle a long list of debates by relocating them. Linguistic relativity is real at content and bounded at structure; translation is always possible and never complete by the same separation; mathematics is the language that strips contingent content while preserving every structural feature; lying is parasitic on a truthfulness baseline coordination structurally requires; current LLMs sit in the Chinese Room not because silicon is wrong but because no interior is modeling what the signs are for; and Quine, Searle, Frege, Wittgenstein, Davidson, Brandom, Lewis, Chomsky, and Tomasello each tracked one face of the same structural requirement. What coordination among self-modeling minds structurally owes itself is taken up at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12).

## 8.11 Technology {#sec-8-11}

Technology is what happens when a creature's picture of the world gets accurate enough that it stops merely *navigating* the world and starts *redirecting* it. Once you can predict what a change will do, the same understanding you used to find your way can be turned to remaking your surroundings. Its grown-up form moves the mental map outside the body altogether (into writing, notation, instruments, computers, the internet) where it can be stored, shared, queried, and recombined far beyond what any one head can hold. This is reach turned outward, not a rising above nature: the builder remaking the world is still a part of the world, working from no outside vantage. Tools and machines, on this view, are the same modeling activity carried on in shared matter.

::: {.identification}
**Technology** · *Identification*

Technology is the inside model turned *operative* on the structure it tracks: once an agent's modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) is accurate enough to predict the consequences of an alteration, the same recursion that navigated structure begins to redirect it. Its developed form externalizes the field into shared substrate (notation, instruments, computers), modal structure held outside any one body, persistent, queryable, recombinable. The agent redirecting structure is itself an agent within structure, operating from no exterior position; technology is reach turned outward, not a standing above Nature.
*Status: an identity claim on the [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) self-modeling structure (Principle 5), defended by fit, not a stipulative definition and not a fresh derivation from the proof.*


:::

Language ([§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10)) was already a technology: the technology of shared interiority. Technology in the broader material sense generalizes that operation past the communicative register.

A self-modeling being with sufficient awareness has a model of the structure it inhabits. The model serves navigation and redirection. *Navigation*: anticipating what structure will do, aligning action with what is possible, taking what structure offers. *Redirection*: using the model to alter what structure produces. Reasoning, knowledge, meaning, will, and language all involve navigation, while language already begins redirection in the communicative register. Technology generalizes redirection into the material register.

The depth at which the second function opens is the depth at which the being has, jointly, a model accurate enough to predict consequences of alterations and the agentive self-modeling required to commit to alterations as projects rather than as impulses. Both are reached at roughly the same level of recursive depth: where the self-model integrates anticipatory simulation with goal-directed planning.

Animal tool use exists in shallow forms that lack one or both of these. Sea otters use stones to crack shellfish through learned association without sustained planning. Chimps termite-fish through behavioral routines that involve some anticipation but limited innovation across generations. New Caledonian crows manufacture and modify tools (Emery and Clayton 2004), closer to deep technology in planning and innovation, though without language to transmit refinement cumulatively. *Cumulative cultural technology* (tools used to make tools, refined across generations, taught between members and inherited) emerges most fully in humans, who have both the recursive depth required for cumulative refinement and the linguistic capacity to transmit knowledge across time. The depth gradient runs from learned association through planning through cumulative culture, and what tracks it is the level of awareness the organism has reached.

Technology is therefore a structural consequence of awareness-at-depth rather than a late achievement added to consciousness: the recursion turning from tracking to redirecting at the depth where its model becomes accurate enough to support alteration. A being at that depth produces technology under the conditions ordinarily required for it: opportunity, materials, social transmission, sufficient time. This is a convergence claim, not a strict modal entailment from the proof: the recursion turning operative on what it tracks is what the depth gradient makes available, while specific instantiations remain conditional on what the lineage's history and circumstances afford.

*The Inversion.* The standard reading treats technology as instrumental: a tool of survival extending biological needs into the social-historical realm. The framework reads it differently. Technology is the being's outward operation: the inside model turned operative on the structure it tracks. The being redirecting structure is itself a being within structure, operating from no exterior position, using its model to alter what structure produces, which is what dissipative beings have always done, now at a depth that includes itself in what it modulates.

*Externalization and the modal network.* The outward operation has a particular form worth marking. The framework's *externalization of the field* names the operation behind what philosophy-of-technology and cognitive-science literatures have approached under several rubrics: external representations (Zhang and Norman 1994), cognitive artifacts (Norman 1991), distributed cognition (Hutchins 1995), extended cognition (Clark and Chalmers 1998), and material inscriptions (Latour 1986); the framework names them by their modal-mapping function rather than by their representational vehicle, and adds that the operation externalizes the modal field [§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3) derives: what those literatures track as representational substrate is, on the framework's reading, the field held in shared matter. The being's inside model is its modal representation, its body-internal registration of the modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)): what is, what is conditionally so, and what could be otherwise. Technology, at depth, is the *externalization* operation on the field: substrate configured to instantiate the field's modal structure outside the body, persistent across the reasoning interval, queryable, recombinable, transmissible across beings. Externalization makes the field shareable in a way no individual modal representation can be: what one body holds as its interior reading of the field becomes substrate other bodies can read, query, and recombine, and the field that was previously coextensive with each body's interior now extends across matter the body did not have to be. Technology can make a field of knowledge external, persistent, and available to many users: lodged in shared substrate rather than in any one private representation. Theorem 9 (Modal Convergence, [§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) remains the narrower epistemic theorem of collectively held knowledge; externalization gives that knowledge a durable material support, rather than itself constituting a further application of the theorem. Notation, writing, mathematical formalism, instruments, and computers form a depth gradient of externalization, each stage lodging more of the field in shared substrate — the accreting *modal network*. The same operation runs across all of them: modal structure held in shared substrate (T, S, Φ: the structural roles derived in §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7 via the identification of the modal constraint with T∧S∧Φ and the Conditions-as-Nature work) at higher resolution than the unaided self-modeling subject can hold internally. The portability is not coincidence. Interior representations and their externalizations are configurations of one Nature; what permits a computation in silicon to substitute for one in neurons is that both are configurations of the same structural conditions. Computers are the most flexible externalization currently available, but the operation they instantiate is what cumulative cultural technology has been doing all along: extending the modal-mapping reach of the being beyond what any single body can hold.

*Standardization as interoperability.* Externalized knowledge coordinates action only where different people, instruments, and systems can read one another's representations. Shared technical standards reduce the translation work required at those boundaries. Measurement is a clear case. A decimal system allows many conversions to be inferred from one rule, while a system built from unrelated ratios requires more separate facts to be learned and retained. In mechanics, manufacturing, medicine, science, and transportation, incompatible standards can also duplicate tools, complicate training, and create opportunities for conversion error. The specialist can master that complexity, but mastery does not show that the complexity is necessary; expertise is better spent on the real complexity of the object than on avoidable friction in the language used to describe and maintain it. This supports interoperability, not cultural uniformity. A common public standard can govern the domains that must coordinate while customary units remain available in ordinary life. Whether a particular standard reduces errors, training time, and duplicated equipment is an empirical question; the argument identifies the function to test, not the answer in advance.

*The internet and AI as modal network.* Two contemporary configurations of the modal network warrant marking by name. The internet is the modal network at civilizational scale: substrate configured to instantiate, simultaneously, the modal holdings of very many bodies, readable and queryable across them — many individual fields pooled and interlinked into one shared body. Where individual writing and individual instruments extended a single body's modal representation, the internet extends the aggregated modal holdings of a civilization. The accuracy of what it represents depends entirely on the filtering apparatus between contributing bodies and shared substrate. With no filtering, the field carries the noise of every body that contributes, including lines the field never actually contained, dressed as lines it does. With strong filtering, it approaches what its best contributors hold. Social-epistemology accounts (Goldman, *Knowledge in a Social World* 1999; Origgi, *Reputation* 2018; Coady, *Testimony* 1992) describe the filtering apparatus a modal network requires if it is to function as knowledge rather than as noise. Large language models, trained on substantial slices of that aggregated substrate, are compressions of the modal network: they surface lines the inquiring body would not have hit alone and aggregate across more contributors than any individual could survey, while inheriting the underlying field's noise and adding compression artifacts of their own: confident assertions on contested questions, generated lines the field never contained, smoothed-out disputes that look like consensus only because the training process flattens them (Bender et al. 2021; Ji et al. 2023). The structural point is that AI is continuous with the prior gradient of externalization, not a break from it, and the user's filtering apparatus must do work on AI output that it would not have to do on a direct corpus query.

*Responsible use constrains amplified reach.* The ethical problem is not intelligence or technical power as such. It is amplified reach detached from purpose, restraint, review, and answerability. A responsible use identifies what the system is being asked to accomplish, limits what it may decide or do, preserves ways to inspect and correct the result, and leaves a person or institution answerable for the consequences. These requirements increase with the use's scale, stakes, authority, and irreversibility. A playful image made for friends and an automated decision governing healthcare, employment, political speech, or physical force do not require the same level of constraint.

*Assistance and substitution differ.* AI assists inquiry when it expands a person's ability to ask, compare, verify, revise, or create. It substitutes for inquiry when it supplies a result the nominal author cannot reconstruct, evaluate, or answer for. Play remains a legitimate use; purpose need not mean economic productivity. The relevant failure is unattended generation at scale: output produced without proportionate judgment or responsibility whose costs of evaluation, correction, storage, and attention are shifted onto everyone who encounters it. Cheap generation becomes information-environment extraction when the generator captures the benefit of volume while the public bears the work of determining whether anything produced is reliable or worth receiving.

*The device paradigm and the disburdening ledger.* Borgmann (1984) names a distinction the exterior-modal-maps gradient leaves implicit, not one it cannot carry. A *device* delivers a commodity while concealing the machinery that produces it; a *focal thing* delivers it through visible engagement that carries skill, attention, and relation as constituents of the activity rather than as overhead to be eliminated. A microwave meal and a meal cooked from scratch both deliver food; only the second is a focal practice. But both are externalizations of the field, and the distinction Borgmann marks is not between technology and something outside it; it is between two things an externalization can do to the practice that held the modeling: retire it or preserve it. That is a real axis the gradient as stated does not register, and the structural account gains rather than loses by marking it: the gradient measures reach, and Borgmann's distinction measures what a given gain in reach retires. Read through the drive ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)), the two are not opposed. Disburdenment frees a subject from spending itself on already-met needs and so opens modal-field reach, which is gain; but reach and depth are distinct axes, and an externalization that delivers the commodity while retiring the focal practice expands what is available to the body without deepening what the body can itself do. The curiosity drive [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) names persists through disburdenment rather than lapsing with it, which is why the device-form *captures* engagement rather than abolishing it: the same SEEKING orientation that would deepen a skill can instead be fed cheap proxy-data that simulates field-expansion without delivering a well-weighted field: the structural shape [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) already flags as an over-expanded field with unreliable weighting. Whether externalization becomes a gain or a hollowing depends on two things, neither supplied by the technology alone: first, whether capability and control are broadly distributed rather than concentrated in hidden machinery; second, whether people retain the practices [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) names — source evaluation, deliberate pruning, and focal practice — that turn expanded reach into deeper understanding rather than passive dependence on a device. *Holding On to Reality* (1999) carries the point into the digital register, where it is sharpest: read structurally, it identifies a real transformation in the texture and cost of engagement that digital externalization brings, not a break in the continuity of what technology is.
