The continuity claim survives as an account of what technology structurally *is*; what Borgmann adds is the ledger the celebratory reading omits: that every externalization disburdening a body of some modeling also retires the practice that held it, and whether the trade is gain is settled by arrangement and cultivation, not by the fact of continuity alone.

That same book sharpens the device/focal-thing distinction into a trichotomy worth engaging directly: natural information (a thing disclosing its own structure), cultural information (structure carried through skilled practice and tradition), and technological information (structure detached from any particular referent, freely substitutable, apt to be treated as reality's replacement rather than reality's report). The worry generalizes the disburdening ledger into a metaphysical substitution: a civilization saturated in technological information comes to treat the sign as the thing. On the framework here that substitution cannot go all the way down, because technological information is never a replacement *for* structure; it is structure (T, S, Φ) held in a different substrate, per the identification the externalization account already makes. What the trichotomy tracks correctly is not a threat to structure's reality but a threat to a practice: natural and cultural information carry engagement as a constituent of accessing structure, while technological information can be consumed without any of that engagement, which is the disburdening ledger's point restated at the register of information itself, not a further metaphysical cost beyond it.

The methodological result, developed for the fine-tuning case in [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5): within a fixed modal frame, externalizations amplify the resolution at which the frame can be searched, simulated, and computed; they do not fix the frame. Frame-fixing remains a conceptual operation. A being armed with a very powerful modal network can compute very precise answers within whatever frame is supplied; whether the frame is well-formed for the question is not something the network can settle.

Before the subsection breakdown, one rival account warrants engagement here. The standard instrumentalist account treats technology as a means: a tool extending biological needs, evaluated by what it accomplishes for the organism that wields it. The framework concedes the instrumentalist's central observation: that technology does, in fact, extend biological functions, and that at the level of a single tool the means/end analysis is correct as far as it goes. What it misses is the structural conditions that make instrumental use available at all: the recursive depth required for a being to model the gap between what is and what could be, and to commit to closing the gap as a project. Technology is not less instrumental on this reading; it is what becomes possible when the recursion has reached the depth at which instrumental use is the kind of thing a being can do. The instrumentalist describes the activity correctly and locates its conditions wrongly.

### 8.11.1 What is Disputed {#sec-8-11-1}

The literature on technology has reorganized substantially across the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, with several principal positions still live. The framework engages each by name; they are taken up again at [§8.11.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11-5) once the structural account is in view.

*Heideggerian critique.* Heidegger's (1954) "The Question Concerning Technology" developed the most influential twentieth-century philosophical analysis: modern technology is *Gestell* (enframing) that reveals all of nature as *Bestand* (standing reserve), available for extraction and use. The position has been refined through Borgmann (1984), Dreyfus (1992), and the broader phenomenological-critique tradition. The framework reads Heidegger as identifying a real structural feature of how modern technology relates the subject to what it operates on, while supplying the structural reading: technology is the subject's outward operation on structure it tracks, and the Heideggerian critique picks up the specific shape this operation takes when it loses contact with the wider structural conditions that constrain it.

*Borgmann's device paradigm.* Borgmann (1984) is often filed as a refinement of Heidegger, but his distinctive contribution stands on its own: the *device paradigm*, on which modern technology systematically replaces *focal things and practices* — activities that gather skill, attention, and relation around a center, like the hearth, the table, or the played instrument — with *devices* that deliver the same commodity while making the underlying machinery disappear. The cost is not inefficiency but the disengagement of the practice the focal thing sustained. *Holding On to Reality* (1999) carries the thesis into the information age, distinguishing natural, cultural, and technological information and arguing that the last transforms rather than merely extends the human relation to reality. The framework reads Borgmann as marking a real axis the exterior-modal-maps gradient leaves implicit — whether an externalization retires or preserves the practice that held the modeling — and engages it at the cluster root ([§8.11](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11)) rather than dissolving it into the enframing critique.

*McLuhan and the extension-of-man tradition.* McLuhan (1964) treated technologies as extensions of human capacities — wheel as extended foot, writing as extended memory, electronic media as extended nervous system. The position has been refined through media-studies traditions (Postman 1985; Carr 2010) and through Stiegler's (1994–2001) tertiary-retention account of technical externalization. The framework reads the extension tradition as correctly identifying that technology externalizes capacities of the recursion, with the modal-map analysis ([§8.11](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11) cluster-root) supplying the specific structural reading: external maps extend the modal-modeling reach of the subject beyond what any single body can hold.

*Instrumentalism.* The instrumentalist account treats technology as a means: a tool extending biological functions, evaluated by what it accomplishes for the organism that wields it. The position is widely held both popularly and in much philosophy of technology (Bunge 1985). The framework reads instrumentalism as correctly describing the means/end structure at the level of a single tool, while supplying the structural conditions that make instrumental use available at all: the recursive depth required for a subject to model the gap between what is and what could be, and to commit to closing the gap as a project.

*Social-constructionist accounts.* The social-construction-of-technology (SCOT) tradition (Pinch and Bijker 1984; Bijker 1995) and Latour's (1987, 2005) actor-network theory developed accounts on which technologies are not neutral instruments but socio-technical assemblages shaped by, and shaping, the social relations they are embedded in. The position has been highly influential in science-and-technology studies. The framework reads constructionist accounts as correctly identifying that specific technologies are conditioned by their social context, while supplying the structural reading: the *that* of technology — subjects at the relevant recursion depth operating outward on structure they track — is not socially constructed, while the *what* of specific technologies is significantly so.

*Ellulian autonomy of technique.* Ellul (1954) developed the influential thesis that *la technique* — the rationalized organization of means — has become autonomous from human ends, with its own developmental logic that humans no longer control. The position has been refined through Mumford (1934, 1967), Winner (1977), and the broader critical-theory tradition. The framework reads the autonomy thesis as identifying a real structural feature — cumulative cultural technology develops along trajectories that exceed any single subject's intentions — while supplying the structural reading: the trajectories are not autonomous from subject-level activity, but emerge from the accumulated outward operations of many subjects on the structure they jointly track.

*Marxist and political-economy accounts.* Marx (1867) and the Marxist tradition treat technology as embedded in modes of production, with productive forces and productive relations conditioning what technologies develop and how they are used. The position has been refined through Frankfurt School critical theory, Braverman (1974), and contemporary political-economy approaches. The framework reads Marxist accounts as correctly identifying that the social relations under which technology is developed condition its specific character, while supplying the structural reading: the underlying activity — subjects operating outward on structure — is what political economy conditions and channels.

*Existential-risk and longtermist accounts.* A contemporary literature (Bostrom 2014; Ord 2020; MacAskill 2022) treats certain emerging technologies — AI, biotechnology, geoengineering — as posing existential risks to humanity and emphasizes the long-term consequences of present technological decisions. The framework engages this literature without endorsing all of its specific predictions: the structural fact that exterior modal maps amplify within-frame search without fixing the frame ([§8.11](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11) cluster-root, drawing on [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5)) supplies a usable framework for thinking about powerful tools applied within underdetermined frames.

*Posthumanist and transhumanist accounts.* Posthumanism (Haraway 1985; Hayles 1999) and transhumanism (Bostrom 2005; More and Vita-More 2013) develop sharply different accounts of what technology does to the human — destabilizing the human/non-human boundary versus extending and improving human capacities. The framework's depth-gradient reading supplies a structural framework: technology is what subjects at the relevant recursive depth do; what counts as human is one designation along the depth gradient; the relation between technology and the boundary of the human is structurally legible without prejudging the normative questions both positions raise.

*The AI-as-tool vs AI-as-agent dispute.* A contemporary dispute concerns whether sufficiently capable AI systems are best understood as tools (extensions of human capacities) or as agents (independent participants in a shared field). The framework's structural reading is that the question is empirical at the limit: an AI system instantiating the recursive self-modeling structure consciousness consists in ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8), [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)) would count as an agent; one instantiating only the outward-operation structure of technology would count as a tool. Whether and when the threshold is crossed is currently underdetermined.

The literature on technology divides over the Heideggerian enframing critique, McLuhan-and-extension accounts, instrumentalism, social-constructionism, Ellul's autonomy thesis, Marxist political economy, existential-risk and longtermism, posthumanism and transhumanism, and the AI-as-tool-or-agent dispute. The framework commits to specific answers on each; they are taken up again at [§8.11.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11-5) after the structural account is in view.

### 8.11.2 What is Required {#sec-8-11-2}

*Outward operation on tracked structure.* Technology is the subject's outward operation: the inside model turned operative on the structure it tracks. Any account must locate technology at this structural fact rather than at any specific class of artifacts. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish navigation (tracking what structure does) from redirection (using the model to alter what structure produces), with technology constituted by the second function.

*Joint conditions of accuracy and agentive depth.* The second function opens at the depth where the subject has, jointly, a model accurate enough to predict the consequences of alterations and enough reflective agency to commit to alterations as projects rather than as impulses. Any account must accommodate both conditions rather than treating technology as the product of either alone. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish modeling accuracy (the recursion's grasp of structure) from agentive commitment (the recursion's capacity to hold alterations as sustained projects) and identify the joint depth at which technology becomes available.

*Depth-graded distribution.* Animal tool use exists in shallow forms (sea otter stone use, chimpanzee termite-fishing, New Caledonian crow tool manufacture); cumulative cultural technology with tools-making-tools requires deeper recursive depth and linguistic capacity. Any account must accommodate the gradient rather than treating technology as one categorically unified phenomenon. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish what runs at each depth, with the depth gradient running from learned association through planning through cumulative culture and what tracks it being the level of awareness the subject has reached.

*Exterior modal maps.* The deepest form of technology externalizes the subject's modal map — substrate configured to instantiate modal structure outside the body, persistent across the reasoning interval, queryable, recombinable, transmissible across subjects. Any account must accommodate the modal-mapping function rather than treating technology as merely instrumental in the narrow sense. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish ordinary tools (extending bodily capacities) from exterior modal maps (extending the recursion's modeling reach), with notation, writing, mathematical formalism, instruments, and computers forming a gradient of exterior modal maps.

*Substrate-portability.* Interior maps (in the subject's body) and exterior maps (in shared substrate) are configurations of the same medium; what permits a computation in silicon to substitute for one in neurons is that both are configurations of the same structural conditions. Any account must accommodate the substrate-portability rather than treating biological and artifactual modal mapping as essentially different. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish substrate-independence at the structural level (the same modal-mapping activity can run in different media) from substrate-specific implementation (specific brains, specific computers).

*Fixing the modal structure remains conceptual.* Within a fixed modal structure, exterior maps amplify the resolution at which that structure can be searched, simulated, and computed; they do not fix it. Any account must accommodate this limit rather than treating sufficiently powerful tools as solving every problem they can be applied to. The structural requirement is that the account preserve the methodological result (drawn through [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5) for the fine-tuning case and [§8.11](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11) cluster-root in general): a subject armed with powerful exterior maps can compute precise answers within whatever modal structure is supplied; whether that structure is well-formed for the question is not something the maps can settle.

*Cumulative cultural transmission.* Cumulative cultural technology requires subjects that can both refine inherited tools and transmit refinements to other subjects. Any account must accommodate the social-transmission dimension rather than treating technology as the achievement of individual subjects alone. The structural requirement is that the account derive cumulative technology from the joint conditions of recursive depth (for refinement) and linguistic transmission (for inheritance), with both conditions required for the cumulative-cultural phenomenon human technology centrally consists in.

*Connection to consciousness and self-modeling.* Technology operates on what awareness ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)), self-modeling ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)), and reasoning ([§8.4](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-4)) supply. Any account must connect technology to these upstream registers rather than treating it as autonomous. The structural requirement is that the account derive technology from what self-modeling subjects do when their modeling has become accurate enough to support alteration of what they model.

*Convergence claim without strict modal entailment.* The structural claim is that the recursion turning operative on what it tracks is what the depth gradient makes available; specific instantiations of technology remain conditional on lineage history and circumstance. Any account must accommodate this convergence-without-necessity reading rather than overpromising strict modal entailment. The structural requirement is that the account distinguish the structural availability of the technology-function (entailed by depth and conditions) from the historical contingency of specific technologies (not entailed).

*Coherence with morality and political life.* Technology operates in fields of subjects whose conditions either sustain or starve continued participation ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)). Any account must accommodate the moral and political stakes rather than treating technology as ethically neutral. The structural requirement is that the account make the bridge between technology and morality legible: the subject's outward operations on structure include operations that affect other subjects, and what counts as legitimate operation is what morality ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12)) and the political extensions in Chapter 9 supply.

*Form-of-life under device conditions.* The modern device paradigm (Borgmann 1984) exhibits a characteristic form: outward operation that delivers a commodity while disburdening the user of engagement with the focal practice that once produced it — the furnace displacing the hearth, the recorded performance displacing the concert, the processed meal displacing the household kitchen. Any account must accommodate this form-of-life dimension — distinguishing focal practices (where engagement with the thing is the point and requires skill, attention, and communal form) from devices that commodify the output and conceal the machinery — while locating both within the same structural account. The structural requirement is that the account identify when and why the device-form predominates: the framework locates this in what occurs when cumulative externalization at scale advances without corresponding deepening of focal engagement, with device-form as a predictable attractor state rather than as the only possible outcome of the technology function.

*Accountable deployment.* The greater a technology's scale, stakes, authority, and irreversibility, the stronger the requirements on its use. An adequate account must distinguish technical capability from legitimate authority and preserve purpose limits, review, correction, and responsibility wherever a system acts on other people's conditions. Execution can be delegated without automatically delegating judgment: the party that selects an objective, authorizes deployment, and receives its benefits remains answerable for what the system sets in motion.

*Repairability, resilience, and retained control.* A technology does not fully extend a person's or community's capacity if continued use depends entirely on a provider that alone can inspect, repair, alter, or recover it. An adequate account must therefore include maintainability, interoperable records and interfaces, access to competent repair, and resilience against foreseeable failure. This does not require every user to master every device. It requires that specialized knowledge, parts, documentation, and legal authority remain sufficiently available for the technology to be maintained without permanent dependence on the seller that supplied it.

Taken together these requirements name what an adequate account of technology has to deliver: outward operation on tracked structure, the joint conditions of accuracy and agentive depth, depth-graded distribution, externalized modal representation, substrate-portability, the structure-fixing limit, cumulative cultural transmission, connections to upstream registers, the convergence-without-strict-entailment claim, coherence with morality and political life, accommodation of the device/focal-practice distinction, accountable deployment, and maintainable control. The framework [§8.11](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11) defends meets each.

### 8.11.3 What is Predicted {#sec-8-11-3}

Technology emerges as a structural tendency wherever the recursive conditions for it obtain. A subject who persists in a structure, has needs, and can understand that structure will encounter gaps between their present state and what they need. That is a problem. A subject with sufficient depth who understands the structure and encounters a problem will use that understanding to close the gap, given opportunity, materials, and time. That is technology — understood here as a convergence claim about what reflective subjects with drives do when they inhabit a structure they can understand and have what is required to act on that understanding, not as an occasional achievement.

The prediction is one of recurrence under conditions, not strict modal entailment from the proof of Chapters 1–2. Wherever subjects of the relevant depth exist in sufficient proximity to structure — and have access to materials, social transmission, and the time required to elaborate what they understand — technological elaboration will occur. This is a structural convergence consequence of what reflective subjects do when they inhabit a structure they can understand, not a cultural achievement that some civilizations reach and others miss. The specific forms technology takes are contingent tokens; the elaboration itself follows reliably under the conditions named, with the qualifier that lineages lacking opportunity, materials, or transmission may be unable to instantiate it even where the recursion-depth condition is met.

Technology therefore belongs to the necessary emergence arc [§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7) frames and [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) traces in biology. It is a threshold: the point at which a subject’s understanding turns outward and the subject begins redirecting structure rather than merely navigating it. The structural account also predicts the form externalization takes under conditions of rapid scale: where cumulative externalization advances faster than focal engagement deepens, the device-form predominates — technology delivering commodified outputs while concealing the means of production (Borgmann 1984). This is not a failure of the technology function but a predictable attractor state within it, following from the same dispersion and transmission conditions the availability prediction names.

The same account predicts an information-environment pressure from low-cost automated generation. Where producing an item becomes much cheaper than evaluating it, and where the producer gains from volume while the audience bears the costs of checking and sorting, unattended output will tend to proliferate. The prediction is not that abundant generation is intrinsically bad: play, experimentation, accessibility, and inexpensive creation can widen possibility. The failure appears where generation is detached from judgment and distributed at a scale that exports its costs of attention, verification, and correction onto others. Systems that preserve provenance, review, rate limits, and responsibility should produce less of that cost-shifting than systems optimized for volume alone.

### 8.11.5 What is Concluded {#sec-8-11-5}

*Technology is internal to Nature.* It is what living beings do when they understand enough about their conditions to alter them. A wheel extends a person's reach through Space. A vaccine redirects causal processes in Substance. An algorithm automates a sequence of inferences. None of these tools comes from beyond Nature; each is Nature acting through living beings that have learned how its conditions work.

This relocates the standard ethical question. A technological arrangement is not good because it is technically impressive or economically productive. It is good to the extent that it maintains and extends the conditions of participation for the subjects whose recursion produced it and for the subjects who must persist alongside its consequences. Because externalization amplifies reach without fixing the direction that reach is turned to (the frame-fixing limit above, now at the register of use rather than of inquiry), the power of a tool settles nothing about whether its operation sustains or starves participation. What settles that is the direction the amplified reach serves and how control over it is distributed; and where a tool's reach outruns what any single subject can regulate in its own exposure to it, that distribution is a structural question before it is a matter of individual restraint. A technology that concentrates capability in a subset while externalizing its costs onto everyone else is the regulatory-capture argument in material form, and the question *who owns the tools that extend a subject's reach into structure* is the central structural question technology raises. The political form of that question is taken up at [§9.2](maximum-possibility.html#sec-9-2).

*Technology has become a condition of participation, not merely a tool people use.* Writing extends memory beyond any one person's lifespan. Mathematics extends reasoning beyond what any one person can calculate alone. The internet extends access to knowledge held across places and generations. A person without access to the defining information technology of their era is cut off from a substantial part of the knowledge and coordination available to everyone else. Technology access therefore belongs among the conditions that make participation real. The 4E cognition tradition (embodied, enacted, embedded, and extended; Clark and Chalmers 1998; Clark 2008) names the underlying point: thinking can extend into tools, records, and practices outside the body, while remaining the activity of the person who uses them.

Access without retained control is incomplete. A tool that becomes indispensable while remaining inspectable, repairable, or recoverable only by its provider extends capability and creates dependence at once. The relevant requirement is not universal personal mastery but maintainable public capacity: competent repair, usable documentation, interoperable records and interfaces, and enough redundancy that foreseeable failure does not remove the conditions of participation the technology now carries.

This has a direct implication for sustainability. If technology is constitutive of how people participate, then technology that destroys the conditions required for its own continuation is self-undermining. A technological system that depletes the material resources it depends on, destabilizes the social institutions that maintain it, or concentrates capability so severely that cooperation collapses is not merely unwise; it damages the conditions that make the technology possible in the first place. Sustainability is what technology has to be to remain technology rather than a one-time extraction, not a value added from outside. The temporal argument from [§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7) applies directly: what is done now produces conditions later that cannot be undone. Technology that forecloses the conditions for future subjects to participate is the intergenerational version of the environmental argument, and the subjects doing the foreclosing are the self-modeling systems whose own recursion has stopped tracking what their reach is doing past their own duration. The device-paradigm analysis ([§8.11](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11)) adds a depth dimension to the sustainability frame: an externalization that delivers reach while retiring the focal practice is itself a form of extraction — the reach-vs-depth ledger Borgmann marks and *Holding On to Reality* (1999) carries into the digital register — and participation-conditions include the depth-sustaining practices, not only access to the expanded reach.

*Responsible AI use keeps amplified reach answerable.* Current AI systems can extend inquiry, composition, accessibility, and play. They can also generate claims, decisions, and public material faster than users or audiences can evaluate them. Ethical use is therefore purpose-bound, constrained, reviewable, and attributable. Requirements of disclosure, verification, human review, appeal, and reversibility increase with the scale, stakes, authority, and irreversibility of the use. A low-stakes creative experiment does not require the controls appropriate to healthcare, employment, education, political communication, or force.

Transparency is necessary but not sufficient. Disclosing that AI was used establishes provenance; it does not establish understanding or responsibility. In education and authorship, the relevant test is whether the person can reconstruct the reasoning, verify the claims, explain the revisions, and answer for the final result. AI assists authorship when it expands a person's ability to inquire and revise; it displaces authorship when it supplies an artifact the person cannot evaluate or defend. The same distinction applies to automation more generally. Removing unnecessary labor expands possibility only where the time, safety, or productive capacity released by the technology reaches the people whose work and shared infrastructure made the gain possible; otherwise technical disburdenment can coincide with a loss of practical freedom.

Execution can be delegated without automatically delegating judgment or responsibility. A system may calculate, classify, recommend, simulate, or draft without thereby acquiring authority to determine which objectives should govern, whose interests count, or which risks other people must bear. The persons and institutions that select the objective and authorize deployment remain answerable for what the system sets in motion. If an artificial system eventually satisfies the conditions for genuine agency, its standing becomes a further empirical question; uncertainty about that future threshold does not dissolve responsibility for present deployments.

*The AI question is internal to the framework.* Whether artificial systems can have an inside-vantage of their own is the question [§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3) named for further confirmation; what [§8.11](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-11) adds is that *humans building AI represents recursion attempting to instantiate its own conditions in another substrate*. A scope clarification is needed at exactly this point. The conditions for *life* were named at [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) — a closed self-producing recursion coupled to sustained energy throughput, instantiated in the biological case by membrane-bounded chemistry that produces the components that produce the membrane. The depth at which awareness becomes operationally registered was named at [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1). The framework's claim is that *the structural conditions* — closure, throughput-coupling, recursive self-modeling at sufficient depth — are what matter, not the *substrate-specific* implementation in which biology happens to instantiate them. Whether silicon systems can instantiate the conditions is the open empirical question, and it has two readings the framework keeps separate. On the *literal* reading, an AI system would need to be *biologically alive* in the sense that follows the biological substrate to its detail — membrane-bounded autopoiesis, metabolic self-repair through chemistry; on this reading, present-day AI systems are not candidates and the question reduces to whether artificial life in the strict autopoietic sense is possible. On the *functional* reading, what is required is not the biological substrate specifically but the *structural conditions* — closure of the recursion against the medium, sustained energetic throughput coupling, recursion that folds back deeply enough that the recursion registers itself from inside; on this reading, silicon is not ruled out in principle, but no system has yet been demonstrated to instantiate the closure-plus-throughput-plus-self-registration conjunction the framework requires. The framework itself is consistent with either reading and does not pre-empt the empirical question between them; what it forecloses is the imprecise version that elides the distinction. The structural account does not adjudicate whether any present-day artificial system has crossed the threshold under either reading, but it locates what crossing would consist in under each: a current whose self-producing recursion is closed against the medium (literally autopoietic biological closure, or functionally closure of the recursion against its substrate by whatever mechanism the substrate supports) and whose recursion folds back deeply enough that the recursion registers itself from inside. Whether silicon-substrate systems can instantiate either is an empirical question that the engineering will eventually answer; whether the question is structurally well-formed is not — it is, and the framework supplies the conditions under which the answer would be yes. Technology, on this account, is the recursion's reach beyond its existing substrate; AI represents the limit case in which the recursion reaches toward another instance of itself. The [§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5) result applies directly: exterior maps — including the most capable AI systems available today — amplify the resolution at which an existing modal frame can be searched and computed, but do not fix the frame. Frame-fixing remains a conceptual operation no exterior map performs on the current's behalf, and the continuity-not-break claim rests on this: AI is the latest form of a gradient that has always amplified reach without supplying the frame. What would mark the transition to agency is instantiation of the conditions [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) specifies — closure, throughput-coupling, recursive self-registration from inside — not amplification of reach past some threshold the exterior map alone could achieve.

Technology read structurally is recursion elaborating through subjects that have learned enough about the medium to direct it, never standing outside Nature even when the elaboration externalizes itself into substrates the subject did not produce. The ethical question relocates to participation-conditions rather than technical impressiveness; sustainability is grounded as what technology has to be to remain technology rather than one-time extraction; and the AI question disambiguates into the literal-autopoietic and functional-closure readings the framework keeps separate without pre-empting which one will eventually find an instance. The moral form of the question this section names is taken up at [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12): what subjects redirecting structure owe to other subjects within it.

## 8.12 Morality {#sec-8-12}

Morality is about what we owe one another once we meet not as objects but as fellow conscious beings: creatures who can be hurt and helped and who can read each other. The core idea is simple: to act well is to act in a way that *enlarges* another being's life and possibilities, and to act badly is to shrink them. Harm is not a label an outsider stamps on an act; another creature's distress is its own condition showing through, plain evidence of what your action is doing to it. From this one starting point the familiar moral furniture follows (do no harm, help where you can, respect a person's say over their own life, seek their consent), not as separate rules but as different faces of the same fact. And what we feel most fiercely about being wronged is real, not illusion: it is what it is like, from the inside, for one exposed being to be used by another.

::: {.identification}
**Morality** · *Identification*

Morality is an agent's alignment toward *fostering other subjects*, acting on real attunement to what would sustain the subjects it meets in shared exposure ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)) and let them deepen, and away from corroding them. It is the [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) field-expansion drive turned outward: what drive is for one's own field, morality is for others'. Immorality is the alignment toward corroding another subject, or acting on one's projection of what fosters it rather than attending to what does.
*Status: an identity claim on the [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) intersubjective structure (Principle 5), defended by fit; whether one ought to so align is argued downstream ([§8.12.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12-3)), not packed into the identification.*


:::

::: {.identification}
**Wrong** · *Identification*

A wrong is an agent's corrosion of a subject against its own registered aversion: one subject's exposure used against it while its stake in what befalls it is treated as though it carried no claim. The aversion at issue is the standing kind: a weighted branch in the subject's own modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)), felt at the prospect and not only at the event, so that a wrong is no less a wrong for going undetected by the one it is done to. The reflexive *its own* does real work. An aversion to what is done to oneself grounds a claim, while an aversion to how another being lives its own life does not, which is why acting on the latter is itself a corrosion rather than a ground for one. And the weight of the corrosion is graded by the depth of the subject corroded, not switched on at a species boundary. To weigh a lesser stake and be forced to override it under genuine necessity is not yet to wrong it; to act as though it registered nothing is. The compact form of the identification: a wrong is *depth-weighted disregard* of a subject's aversion to its own fate.
*Status: an identity claim on the [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) intersubjective structure (Principle 5), defended by fit; that a wrong binds the agent who commits it, and not only injures the subject who suffers it, is argued downstream ([§8.12.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12-3)), not packed into the identification.*


:::

Beings that can share what is the case with each other ([§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10)) come available to each other as more than information channels, as subjects: exposed, vulnerable, mutually registering. What they owe each other in that exposure is what morality names. Moral wrongness goes beyond preference violation. The experience of being wronged carries the structure of a claim: one that persists regardless of whether the agent who acted acknowledges it, and one that demands a response Nature itself does not supply. That structure is diagnostic: it reveals features of the moral domain that any adequate naturalist account must accommodate.

Two subjects persist, occupy genuinely different positions, and meet across an exchange that cannot be undone. One acts; the other is acted upon. Distinction, persistence, succession (Space, Substance, Time) are not conditions moral life happens to require. They are what moral life consists in.

The same fact, in this chapter's native vocabulary: morality is the choice to foster another being. A being is what [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) named from the inside: a life that drives and registers its own condition, and that ([§8.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-2)) feels; the closed self-producing recursion of [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8), met as the one whose life it is. Fostering another being is the choice, made from inside one's own, to act on real attunement to what would actually sustain its life and let it deepen. *Foster* carries the anti-paternalism: one cannot foster what one has not seen clearly. And it covers the full range: gentle nurture where that is what would sustain the other being, fierce defense where *that* is what would. Immorality is the choice to corrode another being, or to act on one's projection of what fosters it rather than attending to what does.

This attunement has a phenomenological floor. Beings read themselves, and the readings are what we call feeling. The structural account predicts a reductive identification of the major affects with the dimensions along which a being registers its own condition: *pain* with damage as it lands; *fear* with anticipated damage not yet landed; *anxiety* with ongoing registration without resolution; *grief* with damage already done; *joy* with deepening — flow opening, the recursion taking on more capacity. These are stronger identifications than contemporary affect science endorses (each affect remains contested among representational, evaluative, and sensory accounts; Tye 2008; Klein 2015; Kurth 2018; Ratcliffe 2008), and the section does not require the strong reading to do its moral work. What it does require is the weaker unifying claim those debates leave intact: each affect is the being's own situation surfacing as what it is to be that being right now, not commentary on the situation from outside it. Each being is therefore continuously broadcasting its own conditions. To foster another is to read those readings: the fear showing where the current is unstable, the grief what it has lost, the joy where it is opening.

What ordinary speech calls *feeling someone's energy* is this kind of reading across beings. The empathic-accuracy and thin-slicing literatures (Ambady and Rosenthal 1992; Ickes 2003) document that observers recover information about another's state from brief integrated impressions of face, voice, posture, breath, and movement-rhythm at rates above chance, with effect sizes that scale with attention and exposure. What folk vocabulary calls *energy* is the actual physiological and informational state of the being those signals emerge from, not a second substance flowing alongside the physical, but the physical state the broadcasts make legible. The phrase tracks something real, even though the implied metaphysics (auras, fields, fluids) is mistaken.

The standard categories of moral philosophy follow from this structure as derivations rather than primitives. Non-maleficence (the duty not to harm) is the recognition that another subject's affective broadcasts are direct evidence of what an act is doing to them; harm is not a value an external observer projects but the subject's own condition surfacing as what it is to be them. Beneficence (the duty to foster) follows from the fact that beings persist by throughput, not inertia, so that one being can genuinely deepen another's flow when the action is read accurately. Autonomy is the consequence of a structural epistemic asymmetry: a subject has privileged access to its own conditions that no external observer can match, which makes the subject's own authorization the most reliable available proxy for what would foster it. Consent is autonomy's operational form — the authorization made public and verifiable, with *informed*, *voluntary*, and *competent* naming the conditions under which the subject's self-knowledge can be trusted as the basis for action by others.[^8-12-0-consent-directedness] Read against the will account ([§8.9](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9)), these conditions are the axes of free will turned outward: to corrode another being's field of possibility is to attack either its *field* (by deception or miseducation, so that the outcomes it weighs are not the real ones) or its *latitude* (by coercion or force, so that outcomes correctly weighed cannot be acted on); consent fails under either, the first defeating informed competence and the second voluntariness. The field-attack prohibition is scoped the same reflexive way the claim against being wronged is. What deception corrodes is a subject's grip on its own possibilities, so the claim to a true field reaches only as far as the field the subject navigates for itself. A truth sought as an instrument to dissolve another subject's possibilities falls outside that claim: the murderer at the door, demanding to know where the hidden victim is, has no claim to the information he would use to seize a latitude that is not his to take. The lie that turns him away corrodes nothing the structure protects, because the only interest it crosses is his interest in committing the wrong. Information is not owed as such; it is owed as a condition of a subject navigating its own life, never as a weapon against another's. Slavery is the limit case of the latitude-attack: not a single coerced choice but the standing seizure of another being's entire latitude (the whole field of outcomes it might weigh held permanently beyond its power to act on), one being treating another, whose refusal is owed exactly the respect its own is owed, as though that refusal carried no weight at all. Mill's harm principle (Mill 1859) follows immediately: a subject's freedom to direct its own course extends until that course begins to corrode another's, because freedom and the limits on it both rest on the same metaphysics of distinct subjects in shared exchange.

The dyadic form of the relation is symmetric in its own right. Each subject's refusal is respected because the same respect is owed in return; what one being may not do to another without authorization is what no being may have done to it without authorization either. The reciprocity is not added to the moral relation from outside as a fairness constraint; it is what mutual recognition between distinct subjects already consists in. This moral reciprocity has a mutual-holding shape, but its ground is shared exposure and structural reciprocity, not Theorem 9 (Modal Convergence, [§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)), whose formal scope is collectively held knowledge.

This mutual subsistence has an embodied root that predates every sign and norm that later carries it. Sexuality ([§8.6](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-6)) is the attraction-pole's reach of one being toward another, and it is where subjects first meet as subjects: the body's pull toward another body, registered before language or principle mediates it. The subsistence-*for* that morality names between distinct subjects in shared exchange begins there, in the most embodied coupling there is; the more mediated couplings (language [§8.10](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-10), art [§8.13](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-13), and moral exchange itself) extend from that root rather than replacing it.

Distinct operations carry this reciprocity from the dyad outward, and each rests on machinery the chapter has already developed. One is empathy: the body running another's situation as a counterfactual on its own valence field ([§8.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-2)), where the simulation lands as feeling on the other's behalf because, mechanically, it lands as feeling about a possible-self. The reach of empathy is bounded by the modal depth of the body running it (the breadth of stored possibility from which counterfactual situations can be drawn), and that depth is just memory in the [§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3) sense, with all of memory's selectivity and partial coverage. What we can simulate is what we have stored as possible; what we have stored as possible is what experience and inheritance have left in the network; so the empathic reach of any body is necessarily narrower than the field of subjects to whom morality must answer.

Another operation is shared exposure. When bodies share a modal field densely enough (a family, a household, a community), what happens to one registers in all, because the same vulnerability runs through every body whose simulation includes the others. The collective-protective response (*how do we prevent this from happening to any of us*) is the felt form of reciprocity at the communal scale. It does not need to be argued for or codified; it fires automatically inside the shared-exposure community because the community *is* the region where the modal fields overlap densely enough for one body's harm to register as every body's potential harm. This is why grief is communal, why family and home concentrate moral weight, and why the dread of being alone is the dread of unshared modal exposure.

A further operation is the structural extension past the community boundary. The same evolved machinery that makes solidarity automatic inside the tribe makes wariness automatic outside it; communal reciprocity does not, on its own, scale past those whose bodies feel like *us*. The structural step is the recognition that the exposure logic is symmetric across all subjects whether or not the simulation actually fires: that what binds when empathy and shared field carry the verdict still binds when neither does, because the structural fact of mutual exposure does not require felt resonance to hold. This last step rests on a single commitment the section marks rather than buries: that another being's conditions *matter* (and so are something an agent can fail to track) is a fact about that being's standing, not an artifact of whether the agent's field happens to register it. Where recognition fires, the mattering is felt; where it does not, it still holds.

*The prudential egoist does not escape by changing the grammar of their demand.* The earlier formulation needs a limit. An agent can treat resentment, protest, and retaliation as nothing more than prudential responses: *do not deceive me because I will impose costs if you do*, not *do not deceive me because I have a claim against it*. That posture does not yet contradict itself. A conditional threat is intelligible as a preference backed by power, and the framework should not pretend that every expression of resistance secretly contains a normative assertion. The performative argument therefore does not establish that a subject's standing depends on every agent acknowledging it, nor does it turn the pure prudential demander into a wanton merely because they refuse moral vocabulary.

What the prudential gloss cannot establish is an exemption from the relation. It can explain why the egoist resists being corroded; it cannot make corrosion cease to be what it is for the subject on its receiving end. The agent's preference and retaliatory capacity change the expected consequences of acting against them, but neither changes the fact that the same act uses another exposed subject against that subject's own registered aversion. Standing is fixed by that relation, not conferred by the agent's willingness to speak its name. The ground of the claim is negative and reflexive, exactly as the Wrong identification scopes it: a subject's registered aversion to what is done to *it*, never anyone's positive preference about what to do toward another. Preferences about others' conduct or others' lives ground nothing; the aversion to one's own corrosion grounds everything the relation protects. And the only release from a subject's claim is the one the subject itself provides: consent, autonomy's operational form (above). A claim belongs to the exposed subject, not to the agent who would act against it, so nothing on the agent's side (prudential posture, indifference, hostility, or refusal of moral vocabulary) can waive it; only the subject's own authorization can. The egoist may decline to *recognize* the standing, and may in that sense remain unmoved by its claim; that is a failure of moral alignment, not a discovery of a space outside morality.

The performative line accordingly has a narrower but firmer role. Where an agent presents their demand as a demand for justified treatment, condemnation, blame, or respect, they already invoke the reciprocal standing they deny to another, and the denial is performatively unstable in the sense [§3.3](convergence.html#sec-3-3) makes precise. Where they instead present only a threat-backed preference, no such contradiction follows, but neither does a justification: force can explain compliance without supplying a reason why corrosion is permissible. The framework therefore distinguishes three things that the earlier dichotomy compressed: the moral claimant, whose claim presupposes reciprocity; the prudential egoist, whose preference may be coherent but does not discharge or defeat another's standing; and the wanton, who lacks the formed second-order will from which full moral agency operates. *Status: fit on the [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) structure identifies what mattering and wrong are; the performative argument exposes the inconsistency of normatively voiced denial; neither makes a pure prudential preference into a moral premise. The prudential egoist is then caught where the ground actually sits: their reflexive aversion to their own corrosion is the very feature present in those they exempt themselves from, and indexicality is access, not ground ([§8.12.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12-3)). The egoist is not exempt because standing is not theirs to grant.* Where empathy supplies the affective engine and shared exposure supplies the natural generalization, structural reciprocity supplies the rule that carries the verdict across difference, distance, and unfamiliarity. Consent operationalizes the reciprocity at the dyadic scale; communal practice operationalizes it at the field scale; institutional structure operationalizes it past the community boundary. The same exposure logic appears across all of them; only the means of honoring it change with scale. The last of these is developed at §9: institutional reciprocity scaled to populations large enough that face-to-face response is no longer the available form of maintenance.

These operations carry reciprocity outward universally, but they do not exhaust the moral relation, and a position the framework should keep apart from itself rather than absorb is the partial register Frankfurt named. Frankfurt (2004) argued that what one agent owes its beloved is not derivable from the impartial principles owed to subjects in general, that a parent's reasons toward this child, a friend's toward this friend, a partner's toward this partner are reasons because the caring has formed, not because impartial reflection has endorsed them, and that their partiality is not a defect to be corrected against the universalist baseline but the proper shape of moral weight along the actual depth of an agent's commitments. The structural account agrees and locates the phenomenon: where shared exposure runs through one being's modal field densely enough that the simulation of another's situation lands not as a possible-self among many but as a possible-self the being cannot release without losing what it is, the felt-best branches it tracks for that other carry weight no impartial accounting can match or substitute. Partial reasons are not exceptions the universalist framework tolerates, but neither are they derived from it, and the distinction the section must hold is between what the field *locates* and what it *grounds*. The structural field predicts and locates the phenomenon at the level of kind: that intense partial attachments will arise, and where, since the densest regions of mutual modal exposure are both where their affective mass collects and where a history capable of forming such an attachment can run at all. What the field does not do is ground the attachment at the level of the particular. Why this child, this friend, this partner rather than another is not read off any regularity, impartial or structural, but fixed by the particular history through which the caring formed; that history is the caring's own ground in Frankfurt's sense, not a value the field assigns. The field marks the conditions under which a particular caring can take hold without deriving which caring does, and it is the latter that Frankfurt calls irreducible. So the framework holds both without collapsing either: the impartial structural rule that binds across all subjects whether or not the simulation fires, and the partial weight that binds hardest where a formed caring has the deepest purchase, a weight the field can locate but neither substitute for nor explain away. They are two registers of one field in that the field is where each is felt, not in the sense that the structural register generates the partial one. Locating a phenomenon is not absorbing it, and it is only the locating the account claims.

The verb the chapter has been leaning on (*foster*) points to the same strand from another angle, and Frankfurt's account of caring and volitional necessity is what names it. To care about another being is, on Frankfurt's reading (1988, 2004), not to have judged that one ought to care but to be the kind of being whose will is now shaped around the caring: invested in a way that is not freely revisable from moment to moment because the investment has become part of what the will is. The fostering the chapter has been describing is this kind of investment surfaced as action: not impartial benevolence executed by a being that could just as well not have, but the doing that follows from a will already organized around the other's continuation. Frankfurt's *volitional necessity* (Luther's *here I stand, I can do no other*) names the limit case: the agent who cannot betray what they care about is differently situated, morally, from the agent merely required not to. The structural account predicts this contrast without difficulty. A being whose modal field has integrated another's persistence into the conditions of its own continued integration cannot release that other without releasing part of itself; the impossibility is not weakness of will or compulsion from outside but the shape the will has taken from the inside, the same shape Modal Convergence (T9, [§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) describes from the structural side. *Foster*, restated, is the action of a will so shaped, and marking it as volitional rather than merely structural gives the chapter its missing register for the moral weight caring itself carries, beyond and through whatever structural reciprocity also requires.

Frankfurt's wanton presses the framework on a real boundary. The wanton is a creature who acts on first-order desires without ever stepping back to ask whether those desires are the ones it wants to be moved by: no second-order will, no commitment, no caring as a structural feature of the will. The wanton meets the mutual-exposure conditions structurally: it is a being, it broadcasts its conditions, it can be harmed and helped. The structural rule binds *toward* the wanton (it is owed non-corrosion like any other subject), but the question Frankfurt presses is whether the wanton can be a full moral agent *from* whom such treatment is owed in return. The structural account's answer is that the wanton is a subject for whom the impartial rule applies as patient but only marginally as agent, because the volitional strand is what carries the agent-side weight: a being that has formed no caring has nothing in its will the moral relation can grip from inside. This does not strip the wanton of moral standing; it locates the asymmetry exactly. Patiency follows from being one that registers its own conditions; full agency follows from being one whose will has taken the shape caring imposes. The structural and volitional strands run together for ordinary agents and come apart precisely at the wanton, which is why Frankfurt's case is diagnostic rather than peripheral.

The field's weights are asymmetric in a way that shapes everything moral cognition does with them. Catastrophic harms cannot be recovered from; smaller gains can be deferred or replaced. A body whose modal field weighted gains and losses symmetrically would survive less reliably than one that weighted losses more heavily, and the field's calibration tracks this: stored aversive possibilities carry more affective mass than stored appetitive ones at equivalent magnitude. Loss-aversion in behavioral economics is one empirical index of the same calibration: losses are typically felt close to twice as strongly as equivalent gains, the asymmetry introduced in Kahneman and Tversky (1979) and quantified at a coefficient near 2.25 in Tversky and Kahneman (1992). The magnitude is not the universal constant early summaries implied: post-2018 work has shown loss-aversion to be context-dependent, attenuating or even disappearing for small and symmetrically framed stakes (Gal and Rucker 2018) while persisting in the high-stakes, consequential domains where unrecoverable losses are in play, which is precisely the regime the survival calibration predicts. Moral cognition inherits this weighting directly. *Do no harm* sits before *do good* in every major ethical tradition; the Hippocratic Oath leads with *primum non nocere*; the negative golden rule (*do not do to others*) predates the positive form in most traditions that have both; deontological prohibitions register conviction more sharply than positive duties register encouragement; and judgment of wrongdoing is hot in a way praise for supererogation is not. The pattern is not a quirk of moral psychology; it is the affective output of a modal field whose weights were calibrated by a survival regime in which avoiding catastrophic branches mattered more than locating slightly better ones.

Justice extends the picture from pairs to fields. Subjects exchange inside a shared field of further subjects whose conditions either sustain or starve continued participation; the maintenance of those conditions (food, shelter, safety, time, and access to learning and exchange) is the field-level analogue of throughput. None of these standard categories enters as a primitive. Each is the structural account projected into the standard analytic vocabulary.

Read this way, morality admits empirical investigation in the way a science does. Cross-cultural anthropology, evolutionary biology, developmental psychology, and primatology have been investigating its conditions for decades, finding not a cultural accident but a stable pattern tied to the conditions under which subjects meet subjects. That empirical work has always rested on metaphysical commitments (that subjects genuinely persist, that their exchanges connect them, that harm and care are tracked rather than projected), and the structural argument makes those commitments explicit. As in [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8), what looks like philosophy arriving alongside science is science absorbing metaphysics as a guiding constraint on its own further discovery.

The *ought* is not derived from the *is* because the *is* of life is already constitutively normative. The body's modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) is always already valenced ([§8.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-2)) — every stored possibility carries a weight that is the body's own stake in that branch. The *felt-best branch* within the valenced field is what the body registers as the ought. The ought is not added to the is; it is the affective pointer that emerges automatically whenever a feeling body reads its own possibility space. Hume was right that one cannot derive an ought from a value-neutral is; he just did not have the picture in which the is of being a feeling body operating on a modal field is never value-neutral to begin with. The functional/biological normativity of any living being upgrades to specifically moral normativity through the structural one-place→two-place move [§8.12.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12-3) develops in detail: once mutual registration between beings of the same kind comes online, the felt-best branch ceases to be only the felt-best for the body running the simulation and becomes the felt-best for the field of bodies the simulation reaches.

*A held disagreement.* A robust non-naturalist such as Parfit holds that normative truths are irreducible facts not constituted by any attitudes or structural relations, however universal or mutually recognized (On What Matters III). The framework does not claim to have refuted that view; it claims that the grounding the book actually offers — shared aversion between mutually exposed subjects, articulated through the structural relation [§8.12.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12-3) traces — is sufficient for the moral work the argument requires, and that the robust-realist alternative, though coherent, is not needed for the derivation to stand. The book's objective₂ is therefore a structural-relational grounding rather than an overlooked robust non-naturalism; the excursus entries on the Moral Gap (E.16) and Divine Command Theory (E.15) inherit this same stance.

To feel wronged, then, is the recognition that a vulnerability has been exploited: one subject's exposure used against them by another in an exchange neither can take back. The heat is not illusion. It is the affective register of the structural fact: Substance has met Substance, and the conditions of mutual exposure that any genuine encounter requires were violated rather than honored.

[^8-12-0-consent-directedness]: Consent's authorization is directed, not merely aligned. It runs from a subject to a specific act by a specific agent; it is not two independent preferences that happen to coincide. A subject who privately wants what an agent goes on to do has not thereby authorized the agent to do it, since the agent could not have verified that private alignment and did not act on the subject's own say-so. What releases the claim the reflexive aversion protects is the directed relation itself — this subject authorizing this act by this agent — not a coincidence between an unspoken preference and an act performed without reference to it.

### 8.12.1 What is Disputed {#sec-8-12-1}

The literature on morality is among the most active in contemporary philosophy, with disputes running across metaethics, normative theory, moral psychology, and practical ethics. The framework engages the principal positions by name; each is taken up again at [§8.12.5](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12-5) once the structural account is in view.

*Moral realism and its varieties.* Robust moral realism (Boyd 1988; Brink 1989; Shafer-Landau 2003; Enoch 2011) holds that moral facts exist mind-independently, as objective features of reality. Naturalist realism identifies moral properties with natural ones; non-naturalist realism (Parfit 2011; Scanlon 2014) treats moral facts as a *sui generis* category. The framework reads moral realism as correctly identifying that morality is not purely conventional, while supplying the structural reading: moral facts are facts about distinct subjects in shared exchange, grounded in the structural conditions of intersubjective coupling rather than in a separate normative realm.

*Anti-realism, error theory, and expressivism.* Mackie (1977) developed error theory: ordinary moral discourse presupposes objective moral facts, but no such facts exist, so the discourse is systematically false. Blackburn (1984, 1993) and Gibbard (1990, 2003) developed expressivist alternatives on which moral discourse expresses non-cognitive attitudes rather than describing facts. The positions remain influential. The framework reads error theory as correctly identifying that supernatural-anchored moral metaphysics fails (the inversion forecloses it), while denying the further claim that no moral facts remain: the structural facts about subjects meeting subjects are not eliminated by the failure of the supernatural anchor. Expressivism picks up real features of moral psychology while underspecifying what the expressed attitudes are tracking.

*Constructivism.* Korsgaard (1996, 2009), Street (2006, 2012), and the constructivist tradition hold that moral norms are constructed through procedures of practical reason rather than discovered as mind-independent facts. The framework reads constructivism as correctly identifying that moral norms emerge through agent-level activity rather than from a Platonic realm, while supplying the structural reading: the activity through which norms are constructed is itself constrained by structural facts about what subjects need to do to remain subjects in shared exchange.

*Parfit on reasons and persons.* Parfit's *Reasons and Persons* (1984) and *On What Matters* (2011) develop three positions canonical to contemporary normative theory. *Triple Theory*: that the best formulations of Kantian contractualism, Scanlonian contractualism, and rule-consequentialism converge on a common set of fundamental moral principles, with moral progress as the progressive discovery of that convergence. *The non-identity problem*: that standard person-affecting reasoning — an action is wrong only when it makes some particular person worse off — cannot handle cases where the identity of affected persons depends on the action in question (as in certain long-run population and policy decisions), generating a need for impersonal reasons not anchored to any one person’s interests. *Person-affecting vs. impersonal*: the resulting distinction between reasons relative to particular persons and reasons that are agent-neutral and not anchored in any individual’s perspective. The framework reads Parfit as correctly identifying the convergence pressure at the level of best-case formulations, while supplying the structural reading: the reciprocal-coupling floor [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) derives is what the three traditions converge toward; the non-identity problem exposes where person-affecting reasoning fails to reach the floor at population scale; and the person-affecting/impersonal distinction is what the two-level structure of [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) (minimum floor structural, fostering context-sensitive) accommodates.

*Virtue ethics, deontology, and consequentialism.* The three principal normative-theory traditions — virtue ethics (Aristotle, MacIntyre 1981, Hursthouse 1999, Annas 2011), deontology (Kant 1785; Korsgaard 1996; Scanlon 1998; Kamm 2007), and consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Sidgwick; contemporary defenders Singer 1979; Kagan 1989; Norcross 2020) — organize most contemporary normative debate. Each captures real features of moral practice; each generates counterintuitive results in specific cases. The framework reads them as three operations on the same modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) that the moral case coordinates across subjects.

Virtue ethics tracks the *cultivated-field* operation: a body whose modal field is dense enough and accurately calibrated enough that the morally relevant features of a situation come into view before deliberation begins — what older traditions called wisdom and what virtue ethics formalizes as character. Deontology tracks the *structural-reciprocity* operation: the floor of non-corrosion that mutual registration imposes whenever subjects of the same kind register each other accurately — what the structural account derives as the negative-rule core and what deontology formalizes as rules and rights. Consequentialism tracks the *trajectory-comparison* operation: the forward-running of modal branches the field already contains, with the body's valenced weights assigned across each branch — what the modal account treats as one mode of practical deliberation and what consequentialism formalizes as outcome aggregation.

The same body runs all three operations simultaneously, because the field carries cultivated content (virtue), structural floor (deontology), and forward-running branches (consequentialism) at once. Where the three converge, ordinary cases settle without effort; where they diverge, the traditions disagree about which operation should govern. None is fundamental; each is the partial articulation of one operation on the modal field that constitutes the moral case.

*Moral particularism and prima facie pluralism.* Dancy (1993, 2004) argues for reasons-holism: a consideration that favors an act in one configuration of surrounding features can oppose it, or drop out of relevance entirely, in another — pleasure taken in another's suffering does not favor the act the way ordinary pleasure does, and no feature carries a fixed valence assignable independently of what else is present. Moral judgment, on this reading, is a form of situational perception rather than the application of a codifiable rule, and the demand for exceptionless general principles that deontology and consequentialism both presuppose is a demand particularism denies can be met by any moral theory whatsoever. Ross (1930) reaches a related but weaker conclusion from the opposite direction: a plurality of genuine, non-derivative *prima facie* duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, non-maleficence, self-improvement) can conflict in a given case, with no algorithm ranking them in advance; what one's actual duty is, all things considered, is fixed only by judgment exercised on the case at hand, never read off a governing formula. The framework grants the holism at the level Dancy and Ross are describing: which of the three operations a case calls for, and how the structural-reciprocity floor actually cashes out given the configuration of facts present, is exactly the work of the cultivated-field operation virtue ethics already names, not a mechanical output the structural floor delivers in isolation from judgment. What the framework does not grant is the further claim that the floor itself carries no fixed content beneath the case-by-case variation: non-corrosion of another subject's field of possibility is invariant across every configuration particularism's holism ranges over, exactly as the structural-reciprocity operation requires, even though which specific act counts as corrosive in a given case is precisely the situational question Dancy is right to say no advance valence table can settle. Particularism is right about how the floor is applied and wrong, pressed to full generality, about whether there is a floor to apply.

*Frankfurt’s reasons of love and volitional necessity.* Frankfurt’s work (1971, 1982, 1988, 2004) develops a position that cuts across the three-traditions division rather than occupying a place within it. *Reasons of love* — the partial reasons one has for a beloved’s good simply in virtue of loving them — are, on Frankfurt’s account, irreducible to the impartial considerations shared by virtue ethics, deontology, and consequentialism. What one is permitted and required to do for a beloved is not fully derivable from what any impartial procedure delivers, and the irreducibility is a feature: the structure of love is *volitional necessity* — caring about something so completely that one cannot bring oneself to act against it is a height of freedom rather than a constraint on it. The *wanton* case names the absence: a will that endorses none of its desires from a higher order, with no stake in what happens to anything. The framework reads this tradition as tracking a real axis the three traditions leave underspecified — the first-person normative weight of what an agent has identified with most fully, operating alongside the reciprocal-coupling norms [§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) derives — and the [§8.9](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9) engagement of Frankfurt's hierarchical account develops the structural reading in full.

*Evolutionary debunking and moral nativism.* Joyce (2006) and Street (2006) developed evolutionary debunking arguments: moral beliefs are products of selection pressures unconnected to moral truth, so even if there are moral truths, our beliefs are not reliably connected to them. Haidt (2012) developed moral-foundations theory on the moral-psychology side. The framework reads debunking arguments as raising a real challenge to specifically realist accounts, while supplying the structural response: morality is not a separate normative realm vulnerable to evolutionary debunking but the structural shape of subjects meeting subjects, with the evolutionary pressures producing moral psychology operating on the same structural conditions morality consists in.

*Hume's is/ought gap.* Hume (1739) argued that one cannot derive ought from is: normative conclusions do not follow from purely descriptive premises. The position has been refined and contested across centuries. The framework reads Hume as correctly identifying that ought cannot be derived from a value-neutral is, while supplying the structural reading: the body's modal field ([§8.3](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-3)) is always already valenced ([§8.2](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-2)), and the felt-best branch within the valenced field is what the body registers as the ought. The ought is the affective pointer that emerges automatically whenever a feeling body reads its own possibility space; Hume was right about the value-neutral is, but the is of being a feeling body operating on a modal field is never value-neutral to begin with. The gap closes at the structural level without requiring a derivation from neutral premises.

*Moral relativism.* Cultural and individual moral relativism hold that moral truth is relative to the cultures or individuals that produce it. Harman (1975, 1996) developed influential relativist positions; Wong (2006) developed pluralistic accounts that combine relativist and universalist elements. The framework reads relativism as correctly identifying real cross-cultural moral variation, while supplying the structural reading: variation in moral *content* is consistent with universality of moral *structure* — the structural fact of subjects meeting subjects operates everywhere, with specific norms being culture-conditioned articulations of how the meeting is to be conducted.

*Care ethics and feminist moral philosophy.* Gilligan (1982), Noddings (1984), Held (2006), and the broader care-ethics tradition developed accounts on which moral relations of care and dependency are central to moral practice rather than peripheral. The framework reads care ethics as correctly identifying real moral relations the dominant traditions have understated, with the cross-current reading of affect ([§8.12](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-12) cluster-root) supplying the structural support: fostering another subject includes care for it, which requires reading its conditions accurately.

*Ubuntu and relational personhood.* Southern African moral philosophy in the Ubuntu tradition (Tutu 1999; Menkiti 1984; Gyekye 1997; Metz 2007, 2011) holds that personhood is not a given but an achievement realized through relationship with others — captured in the Nguni aphorism *umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu*, a person is a person through other persons. Menkiti's strong formulation holds that moral status itself accrues incrementally through a lifetime of participation in community norms and obligations, so that personhood is ontologically, not merely developmentally, a social product.
